Morro for bootblacks—After the rain comes the hine. A DIVINING rod to discover a woman's real thoughts would have an immense sale. IT is said that only male grasshoppers sing, So happy that their wives are dumb, eh? Q. Wao was the first striker ?—A. Cain; and he knocked his brother out of a job, ton, MISS-FORTUNES come to some men when they get raarried, and they don't mind it a bit. ON a card in a street car this great truth is heralded: "Advertising is a great deal like mak- ing love to a widow—it can't be overdone." Is a hen fails to come up to the scratch in the morning, but defers her lay until the evening, she has something egg-citing to cackle-late over. "WHICH is right, Edward, the wages of sin is death,' or the wages of sin are death? " "Neither, Annabel. The wages of sin is wealth." THERE is a famine in Boston for cents. Boston never had much cents. NEW YORK is fighting for cheap gas. Washington has it—while Congress is in session. A MAN was buried alive at Barbastro, in Spain. People think that was very atrocious, yet men are buried alive after every election. SHOE-DEALER--" What size, madame ?" Madame —4,l—er—think twos." Shoe-dealer (taking her measure)—" Ah, yes, twos. A pair of two twos, four altogether. (To boy)—jarnes, a pair of ladies' French kids, No. 4." AT a meeting in Whitechapel a pertinent answer was given to a question asked by a candidate for Parliamentary honours. "What," said he, "did a Lord Mayor ever do for you ?" "Give you six months," was the reply. "How was your son, when you heard from him last ?" "He wrote me that he was so ill that he could neither sit nor stand." "Thou if he tells the truth he must lie." ifon—" Say, Jack, where can I get a two-foot rule ?" Jack—" Here." Torn— • Thanks, hand it over." Jack "Well don't wear tight shoes." SOMEBODY has written a book entitled "What shall my son be ?" Upon which someone frankly replies, " If the boy is as bad as the book, the chances are he will be hanged." NIAGARA FALLS are said to be receding inch by I inch, as time goes on. There are so many American thieves living in that vicinity that the Falls are probably afraid of being stolen. A LADY writer asks: "Why don't batchelors marry?" That's so—why don't they? Come to ; think about it, we have never yet seen a batchelor who was married. It's lamentable, too. "What is a swell affair, Jim?" "Swell affair? lemme see. Ah, yes, I know—a boil." " Seine- thing else. Try again." "No. Give it up. I hate conundrums anyhow." "A hill, ye know. Don't ye see, a bill is a swell affair, and besides , all hills have got crests." "Are you acquainted with Pete Johnson?" I "Yes, he is a perfect brute." "I don't think he Is a perfect brute. He may be a brute, but he is not a perfect one, because he lacks instinct. A perfect brute has instinct." FRANK WALLER was arrested in Butler, Ga., on the supposition that he was Bill Walker, who was .charged with murder. When taken to Forsyth for identification and told that he didn't look at all I like Walker, he grinned and said, "1 knowed wasn't Bill Walker." "HAVE you voted, Uncle Johnson ?" "Yes, sah! I voted early dis mo'ning de Republican ticket, sah! Den at noon I voted for de Dimmycrats, and jist afore de polls closed I deposited a ballot for de Prohibitionist. Yes, sah, I allers vote. I'm too good a Christian to neglect my duty, sal." A PHYSICIAN, p.issing by a gravestone cutter's shop, called out—"aood morning, neighbour, hard at work, I see. You finieh your gravestones as far as 'ln memory of,' and then wait, I suppose, to see who wants a monument next." " Why, yes," replied the old joker, "unless somebody's sick, and you are doctoring 'em, then I keep right on." THEY were talking about expenses and how some men got r_ch. Said one—" My butcher and baker have made money enough out of me to build them- selves splendid residences." "And," responded the other, "the piblicans I patronised have built whole blocks out of what I owe them." AN exalted Irishman who was declaiming about justice to Ireland, was asked by a friend, "What is it really that you and your countrymen want ?" He replied, "We do not know what we want, sir ; but by the powers, we are determined to have it I" TEACHER—" Miss Sinnico, please parse the sentence, 'Adolphus married Caroline.'" Miss S.—" Well, Adolphus' is a noun, because it is the name of a thing; married' is a conjuncLion, because it joins Adolphus and Caroline ; and 'Caroline' is a verb, because it governs the noun." GIVE a man the necessaries of life and he wants the conveniences. Give him the conveniences and he craves for the luxuries. Grant him the luxuries and he sighs for the elegancies. Let him have the elegancies and he yearns for the follies. Give him all together and he complains that he has been cheated both in the price and quality of the articles. hnatrrapro CHILD—" Pa, what is the d:fference between sitting up and sitting down?" Pa, with perfect confidence in his ability to explain: "Why, my child, when somebody is standing up and he seats himself, he sits down, and, when he doesn't go to bed but sits down, he sits up I" Inquiring child—" But, pa, if he sits up, how can he sit without sitting down; and, if he sits down, how can he sit up?" THE Laid of Balnamoon, riding past a high, steep bank, stopped opposite a hole in it, and said, "John, I saw a brock gang in there." "Did ye?" said John ; " Wull ye haud my horse, sir ?" " Cer- tainly," said the Laird, and away rushed John for a spade. After digging for half an hour, he came back nigh speechless to the Laird, who had re- garded him musingly. "1 canna find him, sir,' said John. "'Deed," said the Laird, very coolly, "I wad ha' wondered if ye had, for its ten years' sin' I saw him pug in there." OSCAR WILDE knew the late Miss Bayard very well. He was a great admirer of her wit and power of repartee, and lost no opportunity to meet her during his stay in Washington. One fine day the capital's society people found themselves in- terested in two events which were to take place in the evening. One was a lecture by the champion of the sunflower, and the other.was a brilliant re-
ception. Oscar 'Wilde met Miss Bayard during the afternoon .of the .eventful day, and she asked him,

"Mr. Wilde, will you go wta the reception to: night?" " Well," he replied, "if I am not too much fatigued after my lecture." A short pause followed, and then he said, "Miss Bayard, of course you will be at the reception ?" "Well," came the answer, "if lam not too much fatigued after your lecture." " WHo was Columbus? asked a teacher of his class, in one of the South-side Board Schools. "Columbus was a bird," replied a little girl. The whole class laughed vociferously, and the teacher asked the little girl what she meant by such a silly answer. She explained, shedding bitter tears, that she had read in the book of an older sister, a piece of poetry about the egg of Columbus, and as only birds lay eggs, she could come to no other conclusion than that Columbus was some sort of a bird. You gave me that very six- pence on the car this inorning. I took it from you In change." C. C.—" Well, you see, we are more particular than you are." "I AM a lawyer's daughter, you know, George dear," she said, after George had proposed and had been accepted, "and you wouldn't think it strange if I were to ask you to sign a little paper to the edeet that we are engaged, wouid you ?" Geoi•ge was too happy to tilink anything strange just then, and he signed the paper with a trembling hand and a bursting heart. Then she laid her ear against hi,s middle vest button, and they were very, very happy. " Tcll me, darling," said George, after a long, delicious silence, " why did you want me to sign that paper? Do yhu not repose impheit confi- dence in my love for you ?" "An, ye;" she sighed with infinite content, "indeed I do; but, George, dear, I have been fooled so many times." John Greenleaf Whittier, the American Quaker poet, who died on Wednesday, wrote years ago that, he was" ready to depart and be with Christ, which is far better" ; yet at eighty-five years of age, and after sixty-six or more of writing, he dedicated some new and charming verses to his friend, junior octo- genarian, and fellow-poet, him " of the Breakfast Table," in the pages of the " Atlantic Monthly" to which for over forty years he has been a leading contributor. A volume of his later verse, to be calleu "At Sundown," will shortly be published.

There is quite a colony of artists just now in Somerset. One of the latest arrivals is Pretessor Herkomer, who has acquired an old farmho use six or seven miles from Minehead, has tranaformen a barn into a studio, and contemplates spending much of the year there. Mr. IL W. Macbeth, R.A., is a near neighbour, who spends nine months out of the twelve amid the vales of Somerset. He and Lady Macbeth (as Mrs. M. is called down there) are great hunters, and are always to the fore when the red deer is being hunted. Lady Macbeth is regarded as a sort of she-Nimrod; she is a cross-saddle rider, a l' homtne, and wears knee breeches and gaiters. but covers them from the public gaze with a divided habit.

Sir Spencer Wells sends a useful letter to the " Times "calling attentien to the desirability of instituting compulsory crematiton where cholera has been the cause of death. The doctors in Ger- many are making themselves heard to the same wise purpose. Nothing is more suicidal than the present habit of allowing the germs of disease to multiply in the dead and buried body. Sir Spencer Well says --" There can be no doubt that fire is the swiftest and most effective mode of destroying the bacilli. 11 they are buried in the earth they are almost certain to multiply, and sooner or later to pollute the earth, the water, and the air, and so act as storehouses of disease which ought to be stamped out."

Sir Samuel Griffith, the Premier of Queensland, before he turned himself inside out on the Kanaka question, was wont to ride every day from the (government offices to his home on a prancing steed. That steed is now no longer visible, and its dis- appearance is not wholly unconnected with the unpopularity which Sir Samuel has drawn upon himself by his espousal of "black slavery" in flagrant violation of all his previous primises and pronouncements. It is no longer politic on his part to court the notice of the Brisbane populace, and so, instead of mounting the efstwhile prancing steed, and giving the Brisbaneites a treat in horse- manship, he prefers to go home by a less fre- quented and more circuitous route.

' The enterprising tobacco trader has not accepted the hint we gave that Myrtle Grove, the old resi- dence of Sir Walter Raleigh, at Youghal, in the county of Cork—famous as the scene of the smok- ing of the first pipe in these countries—was for sale and might be had for very little. The historic old manor house was put under the hammer at Cork, on Monday, but, strange to relate, the auctioneer , had the same experience in the city by the Lee as in the big metropolis on the Thames—not a single bid was made. This is all the more curious as the house is a very comfortable, as well as a very histo- ric and picturesque, residence, and Youghal is one of those old-world places in Ireland where one could live for " half nothing," as the natives say. At Kirkham, in North Lancashire, dwell three gentlemen named Birley, Hodgson, and Ramsey The vagaries of a Lord Chancellor have made them justices of the peace, and in the exercise ef their magisterial duties they have just sentenced four boys to a month's imprisonment each for stealing pears from a garden. Probably these worthy Shallows don't know it, but it is none the less a fact that the man who sends boys to gaol for a trival offence is a much greater criminal than the orchard robber. The latter inflicts annoyance, the former converts boys (who will be boys) into thieves. We don't suggest that Messrs. Birley, Hodgson, and Ramsey should " do a month," or even two ; but we do think that the case should be promptly brought to the notice of the Home Secretary. The Gloucester Festival opened full swing on Tuesday morning, witt a grand cathedral function, at which Dean Spence prPached an eloquent sermon in his best style, and all the high life of Gloucester, including mayor and corporation in state, listened respectfully. The Bishop of Gloucester, as usual, was conspicuous by his absence. Not being musi- cal, and much needing repose, his lordship is in the habit of leaving early for Switzerland, but not with- out first handing out the keys of the episcopal wine cellar, with strict orders that everyone is to be duly entertained. So there is open house at the Palace, under the auspices of Mrs. and Miss Ellicot, who are musical. The palace party include Lord and Lady I Coleridge, Lord and Lady Edward Churchill, the 'Dowager Lady Westbury, the Rev. E. R. Haweis, I and several others.

her Majesty proposes to place a statue of the Emperor Frederick in the grounds of Balmoral, which are crammed with memorials of the Queen's deceased relatives and friends, while every hill-top in the neighbourhood bears a cairn. There are only three statues—one of the Prince Consort, by heed ( representing him in in Highland dress) ; the Jubilee statue of the Queen, which was presented to her Majesty by her Scottish tenantry and servants ;and a statue of John Brown, by Boehm, which occupies a conspicuous position on a wooded bank near the garden. Princess Alice is commemorated by a Celtic cross of granite, and ¶he Duke of Albany by a large seat of polished granite. The memory of sir Thomas Biddulph is recalled by a granite fountain. 1 The bronze statue of the Prince Consort in the I - grounds is an exact copy of his white marble statue in the corridor of the castle.

Sir Richard Owen who,in his ninetieth year is fast recovering from a severe illness, is another illus- tration of the remark that,other things being equal, the hardest workers are among the longest lived. Some 400 works, many of them most complicate and bulky, attest his prodigious industry. He has published original papers on every branch of the animal kingdom, living and fossil, and it has been said of him that " from the sponge to man, he has thrown light over every subject he has touched." The doyen of modern English men of science resides in a homely thatched cottage in Richmond-park. It is a quiet spot, embosomed among venerable oaks where the deer come up to nibble and where night- ingales sing. On most fine days Sir Richard Owen may be seen frequenting a favorite path, and a pause now and then to examine some object indic- , sues that the habits of observation of a lifetime are with him even in his retirement. His full, bright, , and kindly eyes are yet undimmed, and the whole face has a delightful blend ot sympathy and power.

kt the Warrington County Sessions on Wednesday Catherine Chenery of Burtonwood, was charged with assaulting Jeremiah Chenery, her husband, on the 25th ult. The complainant, who appeared with his head bandaged, said he bought a pair of trousers from a rag gatherer, and his wife wanted to pot them on, and wear them outside and "disfigure herself in the presence of a lot of men." Because he complained to her about this, they had some words. After that she commenced swearing at the Welsh and at a Staffordshire I man. He remonstrated with her upon which she threw a brick at him, which he now produced, and after that the little lad came out and threw stenes,and one of them caught him on the head. He tried to get away, but his wife met him with the brick and flung it at his head, cutting it open. She dragged him off the sofa and out of doors about a fortnight since,, and threw a pail of water on to him. He did not wial to press the case, as she was his wife, and he loved her as much as the food le ate every day. All he wanted was protection for himself and his goods, which she claimed as hers. She locked him out all one night, and he had to lie under a tree. The defendant pleaded but said her hus- band first threw the brick at her ; and he was so bad- tempered she could not live with him.—She was bound over in her own recognizancPs for £5 to keep the peace for six months.

Slowly the big bell of St. Paul's rang out the hour of midnight, and the answering peals from neigh- bouring belfries re-echoed the note of admonition to the roysterer, of warning to the suicide, while distant harmonies lulled the mighty city to rot. Close beneath the slates of a common lodging-house, which raised its unpretentious outline from out the I shadow of a broad-towered sanctuary, there lay a wasted form doubled up in agony on a camp bed- stead. Roused from his slumbers by the shrill- 1 toned chroniclers of the hours, he raises his head and rests his hollow cheek on the support of his ' trembling arm. "Marie, for God's sake—water," his quivering lips ejaculate,but no response awakens the shadows of the attic. "Water,"- he repeats, and this time his appeal is half gasp, half sob; but there is none to help him ; nothing to cheer his last moments save the glare of the candle which, having burnt down to the socket, has ignited the grease-stained paper which holds it in its place. Attracted by the blaze, the dying:man, with his forehead covered by the perspiration of death, turns; his glassy eyes to the candle as it gutters in the spirit bottle. Its race is almost run ; its vaunting brilliancy will end in smoke, for now the grease paper flares up for the last time, and finds its grave in the neck of the bottle. Even the spilers in the dusty corners are frightened by the intense gloom, and seek the protection of the cracks and crevices which disfigure the plaster. At the same moment the dying man, who had sunk from an upright position in supine feebleness to the hardness of his horsehair pillow, mingles the death rattle in his throat with the mournful ,ion- sonance of the failing wick, whilst the cheery tin- tinabulation of the chimes, and distant murmuring of voices, with the rattling of wheels on the paved roadway, showed well enough that the flood of life still throbbed through the arteries of the great metropolis. But his pulse is stilled for ever, and Darkness reigns supreme with her twin sister Silence. The circling cloud of smoke had hardly found an exit by tke bottle's mouth before the gaping window frames began to echo beneath the distant tread of footsteps on the stairs, and subdued anathemas on their ricketiness to pollute the sacred silence of the death chamber. The top landing reached, two forms, a man—a gentleman in dress—and a woman, are silouetted against the intense darkness beyond the doorway as they make their entrance by the meagre light of the candle. Slight though it was,it revealed to expectant eyes the stiffening form on the mattress, and wrung a shriek from the woman's lips. Straining her ears to catch the slightest sound from the silence of the sick room, she darts forward and instinctively clasps the lifeless wrist to her bosom. As the pulse no longer throbbed, she cried out— "Oh, sir, you have come too late." "Too late,' be repeated, "I do not comprehend. Do you not wish to disturb him ?" "Sir, he is not asleep, he is dead." "Ah God forbid ! Curse on my unsympathetic heart. Why to goodness did you not tell me that you were in such straits? But no—it cannot be. Let me feel his pulse." "Strike a match, sir, and then you can see that it is but too true."

_ "No, I dare not, it would look too ghastly. Go and fetch me a lamp or a candle. I will prepare myself for the worst." Passing through the doorway like a shadow, she waited and listened from without to the cenvulsive sobs of her penitent brother-in-law as he knelt by the bed side, and none but the stars as they twinkled through the skylight saw the smile on her lips. Once more the brothers are united ; the one a corpse, the other on his knees, offering his sacrifice to God on the altar of repentance. Carried away by emotion, he vowed to help the widowed and fatherlass, and to make up for past shortcomings. Soon the shadow reascends the stair with catlike foot- fall, and holds a lighted candle above her hem' as she peers into the pallid face with its clenched teeth, and as she looks the corpse seems to m we, nay it does move, it turns over on to its back with a spasmodic jerk occasioned by a reflex action of the nerves. The man sees it not, for his face is buried in his hands, but the girl—for she is little more than a girl—drops the candle from her nerveless fingers and throws herself into the arms of the penitent, as he rose in terror to his feet clutching hold of his coat. Her grief was so natural, her tears so free that it took sometime to soothe her paroxysms of hysterics. When he had reduced her to an equable frame of mind he lighted the candle and told her that he wished to make some requital for the wrong he had done in being an indirect agent in causing his brother's death. " As you say," he began, "that you have never heard the story of this wrong, some little explanation is owing to you, though it grieves me sorely to think t,,at he never revealed the particulars to his wife. Some years ago, as you probably know, I made my mark by a work which was said to have evinced signs of a remarkable genius. That work was in reality written by your hus- band. In ignorance of my own literary aspirations and of the piles of manuscripts hidden away in my drawers, he made me his confidant and showed me the plot of his tale. It was a wonderful tale, but his confidence was misplaced, Some days afterwards he missed his manu- scripts. Needless to say, they were in my possession. I had transferred them from his desk, which was always open, to my own, this being always kept under lock and key. In his agony of mind he naturally accused me, , but I repudiated the charge, and refused to live in the same house with him. I afterwards heard that he was 11 collecting his notes for a second transcription, but my villany was greater than his genius, for I had my copy accepted by a firm of publishers in my own name before his had grown out of its manuscript state. From that time my name and fortune were made. Deaf to all applications for assistance, I felt no pangs of conscience for the fate of the poor ill- dressed literary hack whom I recognized as the playmate ot my youth, when I passed him unnoticed in the street, and though none of my productions equalled my first, as they were few and far between, I kept up my reputa- tion and obtained a ready sale for my works, which have kept me in affluence. Thus you have the truth, and if you will only tell ma how, I will do my best to place you in a position which will bring in a fair remuneration for the services required." Naturally of a near and egotistical nature, he had already forgotten his vows to devote his ill-gotten gains to the widow and fatherless, and intended to get off as easily as he possibly could. His emtion was gone now, and he began to regret that he had made any offer to help his brother's wife; but, remembering tile hold on his reputation the confession had given her, he was con- strained to reiterate his offer. Nor was the girl slow to comprehend this. " Sir," she replied, "if you could but recognize the injury you have done to me and mine, you could not possibly refuse to give me less than £5O for present necessities." Appalled by her presumption, he retused pointblank, and only the recollection of the advantage she had over him compelled him to draw out his purse and give her what she asked, though he took care to add "Luckily for you, I have that amount on me at present, but I hope that you will have no further need of my assis- tance."
" No ! certainly not at present " she added with cau- tion.

With some misgivings whether he had not made a fool of himself or not by his confession, he turned on his heel and kicked the door open, but, as if prompted by some sudden suspicions, he turned round and said—" By the way I never knew my brother was married. You are his wife, are you not l,: Without hesitation, thfth her lip trembled and her cheek was flushed, she answered 'Most certainly, sir! Row can you doubt it ?" "Oh very well then. No harm meant. You can see to the burial of the body. I have done with you all." Then his iron-shod boots clattered down the wooden stairs. . .

Scarce had the door which opened into the narrow court turned on its hinge ere the sick room was the mute witness of a scene of exultation. The curtain which cut off the corner formed by the dip of the slates was thrown aside by a villainous-looking Frenchman. The mark of Cain on his brow and the subordination of his own wishes to those of his wife showed that he had passed through the hardships of penal servitude. "Why Marie," he exclaimed in admiration," you are a born actress. You have fleeced that niggardly En- glishman to the tune of £5O if I am not mistaken." " Forty-five, Louis, if you please," she answered as she placed a crisp £5 note in the grasp of their deceased lodger. Louis turned inquiring eyes to his wife when he saw what she had done, but dared not make any objection, though he was longing to know the reason why. Irritated by his silent acquiescence in everything she did, she began to lament her impersonation. "Louis, you scoundrel, who do you think is going to bury the body ? I confess I have no liking for my pseudo brother-in-law, but we have been too hard on this poor fellow, and it was all the outcome of your fertile brain. If my father was hanged there is no reason why I should not make a respectable living, and I yeas doing so until! met you. That five pound note is to pay for his burial, so don't sit staring at me like a dummy." " And a fine lot of good it will do him too,'"you bet," added her husband. " But I say, Marie, had we not better clear out ? " " Yes, at once. It has been an awful strain on my nerves." "And on mine too. It scared me awfully to see him kick the bucket as they say in England. Parbleu ! It was horrible." Once more the door opens and they are gone. They had scarcely closed the street door before the
• ,41. k '4os- THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 10. 1892. A BAD B

generous donor of the bank notes made his re-appear- ance on the top landing. When he stepped out into the cold air of the early morning, he felt the reaction of his unnatural grief. No longer haunted by remini- scences of the past or the terrors of the present,he doubly cursed himself for allowing the cherished secret of years to pass the barrier of his lips. " The fact of it is," he said," that woman will make capital out of it unless she gets into trouble with those counterfeit notes. blood Gracious " he exclamed as he examined his purse, " I must have given that genuine five-pound note ; confound it. I have done so, but if persuasion or threatening can recover it, I will have it back again." As he opened the door with his trembling hand and saw that the birds were flown, the crumpled paper in the clasp of the bloodless hand caught his eye. Forcing apart the fingers, the imprecations on his bad luck, which had risen to his lips, gave way to exultation when he found that he had recovered what he sought. Without stopping to think why the note had been ' placed there, he hurried homeward, and in doing 80 passed the woman and her accomplice, as they crouched down to escape his notice, in the shadow of a doorway.

div.head: CREST, MOTTo, AND BADGE.
div.p: CREST, MOTTo, AND BADGE.

(From " Little Folks.") "I vi ant to know," said Wilfred, " why they had mottoes at all, or where they came from ? The knights don't wear them on their heads as they did the crests, did they ?" " Some people," replied Lucia, " fancy that mottoes were originally war-cries, shouted by the-] soldiers when rushing to battle. The yell or war- cry of the Irish chieftains was 800 !' To this the chiet added the name of his family or castle; con- sequently in an engagement would be heard such shouts as ' Crom 'a boo!' or ' Crom for ever !" Shanet a boo !" Butler a boo!' mingled with the cries of A Douglas? A Douglas!' or A Home! A Home !" Mottoes proper were not adopted until after the Conquest ; they were all either in Latin or French, and one belonging to Sir Thomas Cavall tells us to Trust in Thomas when you see his horse.' The crest, as you can guess, is a gallant steed. Many. mottoes allude to some notable event in the family; history; as, for example, the Grip fast ' of the Leslies. Margaret of Scotland, crossing a river, was in danger of being swept down by the current and drowned ; but fortunately caught hold of the belt of Bartholomew Leslie, une of her escort. Grip fast.' cried the knight,as lie struck out for the bank, and the queen, holding on for dear life, was brought safely ashore. Ready, aye ready,' with a bundle of lances for his crest, was granted to Lord Napier by James V. of Scotland as a reward for his fidelity; because he was 'willing to gang wi' us into England when our nob:es and others refused, and was ready to stake all at our bidding.' Another Ready motto was bestowed upon an ancestor of the Trotter family, who being suddenly sent for by James 11., Aide to Court upon a particularly fast trotting horse. " Howdoes it happen that you are here so soon?' asked the king, surprised. "• I trotted, your Majesty ; was the reply.; and the king, pleased with his zeal, altered his name from Giffard to Trotter, and gave him the motto Ready'"

"I swhouldn't like the queen or anyone else to give me the name ot Trotter," said Wilfred. "I am glad people don't have their 'names changed like that nowadays." "Then there are the royal mottoes," went on Lucia," such as Dieu et mon droit,' which you must both have seen many times. Everybody is familiar with this motto, but 1 expect very few know its origin—that it was the parole or password given by Richard Cceur-de-Lion to his army at the battle of Gisors in France. The French were defeated upon this occasion, and Richard to com- memorate the victory, made • Dieu et mon droit God and my right,' the motto of the royal arms of England, and it has retained its position ever since. " Queen Elizal etli'a favourite motto was ` &roper eadem '—` Always the same' ; her mother the unfor tunate Anne Boleyn, adopted the selfish one of For me and mine' ; and her successor on the throne, Jane Seymour, the humble' Bound to obey and serve.'

"In the senate-house at Frankfort hang portraits of all the emperors, and under each is the motto assumed by him at his coronation. One is Among swans, the goose maketh a loud noise,' but whether Otho the Superb, whose choice it was, considered himself a goose, I reall cannot tell you. " One of the Emperors, Frederick 111., had a fancy for placing upon the covers of his books, furniture, and plate, the initials,' A. E. I. 0. U.,' and he was continually asking his courtiers to guess what they stood for. They did their best, no doubt, but no one could succeed in deciphering ttie royal puzzle, and I expect they grew very tired of it in time. It was fortunate for them that their heads were not cut off for making wrong guesses, as so often happens in fairy tales. After the emperor's death the secret was disclosed, and from a paper in his own handwriting it was found that the mys- terious 'A.E. I. 0 U.' stood for Austria est im- perare orbi universo The whole world is subject to Austria.'

"Before I end, I want to tell you some mottoes of Companies, which seem very applicable ones. For instance, the Blacksmiths have ' By hammer and hand all arts shall stand' ; the Waxhandlers, Truth is the light'; the Weavers, Weave truth with trust ' ; the Woodmongers, The axe is laid at the foot of the tree ' ; and the Sadlers, Hold fast, sit sure.'
"Sir Walter Scott's motto was 'Vice la plume r —' Long live the pen r and surely a better could never have been invented for one whose pen has given us so many wonderful and delightful books." , -

div.head: GREAT FROZEN LAKE.
div.p: A GREAT FROZEN LAKE.

On the road from Irkutsk to Kiakhta, the frontier town of the Chinese Empire, the monotony of the journey is broken by crossing Lake Baikal, a won- derful lake frozen for nine months in the year,which has sixty times the area of the Lake of Geneva, and has an average depth of no less than 5,404 ft., or more than smile. The cold is so terrible that when a hurricane stirs the waters the waves often freeze as waves, remaining in hummocks above the surface; but when Mr. J. M. Price, author of "From the Arctic Ocean to the Yellow Sea," crossed, the cold had caught the lake asleep and the ice was perfectly smooth. He bad thirty miles to drive on the solidi- fied water. "For about a mile from the shore, the ice had a thin layer of snow over it, but we gradu- ally left this sort of dazzling white carpet, and at length reached the clear ice, when I saw around me the most wonderful and bewitching sight I ever beheld. Owing to the marvellous transparency of, the water the ice presented everywhere the appear- ance of polished crystal, and although undoubtedly of great thickness, was so colourless that it was like passing over space. It gave me, at first, an uncanny feeling to look over the side of the sledge down into the black abyss beneath; this feeling, however, gradually changed to one of fascination, till at last I found it positively difli- cult to withdraw my gaze from the awful depths, with nothing but this sheet of crystal between me and eternity. I believe that most travellers, on crossing the lake on the ice for the first time, ex- perience the same weird and fascinating influence. About half way across, I stopped to make a sketc% and take some photographs. It was no easy matter, as I found on getting out of the sledge, for the ice was so slippery that, in spite of my having felt snow-boots on. I could hardly stand. The death- like silence of the surroundings was occasionally broken, however, by curious sounds, as. though big guns were being fired at some little distance. They were caused by the cracking of the ice here and there. I was told that in some parts of the lake were huge fissures, through which the water could be seen: It is for this reason that it is always advisable to do the journey by daylight. We reached Moufshkaya, on the opposite coast, exactly four and a half hours after leaving Leistvenitz, horses having done the whole distance of over 30 miles with only two stoppages of a few minutes each. It was evidently an easy piece of work for them, as they seemed as fresh when we drew up in the post yard as when they started in the morn- ing."

div.head: lONIE,
div.p: lONIE,
PRIDE OF THE MILL
A THRILLING LOVE STORY. BY LAURA JEXN LIBBEY.
CITAPTER XI.
"IF WB MEET AGAIN, I WILL BE AS PROUD, AS
COLD, AS INDIFFERENT AS RE."

From the hour when lonie had sent him from her, Arthur Rochester was a changed man. He did not drift recklessly to ruin as many another would have done. He had gone away quietly, and had tried to drown all thought, all memory in hard work. What he suffered no one knew. He had loved her so well. He fougkt a brave battle with grim despair. There were times when he was victor, and for a few hours he would cry out that his work was everything —that a man's life was work, awl that love was play; but after all this was said, he would bury his face in his hands with a bitter groan, muttering that a man's life was nothing without love to brighten it and make it worth the living. . .
Would the time ever come—, he wondered, when he should forget her—when the fair beauty of her face would fade from his memory, and cease to torture him? _ _

He had left New York city to avoid seeing her, and it was the greatest shock of his life, when he was talking with Colonel Whitney, to learn of her presence at Beechvaie Villa, and that she was the colonel's niece and prospective heiress. How strangely the wheel of fortune had revolved. "What cruelty of fate has brought me here to suffer all the old pain and anguish over again I" he thought, bitterly. At first it occurred to him to go away. Then he denounced himself for his want of strength and manly courage.' "I need not see her. We shall not be likely to meet," he told himself, for her social position was far above the one he found himself occupying now. It was as though they were living in two different worlds. Once the colonel invited him to a lawn fete, to be held at the villa. Arthur declined with graceful courtesy. He remembered how shallow the social world was; that a man was measured, not by his Intellect and noble qualities there, but by the amount of his gold; and he thought of the lines: I sometimes wonder if heaven will be A place of distinction 'tween wealth and worth, And will they ask o'er the crystal sea How many thousands we owned on earth? 'She is RP heiress of untold wealth, And fame has laurelled her woman's brow, While I am a workman, with nothing but health, And a heart full of love to offer now." On the day he had met lonic while driving, he saw her for the first time since the hour in which she had sent him from her. Arthur Rochester had raised his hat with a cold, courteous bow; but only Heaven knew what it cost him to pass her by like that.
lonie had arranged that second lawn fete pur- posely that he might be invited; had even suggested his coming to the colonel; and now her pretty plan of reconciliation had failed.
"He wants me to clearly understand he loves me no longer," she sobbed. lonie thought )ong and earnestly over the matter. His love must have changed to indiffer- ence, and
" 'Tis easier to move a mountain than to change Indifference to love."

Of what use were her beauty, her grace, her wealth and talent, if she could not win him I The whole world was as nothing compared to that. As the weeks lengthened into two long, weary months, and he had not come near her, she knew her surmise was correct—he studiously avoided her. "Oh, if I could but tell him bow I have repented those hasty words that sent him from me," she would murmur.

Should she send for him and tell him so? She thought of the sad plaint of Elaine, the lily maid of Astelot, who said: "And must I die for want of one bold word T" She would take a little time to think over the matter. Even Miss Carriscourt noticed how pale and thin beautiful knie was growing. "We are going to hear an opera to-night, uncle," said lonie, one day, to the Colonel, "will you come with Miss Carriscourt and myself as our escort T" "You will have a box filled with noisy chatterers the whole night," he said laughingly. "Not if you dislike it," she said affectionately, "It is to be 'La Grande Duchesse,' with a very famous prima donna in the title role." "I have net heard it yet," rerturned Colonel Whitney, adding: "1 oannot say that I have any great admiration for that school of music, but if you wish it, I will go, lonie." "It will increase my enjoyment a hundred fold," she said, gently, "if you go. "How can I refuse when you say that T" cried the colonel, cheerily. "I will be on hand punctually." In the theatre the Colonel saw lonie attracted more attention than any one else, even though the house was crowded; he saw opera glasses turned constantly towards her beautiful face.

lonie noticed that the colonel did not evince any great interest in the opera. "You do not care for La Grande Duchesse she said, suddenly. "No—frankly, I do not," be replied. "Tell me why V said lonie. "Can you ask me?" he returned in surprise; and then he added: "I should not have brought you to see this • I do not like it."

"Tell me why 2" she said again. She never for- got the conversation that followed. It made a great impression on her mind. "That which they are applauding lowers my idea of womanhood. I could not forgive the woman, let her be duchess or peasant, who could so deliber- ately set about to win a man's attention." She looked tip at him quickly. He continued. "Beauty is very charming, I grant, as are grace and talent; but the chief charm to me is a woman's .modesty, just as the great charm of a lily is in its whiteness. Do you not agree with me, lonie '1" "Yes," she replied, piteously, "must certainly I do; but you are so hard upon our sex, uncle. Sup- pose," she faltered, "that a young girl loves a gentleman ever so truly, and fate part them—and it was all her fault. If they meet again, and he holds aloof, must she not put away her pride and re-call him? Must her heart ache at being so near, and yet so far from him, and make no sign ?" "Any sign she might make would, most certainly, in my opinion, lessen her greatest charm," he said. "But," she persisted, "do you not think that is rather hard? Why, must a woman never evince a preference even for the man she loves 2 Must she break her heart in silence 2" "If he still cares for her, he will find at way to present himself before her again, and attempt to urge his suit." "Do you really believe that uncle 7" she said, in a very low, faint voice. . _ . .
"Certainly," he replied, with energy; "where there's a will, there's a way. If he holds aloof from her, he does not love her—depend on that." . . .

To the last, that night, the light shone in bale's eyes—the scarlet lips were wreathed in smiles, but when she gained her own room, and the door was closed and firmly locked to keep out all intruders, even her maid, the haggard, terrible change that fell over the young face was painful to see. The light, the youth, the beauty, seemed all to fade from it. It grew white, stricken as though the pain of death were upon her. She clasped her hands as one who had lost all hope. " How am I to bear It?" she cried. " What am I to do My life will be a waste unless I can win back the lOve I once cast so lightly from met" She was of dauntless courage; she knew no fear; but she did tremble and quail before the future stretching out before her—the future that was to have no love and was to be spent without him. • She must be like poor Elaine, then. She "must die for want of one bold word" to try to recall her lover. "If we meet again I will be as haughty and cold, as proudly indifferent, as he," she told herself. And very soon an opportunity occurred. The colonel was attacked with his old enemy— the out;g and it so happened that an important matter tame up for consideration at the iron works. It was decided that the young overseer should go to the villa in person to learn the colonel's views and wishes. Arthur Rochester's noble fate paled. What I Go there and meet her! How could he do it? But he must pot flinch. He must go where duty pointed. He ,et ont with a heavy heart. The footman recognised him, and be was shown at once into the library, where he found Colonel Whitney, who looked up with a smile when he saw who his visitor was. The business matter was soon concluded, and the colonel pressed his young overseer vrarmiy to remain for luncheon, but Arthur declined, even though his heart yearned for iust one more glimpse of the

sweet girlish face tliat had been dearer than life to him. "There are a few guests—girl friends of lonie's —stoppMg a few weeks with us, and a party of young gentlemen have just driven up from the city. "Do stop!" repeated the colonel. "You will be a valuable acquisition to their number, Mr. Rochester."
Before Arthur could frame a reply there was the sound of voices in the corridor without. Evidently the whole party were coming to the library in search of the colonel.
The first voice that he heard was that of his old friend, Frank Lyths. Arthur started as though a sword had been placed in his breast. Lyons here 1 What could it mean?

It may as well be stated here and now that lonia's cut direct, on that day he came to renew his .suit, had not daunted him. He still persisted in coming to the villa, but he was always wise enough to bring two or three of lonie's acquaint- ances with him, in order to be sure of being re- ceived.

The door opened, and Frank Lyons was the first on the threshold. His amazement knew no bounds upon beholding Arthur Rochester there. He acknowledged the preser.tation stiffly, not as much as a look revealing he had had a previous knowledge of him. The young overseer of the iron works was quite a different personage in Frank Lyons's eyes from the millionaire's son.
Then the colonel turned to lonie. She had attempted to turn about and fly, but fate was not propitious; the colonel was calling to her.

"lonie, my dear niece," he said "this is Mr. Rochester, of whom you have heard me speak." Arthur saw her start and turn suddenly pale. She recovered herself by a violent effort, and said, falteringly, as she held out her little white hand:
- " Xr.'koCheater and I have met before, uncle."
_ CHAPTER XII.
MAR MY VOW—SHE SHALL BE MY BRIDE, NEVER Ens."

For one brief second Arthur Rochester held that trembling white hand then reluctantly dropped it. The rest of the party were engaged in lively con- versation with the colonel. No one was watching them.
" I did not know you were here, Mr. Rochester," she said, in a voice that indicated she would not have entered had she known it.
"Nor did I dream of seeing you, Miss Lawrence," he answered.

She walked to the window, and he followed her. "If my presenceannoys you, I will leave at once," he said, "and never come here again." And she could not help but detect the ring of eagerness in his voice. . _ . . _

" Why should you 7 " she returned, proudly. "It can make very little difference to me whether you go or—or—stay." He knew that he should have turned then and there and left her ; but his mighty love was more powerful than his strength of will. „ . . . .

He stayed to luncheon, and, to his surprise, lonia gave him the place by her side. Now that fate, or fortune, had brought them together again— now that he was once more in her presence—the old glamour fell over him, the old love stirred in his heart. The coldness melted from her manner. lonie was so kind and gracious to him that he grew be- wildered. When luncheon was over and music began in the drawing-room, he found himself once more by her side, and his heart beat quickly. She had taken him to a little table which was scattered over with choice engravings, and was showing them to him. Suddenly he turned toward her. She saw that he had grown pale, and trembled. "How good you are to me," he cried, "and yet how cruel. It would be more merciful a thousand times to drive me with cruel words from your presence. lam drinking poison." "I have no wish to drive you from me," she answered; and the proud face drooped and a burn- ing flush came over it. Arthur was dazzled and bewildered.

"Shall I tell you the beautiful lines that have haunted me for the last hour 7 " he murmured. She bowed her head, and he whispered: "Every word finds an echo in my own heart. " Had I met thee in thy beauty, When thy hand and heart were free, , When no other claimed the duty Which thy soul might yield to me; Had I wooed thee, had I won thee, Oh I how blest had been my fate, But thy sweetness hath undone me, I have found thee—but too late I " Like the fawn that finds the fountain With the arrow in his breast; Or the light upon the mountain, Where the snow must ever rest ; - I have known, but must forget thee, For I feel that ills await. Oh ! 'tis madness to have met thee, To have found thee—but too late I'" "Why do you not remind me of the folly 7" he went on. "Remind me that our paths lie the whole world apart? Send me away fram you again, this time with well-deserved coldness and rebuke and bitter words, for the reckless words will break from my lips. I love you as madly as ever; and, ah, Heaven 1 how utterly in vain I" But no rebuke came from the sweet, proud lips. No anger was in the beautiful eyes. He saw a warm, tremulous flush which rose even to the roots of her dark, curling hair. He saw a tender, wistful smile on her face, and his dismay increased. "Send me away from you while I have the strength to go," he said, huskily. "Could any man keep sane while you smile so kindly? I love you more madly than ever. As I stand here I could worship you. The sunlight kisses your beautiful face—ah I happy light! The sweet wind through the open window caresses you, stirring the roses you wear—oh! happy wind! For one touch of your white hands I would die! It is worse than madness, this outpouring. Send me away while I have the strength to go.' But no words came from her lips, which had grown strangely pale. "You will never forgive me, lonie—Miss Lawrence. I—l cannot help it; I love you so well that, stand- ing here, I swear to you that for one loving word from your lips I would die. Yes, I would die," he repeated, and his voice died away in a long, low sob.

Had be gone mad, or was he dreaming? A little hand was laid on his, and a tremulous, faltering voice whispered: "You need not die." For one moment his brain reeled; then he turned abruptly. "I will go at once," he said. "You will forgiVe me; you will pardon my folly. I will go and pray Heaven to never bring me near you again, for I remember now those words you uttered once: 'I am sorry you love me, for my heart is given to another.' In the delirium of the moment, I had forgotten that."
"You need not go," whispered the sweet voice again. _ _ .

- She never forget the cry that fell from his lips —a cry of wonder, fear, pain, and love. " You do not mean to be cruel to me. You mean to be kind and gracious; but your words are sweetest poison. You do not understand how you torture me.'

She laid her other hand upon his. "I am not the one who does not understand," she said, shyly and sweetly. She bent her beautiful dark head nearer him, her face crimson, her eyes drooping from his. "You—you will not understand ? " she interro- gated. "I dare not," he cried. "Come out into the garden, will you ?" he pleaded. "Just for a few moments."

And, to his surprise, she went with him. Together they walked in silence, until they reached the shell-bordered fountain, glinted by a touch of crimson and gold by the setting sun. Then he turned to her suddenly. "I dare not believe that you -mean to give me hope," he repeated. "You told me that it could never be. You sent me away with my heart crushed, these words ringing in my ears; lam sorry, but my heart is another's ; I am soon to be his wife.'" And he turned away, with the sound of tears in his voice. "Listen to me, Mr. Rochester," she murmured. "I —oh, if you said the same words now, my answer might be different." She was covered with the greatest confusion lest she had said too much. He could not believe that he had heard aright. It was incredible to him, and he said so. "It is true," she replied. "I will tell you the truth. I thought then that I cared for another, but It was only the glamour of fancy. I soon found out my mistake, and I parted from him for ever. I found that I had sent away with you the happiness of my whole life. I should never have sent for you; but Providence has brought you back to me."

be never forgot the cry of rapturous deiignt tnat broke from his lips, nor the sudden joyful radiance that overspread his face. "lonie,' he said, gravely, "you do not know what your words have done for me. I feel as though I were coming from death to life. Oh my darling, my love, how shall I thank you!" He whispered the words as he gathered her to him, and kissed the beautiful face that he never dreamed would rest on his breast. "I have not realised my great happiness yet," he answered. "I feel dazed and blinded, as though I had been looking at the sun. Oh, lonie--sweet can it be true that you love me 7" Zo love you," she replied, with all a young .ra pretty shyness. "Can it really be true that yon will be my wife, mie " "Yes, if you ask me," she anwered. "But Arthur, a haven't asked me yet." The clasp of his strong arms tightened about her. "Let me hasten to ask you now," he said eagerly. "Will you be my wife, my beloved?" The answer contented him. How little either of them dreamed that it would have been better had they both been stricken dead than that love should have brought them together again, for their hearts were destined to be wrung as hearts were never wrung befetre. The time was corning, and full soon, when h'b should turn with almost a curse on his lips from the beautiful face he loved so madly, and cry out to heaven: "Why were women made fair to torture the hearts of men?" There followed for them half an hour in Paradise. Still the lovers lingered by the fountain. Arthur was slowly beginning to realise his position. "What do you think Colonel Whitney will say. to this 1" he asked. "You know I have no prospective fortune now, lonie. I am now one of the bread- winners, and you are his heiress, dear." Joule laughed a glad, happy laugh. "He will say that I have chosen wisely and well she said. "It is a compact between us that he will raise no objections to my love affairs. He likes you very much, and I think he will be pleased." "The world will say that you have thrown your- self away, darling," he said, slowly. He deteireined never to tell her that he had been disinherited en her account. No, no, she should never know that. "I am content," she replied. "I shall have love and happiness with you. I should have neither away from you. Can what the hallow, uncating world may say make up the loss of a loveless exist- ence to a lonely heart ?" They passed on to the house.

A moment later the tall lilac btrTheF. parted close by, and Frank Lyons, who had gone into the grounds to smoke, and had by accident heard all, gazed after them with a face full of rage and deadly hatred. "She loves him!" he muttered. "She has pro- mised to wed him, but here and now I register a vow to Heaven that it shall never be. I shall part them just so sure as I live, let the cost be what it may. She shall be my bride—never his." (To be coainued.

div.p: IT'S GONE, ALL GONE, AND I'M GOING

For many a year did the same man sweep a c,ertain street-crossing in Flampstead. Through all seasons and in all weathers, there he was, sweeping the crossing and taking such gratuities as were given him. Time wore away, and he came to be eighty years old. He apPeared at his post no more. A lady district visitor looked him up at his lodgings. What a picture of squalid destitu- tion. No fire, no food, no friends. Wife and lama)" he had none—never had. The poor old fellow was perish- ing of starvation, of want. Some money was raised for his benefit and he was removed to a London Hospital. Here he lay several weeks sinking daily. One night he was clearly very low. Near him stood one of the hosPital physicians and a nurae. Seeing him clutch nervousl9 at his pillow, the nurse, supposing the patient desired to be raised up, put his arm beneath him to perform that service. In doing so the nurse's hand come in contact with an object which he withdrew. It was a dirty little canvas bag tied with a leather string. As it Was laid aside the old man perceived what had been done* lifted his skeleton frame partially from the bed and, trembling with excitement, said in a shrill whisper. ,! Ala my treasure, my treasure ! It's gone, all gone'. and I'm going too I" and sank back dead. The tag ..co- tained £5OO in notes—the savings of his miserly life' And he, there, dead of starvation, even more than of age. Well, what of it ? you say. The wretched °ld man was better dead than alive. Quite so, but most human events have a moral, a lesson, about thorn,

we keep an eye out for it. What, for example, can we learn from the following facts P—One night about ten years ago a man vollds° name we can furnish, went to bed as usual, anParentlY in good health and spirits. A few hours later he lay ufl conscious on the floor. In explanation he stated that he had been seized, suddenly, with a pain of such violence that he was compelled to rise—a pain in the chest. After rising he lost his senses and sank down on the sP°t where he had stood. His wife aroused by the noise, struck a light and saw her husband in that situation. She afterwards declared he had gone black in the facB; and that his eyes looked as if they were starting 490 °' his head. Restoratives were applied which brought him to, but he was not as before. So quickly and unexpectedlY d° we cross the boundary line between two opposite bodily conditions. It is like stepping from the broad blazefelt 01 day into a damp cavern packed with darkness. lie weak and sick, with a strange "all-gone sensat.— throughout his whole system. His mouth tasted badlici and was filled with a slimy sort of phlegm, his beild ached, he was unable to draw a deep breath, he walke with difficulty, and went about his business like a man who is haunted by a paralysing dream. Perplexed and alarmed he consulted physicianSi w" prescribed for him, without, however, producing align 1 noticeable improvement. The strong clear-headed /21210 f of previous years was gone--changed as by the wand . a vicious magician into the feeble being he now yra9,l Even with this dismal prospect before him our friend,: travelled not on level ground ; his path led downy/4r he grew worse. In December. 1888, fie had distinct and bad attack, gave up business, and vfen t" to There he remained for a weary painful inonth--thif I days, as long as thirty years of power and IThe doctor said there was something wrong with h 6 a .

stomach and bowels. tt red After he once more rose from his bed he still su.e dreadful pain and could ro,st neither day or Pighti Indeed, some nights he never slept a moment. S° Weilk had he become that when he attempted a short „n to he was obliged to abandon the effort, return, arlu

bed. His own words are these :—" To give you an irmt how reduced I had become I may mention that I over three stone weight and ao wa‘ting awaY. I icepf on like this until January, 1891, when Mr. Eversolil,l°,s Occold, told me of a medicine called Mother Sei,,ee, Syrup and the good it had done. I trfed it and in Or / days I felt better. Cheered and encouraged bY this continued to use it, with the result that I wholly recover:l ed from my mytserious malady. lam now strong an.d hearty, and business is again a pleasure. The SyruP cars me more good in a few weeks than all my ten Yeai.o doctoring put together." (Signed) Albert Tholntls7' e' Proprietor of the •'Grapes Inn," Church-street, k.:Y Suffolk. May Ist, 1891. What do we learn from this? We find that While miserly fool like our crossing sweeper Ina' money, a wise man with more reverence for his b7i, temple, seeks and finds a remedy for a tenaency to vation, induced by disease :—that the disease w!s ifg digestion and dyspepsia, and the remedy Mother Seige

Alderman Surron : So it is. Councillor BEAMAN said he was prepared to say that Longford was in a very much improved condition owing to the energy of their manager Mr. Dees, but they had not arrived at a state of perfection yet. That word should not be used just now, for they were in a transi- tion state. Councillor SMETHURST thought that if the resolution were passed they would have an application from the manager in three or four months for an increase of salary. Councillor H. ROBERTS thought the remarks of Mr. Smethurst were just the thing to encourage such an application, and if he were in the position of Mr. Dees he should take the very earliest opportunity of applying for an increase of salary. Alderman SUTTON : He will not get it. Councillor H. ROBERTS thought they would have very great difficulty in refusing it. He thought the mem- bers of the Council could read between the lines in the letter. The fact was that they had now got at Longford, for the first time in the history of the place, got a manager who was not only a good engineer but also a competent manager, a man whose capacities were not even to be limited by the mind of Councillor ' Dixon. (Laughter.) There had been for some reason or other a little friction between those two very valu- able officers of the Corporation, the Borough Surveyor and the manager of Longford depot,and the members of the Sanitary Committee felt that they had taken up far too much of Mr. Longdiu's time. Mr. Longdin had workedjnight and day in connection with Longford, and it was fortunate that they were now in a position to relieve him of responsibility because of the confidence they had in the man who was now at the head of affairs there. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the smallpox outbreak he regretted it had become necessary to occupy the land just obtained for the purposes of the smallpox hospital, and he was very sorry for the people who had to live in the im- mediate vicinity of the smallpox hospital. He hoped the Council would not hesitate when the time came, to secure a smallpox hospital far enough away from dwellings to make the possibility of contagion as remote as it could be made. The present arrangements were only of a tentative nature, and were forced upon them by circumstances over which they had no control. There were many things in connection with sanitary reform which had still to be done. He did hope they would be able to get rid of the nuisance caused by the perambulations of these wretched vans, which were a perfect disgrace to 19th century civilisation, and carried about with them wherever they went a vile stinking odour which was not fit for a Christian to breathe,owing to their construction and to the fact that the material they carried had not been rendered as unobjectionable as it might be. At the present time it was imperative that those vans, which, so far as they knew, might con- vey infection, should, even at the loss of the mate- rial they contained, be rendered inodorous. He had been ashamed many times, as a member of the Committee, in passing those vehicles, smelling as they did do. In spite of the statement that the vans did not smell, the rarity was to pass a van that did not stink abominably. The time had come when they should insist upon their officials who had charge of that depart- ment keeping the vehicles as free from smell as it was possible for them to be. He thought a little attention to that, and a little outspoken opinion about it would not do any harm. (Hear, hear.) Councillor R. T. FAIRGLOUGH thought that if sawdust were used in connection with the vans the smell would be greatly diminished. Alderman BURGESS, in replying, said he knew nothing about the case referred to by Councillor Plumpton, but would make inquiries. Such a condition of things, if existent, should not be allowed to exist. The committee did not expect to receive an application for an increase of salary, as suggested by Councillor Smethurst. With regard to what had been said about the vans he should not at the proper time and on the proper occasion hesitate to battle with the question. As to the matter raised by Councillor Beaman Alderman Sutton had given the right explanation. Councillor BEAMAN : Just leave the word out. Alderman BURGESS : But it was passed by the Com- mittee. Councillor BEAMAN : Mr. Wilson says he put it in. The MAYOR : I made a mistake in saying Mr. Wilson drafted it. Mr. WILSON : The word " perfectly "was in the reso- lution when I read it to the meeting. Alderman BURGESS added that they did not assert that there were no repairs wanted. He also mentioned that they were now getting 11 tons per week of finished material at Longford. The minutes were then confirmed.

The minutes of this Committee recommended that the ' tenders for the forming and paving of the following streets be accepted :—Mr. F. T. Bennie, for Percy-st., at £321 2s. ; Chorley-st , at £535 10s. 3d. ; Collin-st., at £l7l 14s. ; Wellfield-st., at £374 16s. 9d. ; Mr. William Heaton, for passage between Pierpoint-st., and Refuge Square, £l3l 15s. 7d.; Mr. William Williams, for passage between Erwood-st. and Portland-st., £4B 3s. ; Mr. William Williams, for passage behind 1 to 27 Erwood-st., £3B Os. 4d. •, Mr. W. Heaton, for passage from Dallam- lane to Portland-st., £3l Bs. Bd.; Mr. W. Williams, for passage between Dallam-lane and Portland-st., £36 9s. ed. The Committee also recommended that an agree- ment be entered into with the County Council of the County Palatine of Lancaster, for the repair of those parts of main roads taken in by the extension of the Borough Boundary upon payment to the Corporation of the sum of £lO5 for the year ending 25th March, 1893. Alderman WRIGHT proposed the adoption of the minutes. He drew attention to the fact that the ten- dere accepted amounted to about £1,500, remarking that the Council would thus see that the Committee were in practical sympathy with the Sanitary Committee. be- cause they not only attended to public streets but also passages, as fast as the work could be got on with. Councillor HUTCHINSON seconded. Councillor PLUMPTON asked if it was intended to put gullies in Collin-street. He thought it was usual to put them in when the sewer was in. He noticed that Cart- wright-st. was ready for the setts, and was taken up and had the gullies put in afterwards. When the gullies were not put in there was a liability to flooding at this Period. As regarded down-spouts he was under the im- pression that they lead to be carried to the main sewers, but now most of them were turned on to the footpath. and this created a nuisance. Councillor GREENING said he had noticed that most of the fever cases were from those districts where the back passages were not paved, and he was glad to hear that these were beinq paved, and hoped this matter would receive further attention. Councillor DIXON complained of being drenched by a down-spout in Sankey-st. The MAYOR said that was a matter for the Sanitary Committee! kLaughter.) Alderman SUTTON I Wait till the Sanitary Committee meet. Councillor DIXON: (Contemptuously) : The Sanitary Committee. The MAYOR: Mr. Dixon has no hope from the Sanitary Committee. Alderman WRIGHT said the gullies had been ordered for Collin-at., and would be put down before the week was out. As to downspouts the Committee had no fixed principle. The spouts could either be connected with the main sewer or run in a slight channel on the surface. IThe latter was considered by many far better, and he thought so too. The Committee might take the matter into consideration, but he could make no promise
----- - about it. The minutes were adopted.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. Councillor Suew GREEN moved the adoption of the minutes of this Committee, which appeared in the i` Examiner" last week. Referring to Councillor 11. Roberts's resignation as a member of the Committee, he said he sincerely regretted that he found it impossible to continue his attendance. Probably they met at an awkward hour, but it was to suit the convenience of a great number of poor people who had to come before the Committee. Be had also specially to emphasise the fact that every child who could should be presented for special examination at the forthcoming series of exam- inations. Schoolmasters had not previously paid that attention to this matter which it deserved. There had been a great number of children brought before the Committee for non-attendance who would have been exempted from attendance had they been put upon the special list and specially examined by the inspector at the annual examination. The Committee were very anxious that this should not occur again. Councillor Susvuonsmsoconded the motion. He ex- pressed his regret at the resignation of Councillor Roberts and the wish that the members of the Committee would attend more regularly, complaining that at the last meeting of the Committee he was the only member present, and had to go through all the cases himself. The MAYOR made an appeal to the Council to increase their present subscription, 20 guineas, to the training ship Clio, to 50 or at least 40. Councillor SHAW-GREEN said when, two years ago, the Council increased their subscription from -10 guineas to 20 they thought they were doing very handsomely, but if the Council thought it desirable they would be prepared to contribute a much larger sum. They felt that the institution was well worthy of all they could do for it. Councillcr GREENING said it had been proposed in committee to make the subscription 30 guineas, and the matter would be brought before the Council, when, no doubt, after the expression of opinion they had heard, the proposal would be carried. Councillor SMETHURST testified to tie excellent man- ner in which youths were trained on the "Clio." Alderman FIOLMES asked how the institution was sup- ported. Councillor SHAW GREEN said there was a certain grant from the public funds, as well as private subscriptions, the Duke of W estminster being a large subscriber. Councillor BOLTON objected to more money being given until applied for. It did not do to be throwing money around that did not belong to them, when there were a smallpox hospital and a few other things that they required at once. Alderman SUTTON did not think Mr. Bolton had ever visited the Clio. When he (Alderman Sutton) was

mayor he visited the Clio with the committee, and the captain then pointed out that in proportion to the popu- lations of the towns which subscribed to the ship, War- rington had a considerably larger number of boys sup- ported on the Clio, and its subscriptions were the smallest. He believed it was at his suggestion that the Committee increased the subscription to 20 guineas ; and he quite agreed that it should be increased to 30 or even 40 if possible. Councillor HUTCHINSON hoped the Committee would bring the matter forward. If, as he understood, the Council received benefits to the amount of £7OO a year, they ought to increase their subscriptions. Alderman BURGESS said it appeared to him that there was a provision somewhere for the maintenance of a boy sent by the magistrates to the Clio, and if so where was the necessity for subscribing? He should like to know whether this was the case and what other towns were doing before the Council went any further. Councillor SHAW GREEN said whenever a boy was sent to the ship Clio or an industrial school by the magis- trates a payment had to be made by the Committee. He drew attention to the fact that there was an item in the Committee's minutes for payment of £64 12.5., for main- tenance of boys in Father Nugent's Borne and one or two other institutions. The Committee were not com- pelled to pay anything to the Clio but considering the benefits derived from it they were bound in equity to do so. .

The minutes were adopted. MUSEUM, &c., COMMITTEE. COMPLAINTS AGAINST THE COUNTY COUNCIL. This Committee's report contained in addition to a 'natter already published acknowledgment of the receipt of gifts from the following :—Specimens of leather, from Mr. E. Pickavance ; Polecat, from Mr. A. Fryer ; " Life of Galeacious Caraccioius," and " Compleat Servant Maid," 1891, from Mr. Joseph Clare ; A heal broadside, dated 1793, from Dr. Jack ; 28 skins of Canadian birds, from Mr. F. B. Greening. Councillor H. ROBERTS moved the adoption of the minutes. Be said he was glad to be able to present to the Council a financial statement showing the receipts and expenditure on account of technical instruction for the past year, which was in the satisfactory condition of showing a credit balance. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to say also that this was entirely attributable to • the fact that the Committee who were placed in a state of great uncertainty as to the amount of grant repayable from the County Council, still had been fortunate enough to avoid what many of them feared at one time, a balance on the other side of the account. It seemed to him that they had a con- siderable cause ot complaint against the action of the County Council, inasmuch as they had not conceded to the Warrington Corporation anything like the proportion of their grant for the purpose of technical instruction which Warrington as a borough of 52,000 inhabitants would have been entitled to have if it had become a county borough. Therefore the Committee had passed certain resolations which they hoped the Council would see their way that night to confirm; and act- ing in anticipation that that course would be adopted the Town Clerk had sent copies of them to the County Council, and had received an acknowledge- ment from their Deputy Clerk that they would be duly laid before the Technicai Instruction Committee of that body. The Committee could not afford to be hampered in their important work by this uncertainty, and if the County Council did not treat them more upon the lines and in the spirit shown by the Cheshire County Council from whom they had no right to expect the same con- eideratien they would have to come to the Corporation and ask to be supported in a practical form,that was, in making application to the proper authority at the right time that Warrington be constituted a county borough. They could not afford to be losing so large a sum a year because of the action of the County Council in distributing its funds inequitably and unfairly. With regard to the re- solution that the Borough Treasurer be requested to pay the sum of £2OO to Mr. Wm. Owen, treastsrer of the School of Art,in completion of the transfer of the School of Art to the Corporation, Councillor Roberts said the members would remember that as far back as October last year the matter came up. The terms upon which the transfer of the School of Art was proposed to be made were then brought forward, and those terms included the payment by the Corporation of a sum not exceeding £2OO. The Counoil agreed with the terms of the trans- fer, and he did not suppose there would be any difficulty in carrying out the proposal. If the County Council had done what they had a right to expect, and which was included in the scheme submitted by them so far back as November last, they would have been able to have funds without coming on the Corporation. The Cheshire County Council had allotted building grants for technical education, and they thought that the County Council would have included the £2OO as a grant on buildings for the purposes of technical educa- tion. As a matter of fact the money would only be temporarily used for the purpose of paying the debt off, because they would receive in the course of a month or two money from Government in the shape of the School of Art grants on the results, which would practically find them the money. Unless the Corporation passed this resolution the Committee would be in a state of continued debt to the bank on revenue account, and it was not desirable that any department of the Corpor- ation should be perpetually in debt to the bank for main- tenance. ' Councillor GREENING seconded the adoption of the minutes. COllll6llol' JAMES FAIRCLOTIOH and Alderman Sorrow made observations on the subject, the latter suggesting that the General purposes Committee should take the matter into consideration at an early date. Councillor Sitew GREEN considered that the way in whic the Lancashire County Council was treating lie Corp ration was disgraceful. (Hear, hear.) Some of them, he remarked, thought it would be much better if Warrington were absolutely independent of all other counties or boroughs in the kingdom. The MAYOR said the question must not be rushed, but the Town Clerk was corresponding with other authori- ties on the matter and the Corporation must wait results. Councillor H. ROBERTS. said he quite understood that they could not have Warrington a county borough simply for technical instruction purposes. Of course if the General Purposes Committee considered the matter as a whole the Technical Instruction Committee would be guided by their decision. The minutes were adopted.
