As the Council was rising, the MAYOR asked whether it was desirable that the report of Dr. Gornall on the above-mentioned subject should be published. A Councillor asked whether it was alarming. Allerman Famicontis It is alarming. Councillor Sigew GREEN said the reports that had appeared as to the epidemic had created so much alarm at a distance that people declined to visit the town. The new Wesleyan ministel told him that he had almost been afraid to enter the town, as he had thought it was a
plague-spot. The Council pronounced in favour of not publishing the report.

THE NEW WARRINGTON WESLEYAN SUPERINTENDENT. There were crowded congregations at Bold-st. chapel on Sunday, when the Rev. J. Kirtlan, the new superintendent of the Warrington Wesleyan circuit, gave his inaugural sermons. On Monday evening a reception meeting was held in the schoolroom. Tea was partaken of by about 300 persons, and the meeting afterwards was largely attended. Amongst those on the platform were the Revs. A. Freeman, and T. Ross, and Messrs. R. Garnett, J. Bennett, J. Shaw-Green, and W. Brown, (Lymm). There were representatives present from various parts of the circuit. Several addresses were given in which the services of the late super- intendent, the Rev. J. Gunnell, were highly spoken of, and a warm welcome given to his successor. The Rev. J. Kirtlan, in his address said that he was de- lighted to see so many friends address, the various parts of the circuit, and was very gratified at the kindly feel- ing which had been exhibited towards ,him during the few days that he had been in the town. (Hear, hear.) The tone of the remarks of the speakers had also much encouraged him, and the remarks were of such a character that they must inevitably foretell the suc- cess of the circuit. He thought that he might well say that he was standing on ground that even- ing which had been hallowed by his predecessors, who were men of power and of goodness. They were men of ability, and men who had served in the circuit with great benefit to it. He know some of them, particularly the late Rev. G. 'Young. (Hear. hear.) When he met his son quite recently he mentioned casu- 'Jiffy that he was about to take up his quarters in War- rington, whereupon Mr. Young said that of all the circuits he had travelled in he thought he liked Warring- ton the best. Rear, hear.) He felt very pleased at the testimony offered by Mr. Young to Warrington. He had often heard of Warrington, more frequently perhaps than they were aware. On several occasions he had received communications inviting him to come before the quarterly meeting, but he had no doubt that his name had been mentioned in this circuit before. It was more than a quarter of a century since it was done. It had been done by individuals several times since. It was about two years ago since he received the first communication in relation to the position which he now occupied. Bearing in mind that it was not the first time that he had been invited to try the Warrington circuit, he felt that it was a call to leave the South and turn his face towards Northern Methodism. The congregation must be aware that the most of his ministerial life had been spent in the South and West of England. Although they had not in the South the forces which those in the North possessed, yet he had found some of the most gen- uine Methodism that ever he had Come across. (Applause.) He did not say that because he had laboured in the South, or because he was a southern man himself. He was born in the town of York, and was cradled, Methodistically speaking, in the most progressive town in the country. Continuing, the speaker said that three years ago, just before going to the circuit which he had just lett, he received a call to act in a large northern town—Middlesborough. His medical adviser, however, told him that his health would not permit of him going to a district which was then in an unsettled condition. He also felt that it was undesirable to go North, not knowing how the climate might suit him, but it was not without great regret that he relinquished the idea of going to Middlesborough. It was on the score of a fear of a breakdown that he accepted a smaller sphere for his labours. His ministrations were very pleasant in his last occupation, and he had derived a fresh accession of strength. Be certainly never felt that he could labour with greater freedom than at the present time. (Applause.) Referring to Mr. Gunnell,he said that he had not had an intimate acquaintance with Mr. Gunnell of late years, and what he knew of him was gained in the earlier days of their ministry. Be had had the pleasure of corresponding with Mr. Gunnell in reference to the circuit, and had an interview with him a short time ago. Mr. Gunnell then deeply impressed him by his spirit, his godliness, and by his brotherly kindness. He was thank-: ful to be allowed to follow in the footsteps of a man like Mr. Gunnell. Pleased though he was at the kind recep_ tion which had been extended to him, he was the more gratified to observe that Mr. Gunnell's departure was not yet forgotten without a pang. They were not, however, going to lose Mr. Gunnell at once. He was glad to say that he promised to do what he could to assist in the cir- cuit, and he could assure him that it would be his pleasure to take advantage of all the help that he could afford in connection with the work. (Applause. The speaker then proceeded to detail some features of work that he was disposed to push forward, one being that of temper- ance. (Applause.)

div.head: HOUGHTON FLOWER SHOW.
div.p: HOUGHTON FLOWER SHOW.

The eighth annual exhibition of the above society which comprises the townships of Houghton, Myd- dleton, and Arbury, Winwick-with-Hulme, Hermit- age Green, Orford, and Poulton-with-Fearnhead, was held in Myddleton Hall Park, lent by Mrs. Comber, on Saturday afternoon. The weather was most favourable. The show, on the whole, was much superior to its predecessors, as the plants, peas, beans, swede turnips, cabbages, /Lc., were of uncxcep- tionable merit, whilst the cut flowers, potatoes, &c., were I quite up to the average. With regard to the cottagers' window plants, there was a considerable falling off ; and the first prize winner, Mr. H. Hill, was unfortu- nately disqualified, as he exhibited in one or two other classes. The total number of entries was .342, out of which there was a very large number of exhibits, which were nicely staged by the committee in a large marquee. Mr. E. Comber exhibited (though not for competition) a stand of cut flowers, grasses, &c., of various descriptions. Only two nurserymen entered for the prizes offered for the best group of plants for decoration, which were placed in an ornamental manner at each end of the marquee, viz. Messrs. Hilton and Randle, of Newton; and Mr. C. E. viz., of Lyme House Nurseries, Lowton. The judges in this class were Mr. E. Comber and Miss Comber, who awarded Mr. Arnott the first prize and Messrs. Hilton and Randle the second prize. The ether judges were for cottage gardens, plants, cut flowers, fruit and vegetables, Messrs. J. Randle and G. Watkin, of Newton, and for the prizes offered in the farmers' class Mr. S. Thomason, of Croft, and Mr. G. Marsh, of Newton. On account of the un- favourable weather, there was only a small attendance at the opening of the exhibition. Mr. W. Thompson's quadrille band, Warrington, played selections of music during the afternoon, and for dancing in the evening. The prizes, consisting of money, were distributed to the successful competitors by Miss Comber, to whom a cordial vote of thanks was given. THE PRIZE LIST.

RUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY
AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this-Authority was held on Tuesday afternoon. The were present Messrs. J. Mclntyre (chairman), E. Aaron, W. Pick- ering, E. Owen, W. Whistler, J. Brandreth, 11. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams, W. Whitlow, J. Weir, G. Priestner, J. Knowles, T. Lewis, J. Baguley, J. Parr, J. Ashton, (clerk) ; G. Ashton, (deputy clerk) ; Mr. Farrington. (Inspector of nuisances) ; and Dr. Adams (medical offizer.)

FRODSRAIII WATER STIPPLE. The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board sanctioning the borrowing by the Authority of £250 for the purpose of executing preliminary works in connection with the scheme for the water supply of Frodsham.

THM PROPOSED BRIDGE ACROSS THR MERSEY. The Clerk read a letter from Mr. F.' A. Lake, law clerk to the Runcorn 'Commissioners. This stated that Mr. Ashton's letter to Mr. Marshall had been duly re- ceived.. He (Mr. Lake) was glad to find the Authority , were prepared to support the scheme for constructing a vehicular bridge across the Mersey, as the success of the Commissioners' application to the Councils of Lancashire and Cheshire would largely depend upon what the localities immediately interested were prepared to do. He suggested that the Authority appoint a committee to confer with that of his i3oard. It would probably expedite mat- ters very much, and also enable them to ascertain how far the Runcorn authorities, both urban and rural, were prepared to go. He might point out that a large part of the money required for the bridge would have to be borrowed by the localities more imme- diately interested on security of their rates ; and the tolls, if any, levied on traffi7, over the bridge. Important questions would arise as to the extent of the loca.ity on which the charge should fall, and the amount thereof. Be did not anticipate that there would be any actual charge on the rates at all, if they could charge a toll, until such time as the borrowed money was repaid. If [ the Authority should appoint a committee he should be happy to arrange an interview at an early date with the committee of his Board. The Cleilt reminded the Authority that at the last meeting a letter was read from Mr. Marshall asking that he (Mr. Ashton) might attend the conference, and thLi decided that he should. Now Mr. Lake asked that a committee be appointed to confer with the Board as to how far the Sanitary Authority were prepared to go.— Messrs. Aaron, Baguley, Whitlow, Heywood and Brand- reth were appointed a committee to confer with the Committee of the Runcorn Commissioners on the sub- ject.

PRBCACITIONS AGAINST CHOLERA. The Medical Officer submitted a report on this sub- ject. It stated that in view of the occurrence of cholera in seaport towns, which were in direct communication with Weston Point and also in view of the closing of the Runcorn docks in consequence of the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal, whereby all Runcorn-bound vessels must discharge cargo at Weston Point, he had to invite attention to the question of undertaking such precautionary mea.sures as the sanitary condition of the district required. It was essential that some provision should be made for the reception of any cholera patients who might arrive on board ship at Weston Point. In that connection it was, however, to be hoped that the very efficient measures which were being taken by the Port Sanitary Authority of Liverpool would be effeetive in preventing any such patients passing the Sloyne ; at the same time no such guarantee could be given, and it behoved the Authority to be in a condition of efficient preparation for such an emergency. It was further requisite that the general condition of the water supply for the district should be inquired into, and all waters liable to contamination should be prevented from being used until they had been rectified, or directions should be given that all such waters should be boiled before using. Mere filtration in such cases was utterly useless. The report went on to speak of the necessity of the speedy emptying I of the &armies, the burning of vegetable matter, and the thorough cleansing of lodginghouses. He had commun- icated with the harbour authorities at Weston Point, as well as with the Port Sanitary Authority efficials at Liverpool, and could only express his confident hope that their efficient and able precautionary measures might prove an effective barrier to the admission of cholera at Weston Point.—On the proposition of Mr. Heywood the Clerk was instructed to write to the auth- orities ot Runcorn and Liverpool as to what arrange- ments could be made for dealing with cases of cholera that might arise in the Union. SCARLET FEVER AND DIPTRERIA. The Medical Officer reported that two cases of scarlet few r had occurred at Wilderspool, and two deaths from dintheria at Acton Grange and suggested precautionary measures in these districts. THE INSPECTOR'S SALARY. The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Farrington support- ing a motion of which Mr. Aaron had given notice, for the increase of his salary. He pointed out that half of it was paid out of the Imperial treasury, and that he had been the Authority's servant 15 years. Three years previous to that his predecessor's salary was just equal to what he (Mr.Farrington) was now paid, £l5O a year. He had £l2O a year at first, and after three years got £2O, and ultimately, £lO, advance. Through the passing of several Acts of Parlia- ment, and through the extension of the district, and the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal his duties had been largely iucreased.—Mr. Aaron proposed that Mr. Farrington's salary be increased £2O a year. He remarked that he had te deal with a good many fever patients, and his duties were increasing, and he was sure the members of that Board would always prefer to pay men respectably who worked for them—ln reply to Mr. Williams, the Clerk said Mr.Farrington paid the whole of his own expenses.—Mr. Williams said Mr. Farrington's duties were arduous, and his expenses must not be small, and 15 years' experience and knowledge of the locality, must be worth more remuneration, lie seconded Mr. Aaron's motion.—Mr. Parr objected to the increase. He observed that there were many people who helped to pay his salary who had not so much—Mr. Whitlow moved an amendment that Mr. Farrington be re-appointed at his present salary.—Mr. Weir seconded. —Mr. Brandreth said the Authority would have to ap- point an assistant to Mr.Farrington. It would be better to do that and reduce his work than increase his salary. —Mr, Heywood was of the same opinion.—The amend- ment was carried.—Mr. Aaron withdrew his motion,and proposed that Mr. Farrington be paid £lO towards his expenses for the next year.—Thero was no seconder to this proposition. There was no other business of interest to the public.

UNION BOARD OF GUAR- DIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Dutton Union on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Messrs. J. Mclntyre (chairman), E Aaron, W. Whitlow, G. Priestner, J. Brandreth 11. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams, J. Parr, J. Weir, T. Lea, A. R. Norman. J. Knowles, W. Pickering, Mr. Ashton, clerk; and Mr. G. Ashton, deputy clerk.

_ FINANCE COMMITTEE. Mr. Brandreth read the report of this committee. This stated that the balance in the treasurer's hands was £2,696 10s. 4d, Those parishes which had not paid their their calls were Antrobus, £56; Bartington, £lB ; Bud- worth,£B9 ; Clifton, £54 ; Frodsham, £B9 ; Halton.£33 ; fielsby, £BO ; Kingsley, £lO4 ; Kingswood, £27 • Manbv £32 ; Moore, £6l ; Preston o'th' Hill, £6l ; 'Whitley Superior, £36. He moved that the report be received and adopted.—Mr. Heywood seconded, and the report was adopted. ESTIMATE FOR THE RALF YEAR. Mr. Brandreth read the following :—Report and estim- ate of the probable balance in favour of or against each township in the Runcorn Poor Law Union at the end of the current half year ending Michaelmas, 1891, and amount of contributions required from the overseers of the respective townships in the Union to meet expendi- ture of ensuing half year ending Lady Day, 1893. Basis of contributions I.( quired from the overseers for ensuing half year ending Lady Day, 1893, is submitted for con- sideration, being calculated on the rateable value for the valuation lists in force. The total capital for the current half-year ending Michaelmas, 1892, amounts to £8,213, and the net probable expenditure is estimated at £5,452, which shows a balance at Michaelmas of £2,761. The probable expenditure during the ensuing half-year ending Lady Day, 1893, is set out en the detailed esti- mate as under :—Caimmon charges, £2,294; county rate, £3,403; balance and contingency fund, £3,743. The total amount required for ensuing half-year ending Lady Day, 1893, was £9,440, and after thus deducting the probable balance in favour of the townships at Michael- mas, 1892, the amount required by contributions orders from the overseers was £6,679. The rateable value of the union as per valuation lists was £224,620, an in- crease of £4,960 compared with the corresponding; period of last year. A rate of 7d. in the 4 would pro- duce £6,551, and it was recommended that a call for £6,679 be made upon the overseers in accordance with the estimate.—Mr. Brandreth moved the adoption of the report, and said the rate required was the same as for the corresponding period last year.—Mr. Lea S econded , and the report was adopted. TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS. Mr. Heywood proposed that the Guardians for Run- corn, Frodsham, Helsby, and Appleton be a committee

to take steps to bring before the ratepayers the question of the d tiTerinia e said it seem to im, Judging?roitrtfl the letters in the papers, that there was great ignorance among the ratepayers on the subject:" The proposition of Mr. Aaron for increasing the inspectoessalary seemed. to have led to these letters, and the Guardians were accused of false economy both with regard to this and the bringing forward of the question ot triennial elec- tions. He must say that all the arguments that had been brought to bear againq. them 1144 not haken hit opinion that it would be an economy to have the s elections triennially. The figures they had had, before them as to previous elections proved that the alteration would make a -saving of £250 at the very least in six years. It was the Board's duty to save all they could to relilve the rates at the present time when there were complaints all round the country that the farmers were doing badly,and when they were doing badly trade was bad. He nelued the Guardians he did as the Committee, because their districts were most interested, in regard to having con- tested elections.—Mr. Williams seconded the motion.— Mr. Brandreth said the ratepayers seemed to have got an impression that Guardians wanted the elections every three years to cook up things for certain members. He knew that was not the case. He was in favour of triennial elections, because it would be cheaper and better for the ratepayers, to mike this change.—The , motion was carried.—There was no other business of iimportance.
" KOLLUPST !"

When Csin (not Mick!) smash'd A:l;el'iyed, - An' seed aw reawnd him lookin' red, He thrut his club away, an' fled— He Kollupst When Cromwell shorten': Charles the Fobt, He only then fund eawt the cost, An' in his freet he welly host-- He Kollupst !
Wen eawr Owd Canon made a stir I' gripin' fer a Milliner, Death, comin' sadden, closed his clur— He Kollupst !
Wen Bashaves Sammie Brids geet eawt, An' aw flew backerts reaund abeawt, Jack fainted-4er he cudn't 8 heawt— An' Kollupst
Wen Sodom's mon, wi garnrny leg, Took th' number dr-awn o' Tarn o' Pegs, Like th' hen ez seet on addict cags, He kollupst !
Wen eawr Owd Scholar went to Sale, An' " Two" wur aw his bowin' tale, His gizzert welly aeem'd to fa 1- He kollupet

Wen dear Owd Ike becoom a mon, An' sojer togs begun to don, An' wen he put that helmet on, He kollup BP. Wen "Cocker" went, to th' Waxwork Show, He gen sura General a blow He thowt it wur a livin' foe, An' kollupst ! Wen " Birley Bill's" owd Turkey Cock Wur trying' i' eyt a larum clock, Poor William cudn't stood that shock,
He kollupst!
Wen Uncle George went off to bow, He grumbled an' he scratcht his pow; He cudn't t..tond that Wootton's row,
Aa' kollupst !

An' wen Munchau.en Lel a try To cop that Medal wi a lie, An' wen Eaur Jim clean passed him by. He kallupst! Theer ! aw shud think that's quite enough, Eawr Editor is lookin' gruff, An' ez aw wudn't like his cuff, Aw'll kollupse! CUM 0' PEGS. Nyowton, God bless Sept. 9, 1892.

WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.
NEW ARRANGEMENTS.

The re-opening of the School of Art for the ses- sion, took place on Tuesday. The transfer ot the School to the Town Council being almost completed, the new syllabus is issued by the Technical Instruc- tion Committee. The charge of management takes place at a moment when considerable alterations , are being made by the Science and Art Department. in the art curriculum. The old familiar names of " second grade " and "third grade" art have disap- peared, and are replaced by" elementary drawing "and " advanced art" respectively. This represents more than a mere change of name. Important re-arrange- ments have been made in the subjects composed in each, more especially in "elementary drawing." This branch , now includes the first stages of (I) practical geometry; (2), freehand; (3), model drawing ; and (4), drawing in light and shade. The initiated will perceive that here we have a group of subjects which is a distinct advance upon the old "second grade," both in practical value and in interact. The arrangements as to certificates correspond to second grade, and "D " certi- ficates will not be granted in future, but instead "elementary drawing certificates" will be given, and they will have two classes. The second class certificate will be granted to any student who obtains a second class in freehand and modelling and a " pass " in practical geometry. This may be called the irredu- cible minimum of art education, and should be obtained by each and every student who enters the school. It also represents the modicum of instruction in drawing, which the science student should certainly endeavour to secure as part of his course. The elementary drawing certificate of the first class is gained by taking a first class elementary stage in each of the fear subjects named above, and qualifies the holder to teach drawing in elementary schools. The changes introduced by the Committee are all in the direction of simplifying the arrangements as between students and school. The session from September to July will, in future, be divided into three terms, as in most other institutions of the kind, instead of four quarters, and the fees follow ' the same rule, the monthly payments being abolished. I This will be a great advantage to the steady workers, as the new fees for the evening classes are, for them, much lower than the old ones. There is a small reduction in the fees for day students who pursue the South Kensingtro ' course, whilst for the junior and senior students' special day classes the charges remain the same, it being under- • stood that they are paid in three instalments instead of ; four.

div.head: SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC. DEA.TH OF A SCHOOL TEACHER.
div.p: THE SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC. DEA.TH OF A SCHOOL TEACHER.

Mrs. Jordan, head mistress of the infants depart- ment at St. Mary's Roman Catholic School, Butter- market-st.' died on Saturday night is the Warring- ton Fever Hospital, of scarlet fever. The deceased was formerly a Miss Riley, of Sank ey-st., and had for many years held the post of teacher at St. Mary's school, and only two months ago married Mr. Jordan head master at the same institution. She was held in high respect by her pupils and circle of friends, and great sympathy is felt for Mr. Jordan and her other relatives. Requiem mass was celebrated in St. Mary's Chapel on Tuesday. The mass was celebrated by Father Sumner, assisted by Fathers Duggan and Wray. The Dead March in " Saul" was played by Mr. Mather, the organist, the choir also taking the usual part. THE FUNERAL. The remains were interred at the Cemetery on Tues- day afternoon. The cortege left the Hospital shortly after two o'clock., and proceeded to St. Mary's Church, where it was pined by the scholars of St. Mary's Schools, and others. The order of the procession to the Cemetery was as follows :—The children from the in- fants' school (deceased's scholars) ; elder scholars ; the teachers—Misses Fitzgerald, Johnson, Ramsey. Field, Caldwell (2), Price, Broadhurst, Corcoran, and Gannon ; the Children of Mary ; hearse and bearers ; mourning coaches, containing deceased's husband, Mrs. Riley (mother), Miss Riley (sister), Messrs. .1. and E. Riley (brothers), and the Rev. Father Duggan. Mr. Dover and Mr. O'Brien (schoolmaster). representatives from the Orford-lane and King-street Schools, and the Rev. Father Larkin (Liverpool) were also present. The bearers were Messrs. D. Houghton, J. McDonald, W. Lowe, and J. Eckersley. A number of the girls were attired in white, and wore black sashes, and the majority of the boys carried floral wreaths and crosses. Along the route to the Cemetery the streets were lined with spectators, a large number of whom followed the procession to the Cemetery. On arrival at the burial ground the body was taken into the Roman Catholic Chapel, where the Rev. Father Duggan read the first portion of the funeral service, during which a large number of persons congregated around the grave. The service was afterwards concluded at the grave-side, and as the body was lowered into its last resting-place many of those present seemed deeply affected. The • coffin was covered with beautiful floral wreaths and crosses, contributed by the relatives of the deceased,the school teachers, the scholars, and other friends. The : head teachers contributed a large floral cross, and a wreath, on a marble slab, with a glass case. The de- , ceased was referred to by Father Wray.in his diseourse at St. Mary's Church,on Sunday eveningithe rev.gentle- mae describing her as a model schoolmistress, who • taught the children more by her own actions than by her words.

SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 10, 1892.
WARRINGTON is being doubly Disease scourged at the present moment. in _

Warringtcn. There is an epidemic of scarlet fever in tfre town; and, in addition, there is an outbreak of smallpox, which has already reached alarming proportions. Thirty cases were reported to the Town Council, on Tuesday, of which four have had a fatal termination. Where the out- break will end it is, of course, impossible to say; for, like the cholera, it may spread rapidly. In Manchester, in 1888, a single case in St. Joseph's School infected no fewer than 69 inmates. The outbreak of smallpox at Staleybridge, which has resulted already in five deaths, is said to have been imported from Warrington. It will be seen, therefore,that the popular dread of the appear- ance of this disease is well-founded. The moment there is reason to suspect that &case of illness may be one of .smallpox, a doctor should be sent for; and the patient should net,, in the meantime, leave his room,, lest he should be the means of furtherispreading the malady. The doctor will see to it that the patient is, removed to the Infec- tious Diseases,or Smallpox Elbspital. The opinion was formerly entertained that infection could not be conveyed beyond a few yards.; but later know- ledge makes it clear that contagious particles may travel a quarter of a mile and still strike. The importance of absolute isolation is under these circumstances obvious ; and it is of importance, toe, that the smallpox hospital which is being erected at Warrington should not in, itself prove a centreof. infection. It is,. we believe., the opinion of Dr.. GORNALL, the Medical Officer A Health, and of D7.-SPINKS the Medical Officer of the Work- house, that the new- Hospital will be nearer. the Workhouse and nearer various dwell- ing-houses than is deai.rable. If it should prove that a mistake has been made' in this respect it will boa mistake whish will reilect seriously upon. the Sanitary Committee. One medical authority states that the influence of the Sheffield Hospital could be distinotly traced for a circle of 4,000 feet ; that is to say the smallpox contagion was carried in some cases a distance of three- quarters of u. mile. Much, of.aourse, can be done intaking precau- tion to prevent the spmad of both scarlet fever, and smallpox ; and the authorities are doing what they can in, this direction. Cleanliness is half the battle, in ,the first instance, for diseass and dirt go hand in hand. Milk, as well as water, may be

a source, of contagion. Several outbreaks of scarlet fever have been distinctly traced to a contaminated milk supply ;,and it is there- fore prudent to boil milk before using it. With regard to smallpox,,, there can, be no question 'that; vaccination reduces not only the chances of incurring the diseace, but the risk of fatal termia- lation of an attack. The recerds of the Sheffield epidemic are most, remarkable, Amongst the I vaccinated, "out of 4,151 cases of all ages TO died,. equal to a mortalify. a 4.8 per cent." Amongst the umaccinated,,".out of 552 cass of alt ages 274 died), equal to fianortality of 49'fitper cent" From thlit it will be seen that till un- vaccinated, when,attac ked,,died at the rate of 10 ,to.on,e as compared with the vaccinated. There is,, it should be kserved, such a thing as individ- susceptibility to disease from being in, a low ;bodily state; and it therefore behoves < every 'person to endeavour to Irep himself in grzod con- dition. In a similes way a whole- town may be susceptible through its iudifferen4 eanitation ;.and this, we fear, is the chronic condition of Warrington. Scarlet fever has been more, or less prevalent for many years;. and it would be interesting to ascertain, if it be possible, whether or no the fever has increased since tho establishment of the Intercepting Depots. That the Depots have proved a nuisance, and that they have been a cause of disease through lower- ing the vitality of the inhabitants who reside within the sphere of their evil influence, is abso- lutely certain. And what of " The Rack Spots of Warrington ?" The series of articles in the " FAxaminer " upon this subject excited consider- able attention at the time (though they were little more than an amplification of statements officially made by the Medical Officer of Health) , and steps were taken which, it was understood, would lead to the removal of some of the worst of these plague-spots. But after a show of activity, the reign of apathy was resumed; and the town is suffering to-day because of this apathy. One district, in particular, has been described by Dr. GORNALL as an insani- tary area. Its death rate is something terrible to , contemplate; and, as the local authorities are slow to move, it may become necessary tole), the

----- facts of the case before tho al Govel Board, with a view to an official ,i'.tiquiry being instituted, There is certainly preaix4,l need on to the every hand for a reform which shall go bottom in these things. It is vio use laserenth-Ig.a: epidemic whilst tolerating tho conditions will!, produce epidemics. Warrington has been negl' gent, and Warrington is suffering: for its nivOi gence.

Catherine Carey, of Bakehouse-yard, Warring- ton, seems to have been astonished at the magis- trates, on Monday, sending her to prison for a month for being drunk and disorderly and ill- treating one of her children. According to the evidence, she had been most negligent and cruel ; and the bench were certainly not too hard upon lier. It will be a good thing if the sentence astonishes other mothers of this class ;it may cause them to turn over I new leaf. --- Turton Fair keeps up its reputation as a rough- and-tumble institution._ Councillor Tootell will

remember his visit on Monday; for he was sur- rounded by a gang of sharpers who relieved him of a vahmble watch. The story goes that the first time a cab was seen in Turton the whole village was in a state of wonderment. One little boy ran home to his mother and exclaimed—"Eh, mam, do come an look. Here's a fellow coming in a leather cart!"

The German Emperor has no sympathy with Jew-baiting. Lieutenant-Colonel von Mossner has been savagely attacked by a portion of the German Press because of his nationality. The Emperor has responded to the attack,hy promoting the officer to be his aide-de-camp,at the same time expressing his regret for the existence of religious and political hatred. If the Emperor of Russia Would go and do likewise, what a difference it Would make in the world!

Who could have thought it? Mr. Tracy Turn- erelli is still amongst us. The wonder of course is that he should have remained quiescent so long. But he has broken silence to lot it be known that he has devoted 136,800 hours to the service of his Queen and country. "Truth" says this is "a melancholy record of a wasted life "—a dictum which may fairly be questioned ; for if Mr. Turnerelli has not been funny in himself he has been a source of innocent amusement to other People.

As usual, when the Liberals are in office, there are certain Jingoes who try to raise a scare about the designs of Russia in the direction of India. u t despite what is being said, the signs are hope- ful, Lord Rosebery would not be taking a holi- day, if there was a cloud on the horizon ; and, fur- ther, it is reported that "by command of the Czar,Colonel Janoff bas been ordered not to trans- gress the limits of his instructions, and especially not to forget the peaceful character of his mis- sion,"

It seems that cotton spinners are not wholly agreed about the proposal to reduce the opera- tives wages by five per cent.; and this means that the reduction will not take place. It is better to leave the matter alone than have a great strike on the question of five per cent. in wages—it is such a small sum relatively to the total cost of produc- tion. The fact is the cotton trade is bad, as it has usually been bad during the past thirty years, through extra competition and over production amongst the employers themselves. When trade is good, capital is attracted, new mills are built, and old ones extended until the usual crisis is reached. It is a case of periodic ebb and flow Which would continue if wages were reduced by 50 per cent.

A Liverpool contemporary of Wednesday has a short paragraph giving sqme account of what is described as" a disgraceful prize-fight " in Wales. Presumably the fight was " disgraceful " because the stakes were only " a-side "; for, on the same page, a half a column is devoted to the dis- cription, round by round, of "a furious combat "in America—with no suggestion of its being disgrace- ful, as the purse and stake amounted to over £2,000. It is stated, too, that the combatants had "an equally spotless record." That was before the fight commenced ; later on, the record could scarcely be saia to be spotless, seeing that, during the fifth round, " the New Yorker began to bleed Profusely."

The cholera snake is scotched not killed ; and it Will therefore be necessary to keep up the extra- ordinary precautions to prevent it getting a hold Upon this country. As so much risk is run by receiving unclean immigrants on 'our shores, the question is being raised as to whether it is not de- sirable to control, if not prohibit,the influx of des- titute aliens. It would be hard on the aliens who are seeking to better themselves, and contrary to the traditional policy of this country, but charity Should begin at home; and if it can be shown, after looking at the matter on all sides, that the admission of destitute foreigners is a great evil, steps will have to be taken to minimise the evil.

Mr. lodge as President of the Trades Union 'Congress referred to the question, on Tuesday. Prom the workman's point of view, it is not by any means desirable that poverty-stricken foreigners should be allowed to get a footing in Ilingland, and keep wages down through being 44 willing to work at any price." On the other hand it must be remembered that Englishmen have the run of foreign countries; and any steps taken to shut out the poor foreigner might lead to reprisals on the part of the great continental Powers. The matter is beset with difficulties, but the difficulties are not insuperable. The chief luestion is—ls it worth while to endeavour to overcome them?

Whittier death, on Wednesday, of John Greenleaf Whittier leaves a great gap in American singers, for, since the death of Emerson and Longfellow, he may he said to have occupied the foremost Place. 'He had not the range or melody of Long- fellow, but his note was so clear and true that it reminds one of Wordsworth. Like Wordsworth, it 00, he had faith in human goodness. It is not feng since he wrote: Age brings me no despairing Of the world's future faring ; In human nature still I find more good than ill. this is very much in the strain of— Probe nature to her inmost core, There's more of good than evil ; And man, down-trodden man, is more Of angel than of devil.

happily for the nation, Mr. Gladstone was not Permitted to dwell in retirement as he once pro- Posed and devote the remainder of his days to literature. It was a gain to the nation when he I, Nein stepped into the political arena; and if - literature lost 'something it did not lose every- rping, as was seen from the Paper from the Prime nister which was read, on Wednesday, at - "le Congress of Orientalists. Professor Max it uller before reading the article, which was on graceful t ,
patrons ve we ,r taking

an active part in our discussion as a scholar amongst scholars. History will record this event as almost unique. But we have ceased to be sur- prised, if I may borrow an expression from Mr. Gladstone's vocabulary, at his own colossal human- ity—a reference in the forthcoming paper to Achilles. If we had a Homer amongst us, he would have counted Mr. Gladstone as a true " anax andron," the Greek meaning of which you will learn from the paper which I will now read. It should be added, by way of explanation, that, according to the Premier's reading, the Ho.neric phrase " anax andion " means Governor or Satrap.

BRUNSWICK WESLETAN SCHOOLS, RUNCORN. Boy,' School " The school continues to do remark- ably well, both in the elementary and the class subjects. The discipline is now goed."—" Girls' School : " The , girls are in good order, and have, on the whole, done well. The reading of the first standard and the com- position of the fifth standard are the two weak subjects; the latter is a serious defect. The paper work might be better in point of style. The writing lacks character and uniformity. English good on the whole. Needle- work very good."—lnfants' School : " Miss Massey has not yet had a full year's work here. She seems likely to do well, but there is much yet to be done. The read- ing is not more than fair in any class. The second class has not been taught to phrase. The third class read badly. Writing is goed. Arithmetic is not well taught; even in the first class some children work their Sums by strokes. No class does well. The object lessons were worth little and they should be prepared from some trust- worthy book. Kindergarten work is the best subject; it has been taught with pea,. success." As there appears to be aome misconception with regard to the terms of settlement of the above- named strike, the Salt Union desires it to be made known that the entire cost of buying out the non-union men engaged by them has been borne by the strikers' union.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED. —J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-St., Warrington.—Adv. MANAGERS OF TzED HOUSES.

As the result of an agitation by the Liverpool temperance party,it was decided by the magistrates at Liverpool Brewster Sessions, on Thursday, that all managers of public-houses must reside on the premises. and personally supervise their houses. In Liverpool and elsewhere it has been the practice for walking managers to hold a plurality of licenses on bchalf of large brewing firms, and this decision of the justices practically abolishes the system as far as Liverpool is concerned.
HOUSEHOLD LINENS hemmed and maraed free of charge.— J. and W. DurroN, Sankey-et. Warrington.—Adrt. THE CHESHIRE TRAGEDY.

The case of John Griffiths, aged 30, who was charged with the murder of his brother by striking him with a scythe during a quarrel which took place in the harvest field at Little Saughall, near Chester, was before the magistrates at Chester Castle on Saturday. The evidence of the father of the two men, the only witness of what occurred, was taken, and this as well as medical testimony was not unfavourable to the statement by the prisoner that the wound was not inflicted inten- tionally. Prisoner was committed for trial for manslaughter.

On Wednesday evening, Mary Rimmer, Thorpe- et., Widnes, succumbed to the terrible injuries sus- tained, on August 14th, by being burned in a shocking manner about the face and chest, through the upsetting of a lighted parraffin lamp, whilst Phe and several others were " waking " the body of a lodger. De,ceas?,d sustained her injuries by endea- vouring to save a woman'immed Ann Gordon, who was also burnt, and died the same day a: Widnes Accident Hospital. The inquest was held yesterday by Mr. Brighouse and a verdict of accidental death was recorded. IJMI3FLELL RECOVERED.—J. and W. Durrox, Sankey-it., Warrington. —Ad.
THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN TRAIN SERVICE.

Complaints regarding the unsatisfactory and un- punctual train'service between St. Helens and vari- ous towns in Lancashire have given rise to frequent correspondence between the St. Helens Town Council and the railway company. How far this has been successful is seen by the following minute of the Parliamentary Committee, which was sub- mitted to the Council on Wednesday :—" Referring to the resolution passed at the last meeting, a letter was read from Mr. James Shaw, superintendent, stating that he hoped the trains would be greatly improved in punctuality when the four lines be- tween Wigan and Carr Mill Junction have been opened ; that other works are contemplated which will have a very beneficial effect ; that he would give the matter his best attention ; and that when the new time-tables were issued the 3 p.m. train from St. Ilelens to Rainford would leave at 250 p.m. and thus form a connection with the Lancashire & Yorkshire line for Southport.:'—The Town-clerk was instructed to again write to Mr. Shaw pressing upon him the necessity for immediate improve- ment in the matter of the trains by way of St.. Helens Junction.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
That one of the chief topics of conversation dur- ing the week has been the exclusion of Mr. Grice from the Board of Commissioners, after his long servitude as a representative of the ratepayers.
That he was a most attentive Commissioner,punc- tual and constant in the performance of his duties, and took a genuine interest in the work of the town. That he will be much missed.
That the new members took their seats on Thurs- day, and they quite altered the appearance of the Council Chamber.

That by custom each member always occupies the same seat at each meeting, but the new members quite upset this arrangement on Thursday, and the members were in strange and unaccustomed places to which they will no dciubt soon become as at- tached as to the old ones.
That the meeting pf the Musical Society on Tues- day ended like the one held the previous week—in aqizzle, and there will have to be some radical change if the Society has to be kept in existence.
That the School Board election for Widnes takes place next month, and there is expected to be a stiff fight between the upholders of undenomina- tional education and the denominationalists.
That there is a rumour that Mr. Timmis will not seek re-election, but it is to be hoped it is a rumour and nothing more.
That he is a model chairman of the Board, and it is wonderful to witness how he will smooth over the knottiest difficulty, and his removal from the Board would be a great loss to the town.
That we shall have along list of candidates in the course of a week or two.

Boys IN fuounnt.—Thomas Buckley, H. W. Connor, Ed. Brown, and James Metcalf, all of Salford, were charged vith stealing four cakes, the property of Sanuel Jordan, grocer, Bold.—Mrs. Jordan stated that the boys came into her shop on Tuesday, and asked for some bread and cheese. NEGLECT OF A WIFE AND CHILDREN.—Edwin Bond, Widnes, was brought up on remand charged with neg- lecting his wife and two children. Mr. A. F. Mann, clerk to the Guardians, appeared to prosecute. Mr. Hampson relieving officer proved the case.—Mr. Deo, con : You will be sent to gaol for one month.—Prisoner : Thank you, sir, I expected three.
THE MAKING OF PRIVATE STREETS.

At a special meeting of Warrington Town Coun- cil, which was held prior to the ordinary meeting on Tuesday evening, Alderman Wright moved : " That the Nlayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of Warrington, acting by the Council as the Urban Authority for the said borough, do here- by adopt the Private Street Works Act, 1892, and that this resolution shall come into operation on the 11th day of October, 1892." He read a state- ment which had been prepared by the Town Clerk as to the advantages of the new Act. These ad van- tages were summarised as follows :-1. It settles the question of liability before any expenses are incurred, whereas, under the old Act, the Corporation were re- quired to expend money and then contest the liability. 2. It secures the Corporation against any loss by pro- viding more certain and less costly modes for recovery of the expenses. 3. It accelerates the proce- dure, and enables the Corporation to complete a street within three months, whereas under the old Act it took from six to nine months. 4. It takes away the power which was given to owners to construct a street in a piece meal fashion. 5. It gives distinct power to amend plans and specifications in the event of any error being discovered. 8. It gives power to the Corporation to make more equitable apportionment, as, for instance, where a footpath is required on one side of a street only, or where a street is wide at or.e end and narrow at the other. 7. It gives power to the Corporation to charge a fair proportion of the cost upon persons whose property is benefitted, although not abutting upon the street. 8. It gives power to the Corporation to adopt a street when the whole or any part of the paving works have been completed. 9. It gives power to the Corporation to contribute to the cost, and to borrow money for the execusion of the works.
After a abort discussion the special meeting was ad- journed for a month in order to give further time for the consideration of the report.

About 1,000 miners struck work on Monday at the Clydach Vale and Llwyny Pit Colleries Rhendda owing to a wages dispute. The Lord Mayor of London visited Rhyl on Monday, and was accorded a most enthusiastic reception. His lordship during the day performed the ceremony of turning on the water at a new fountain. In the evening he was entertained at a banquet.

RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY, The adjourned meeting of the members of this Society was held on Tuesday in Bethesda Lecture Hall. There was a good attendance, the lady mem- bers preponderating. On the proposition of Mr. R. W. l'ierpoint, seconded by Mr. Taylor, Mr. Thos. Handley was voted to :he chair.—The Chairman expressed sorrow that he was unable to be present at the last meeting, and called upon Mr. R. W. Pierpoint to read the minutes ef last meeting.—Mr. Pierpoint said he was no longer secretary. The season was wound up and the President and vice-presidents were elected. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys was appointed conductor, but he could not get a cabinet to work, and resigned the position. He had a resolution to move which would cause the whole matter to be debated thoroughly, and it was as follows :—" That the Society shall have a professional conductor and that such eon- ductor shall be selected, engaged and con- trolled by the Committee." The/ all knew the block that occurred on Tuesday bat; and he looked upon the society as a nebular hypothesis at the present time -.-(laughter)—but he thought before the meeting concluded it would again be a living reality. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Humphreys was quite right in not at- tempting to conduct the society when he could not get a committee to back him up. He did not wish to do anything to create a division in any shape or form. He advocated a professional conductor, and would give reasons. They could afford such a luxury. He did not believe the statement that had been made, that a pro- fessional conductor had brought about the ruin of socie- ties in the district. He thought such remarks very unfair. Ile proceeded to deal with the history of the several societies, and gave his opinions as to why they came to an end. They failed in obtaining an influential list of vice-presidents, upon whom to rely for contribu- tions. In that respect their society raised £llO last year, which was sufficient to afford the luxury. He also contended that if they had had a professional gentle- man to advise them, they would not have had the ex- travagant expenses for band, &c. From a musical point of view it went without saying that a professional con- ductor for the society would have been a great boon to them. He was not going to pass any reflection upon anyone else, as in his opinion Mr. Humphreys, as an amateur, efficiently fulfilled his position. .(Applause.) He thoroughly believed that if they would pass the re- splution the end of that society was far distant, and there was greater promise in store in the future than in the past. (Applause.) Mr. Marlow seconded the proposition,

Miss Stubbs stated that she understood that they had to decide that night whether the society shouldlir should not be continued. They had two sections,one desiring to see Mr. Humphreys as honorary conductor, and the other wishing for a professional gentleman to wield the baton. There was much to be said on both sides. She trusted that all present would sacrifice their individual wish for the public good. The claims of the society upon them were greater than the mere question of who should be the conductor. She was opposed to party feeling, and trusted that the voting would be by ballot. She moved a resolution to that effect. Miss Jones seconded.

Mr. A. R. Norman, as an outsider and a vice-president, spoke of the satisfaction the concerts promoted by the society had given to the public, who had been delighted with them, and were desirous of their continuance. He believed that the great support received by the society was because it was a local one, and be was afraid that the generous response given in the past would be dis- continued in the future if they had a professional con- ductor.

Mr. W. Handley thought that the time had come when they should get to work. He spoke from experi- ence of other societies, and stated that in his opinion professional conductors had not done very trinch in the way of musical education. They had been dominated with the idea of getting as many concerts as possible, so as to get the fees ; and b.e had known the choruses to have gone on the platform wondering how they were to get through. That could not be said of the concerts of the past few years, and he quoted the opinion of one of the leaders brought down, who spoke in high terms of the accomplishments of the members. He thought their best plan would be, instead of squabbling about the conductor, to form a committee, and see what works they would practice. Everyone was anxious to begin their winter operations. After other speeches, M. Plerpoint replied. He con- tended that the vice-presidents would continue their sup- port if a professional conductor were appointed. The proposition that the vote should be taken by ballot having been carried, Messrs. W. Handley and W. H. Rogerson were appointed tellers. The Chairman announced that 64 votes had been recorded, of which 27 were in favour of the appointment of a professional con- ductor and 35 against, there being two blank papers. Therefore the proposition of Mr. Pierpoint felt to the ground. 'the election of officers was then proceeded with. It was decided that Messrs. James Booth and Walter Jones be joint secretaries. Mr. F. Scott was chosen as trea- surer. The committee selected was Misses Crosby, Comerford, Stubbs, C. Sampson, and Simister ; Messrs. W. Handley, W. H. Rogerson, J. Marlow, Joseph Littler, and C. Pownall.

Mr. Pierpoint suggested that the appointment of con- ductor be left in the hands of the Committee, which pro- position was seconded by Mr. Unsworth. As an amendment, Miss Wright proposed, and Miss Jones seconded, that the selection be made that evening, which was carried.—The Chairman asked for nomina- tions, but none were forthcoming. After a pause of several minutes Mr.lluFriphreys said having regard to all the feeling' exbibited he must decline to permit his name to be brought forward for the position in future. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Rogerson, seconded by Mr. Marlow, to adjourn the meeting to a date to be de- cided upon by the Committee.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.

A special meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday morning. Mr. F. Wiswall presided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speak- man, C.C., J. Prit chard, W. Fisher, 11. Coward, W. IL 'Wass, P. Smith, Dr. Mangan, W. Leach, T. Lea, D. Bisbrown, J. W. Lightburn,S. Taylor. W.Hankinson, E. W. Humphreys,J..Nleadoweroft, and Dr. Mangan, with F. A. Lake;jaw clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor).
THE DECLARATION.
Before the • business commenced, the newly-elected members made and signed the usual declaration as to their qualifications.
HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical Officer (Dr. McDougall) had forwarded the following report :—'Fhe number of deaths registered during the last month amounts to thirty-one. Three were inquest cases, and of the remaining twenty-eight deaths three were due to diarrhoea, three to atheroma, , three to phthisis, three to infantile convulsions, three to mesenteric disease, four to enteric fever, two to pneu- inonia, and one each to cancer, gangrene, pleurisy, , inflammation of the lining membrane of the brain, ap, plexv, premature birth and bronchitis. The thirty- one deaths show an average death rate for the twelve month of 18 6 and exclusive of the inquest cases of 16.8 I I would desire to point out that there is a gratifying I diminution in deaths from diarrhcea, and more especially amongst infants and children of tender years, as for some years past, deaths at this time of the year were very noticeable. Within the last few days the Authority has had placed upon the walls and hoardings of the town, warning notices to all whom it may concern and more especially to some househ-ilders who are apt to forget the obligations which they owe to them- selves and to the public with respect to clean backyards; clean, well ventilated houses, total absence of over- crowding, care in the disposal of green vegetable refuse which should always be burned and never at any time placed in an ashpit, and to give e:,rly notica to the Authority of had smells, insanitary condition of houses, ashpito and privy pits ; also to hoase Owners, who by psompt attention to the insanitary conJitions more , especially c " oniTruirmi themselsthemselveswhen brought under their notice, such as defective ashpits and privy pits, Oefective drains, improper and imperfect stench traps, and dilapidated housuyards, will by co-operation in these matters relieve the authority from grAt anxiety at the present time. The remodelling of the building bye- laws, would be an immense gain and protection to house occupiers,and to the public generally in this respect, and a great future saving to the owners. Mr. Lightburu asked how many cases of infectious disease there were in the town.—The Secretary replied that there had been 56 cases since the first of June up to the pt.( sint date. He could net say how many were actually sick at present.—Mr. Smith asked if it were customary for the I medical officer to be absent when his report was read.— ' Tile Chairman explained that the meeting was a special one. The report was not submitted at the monthly meeting because the returns had not then come to hand. Time doctor was expected to be present during the meet- ing.—Mr. Humphreys considered the doctor should be present at their meetings, especially at a time like the present when there were alaratist reports as to the existence of infectious disease in the town. There appeared to be more cases ot typhoid fever than there should be, and it would be wise to go to the root of the matter and if possible discover the cause of the outbreak, and he should be glad to have an assur- ance from the Chairman of the Health Committe that every effort would be made to do so.—Mr. Lightburn said the health of the town had recently improved very much and there was nothing to be alarmed about.—Mr. Smith said in referring to the absence of the medical officer, he was not finding fault in this sense of grumbling. —At this point Dr. McDougall entered the room, and in answers to questions as to the prevalence )f infectious disease in the town, he said he considered it was inju•ii- cious to discuss the matter at length, as doing so was likely to raise a false alarm among the inhabitants. The death rate was exceptionally low at the present time, and there were nothing like the number of cases they bad in 1890. There was nothing in the condition of the town to cause the slightest uneasiness. Be hcped the Board would give careful and prompt attention to the recommendations received from the medical gentlemen of the town.—The discussion then ceased.

THE LIGHTING OF SALISBURY-ST., &C. A letter was read from Mr. J. R. Frith, secretary of Runcorn Gas Co., stating that he expected the mains would be laid in Salisbury-st., Byron-st., Ac., in the course of the next fortnight.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT W A RRING TON.

As yet I do not hear much talk %bout the coming municipal elections, although the first of November is not so far off now. I will, however, enumerate the councillors who " come oat "this year. These are Councillors R. Heaton, for Town Hall ward ; F. W. Monks, Whitecross ward; S. J. Beaman, Bew- sey ward ;F. A. Roberts, Orford ward ; J. Hill, St. John's ward ; R. T. Fairclough, Fairfield ward ; J. Cannell, Howley ward ; J. Muir, St. Austin's ward ; and L. Greening, Latchford ward. Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Sutton, and Harrison will also retire this November. Alderman Greenall id almost sure to be invited to stand again as 11,iyor.

At the Town Council meeting some credit was ! taken from the fact that smallpox had been imported into Warrington. I confess I fail to see ! that much credit is to be derived firma this. As far ' as I know there has been no claim that Warrington is capable of spontaneously generating a smallpox microbe—or is it bacillus? Many people will admit that the town has the best modern contriv- ances for accomplishing a feat of that kind. If the microbe cannot be generated in the inner recesses of an Intercepting Depot, or a pail and tub van, it cannot be created anywhere. But I believe it is now generally conceded that the amiable creature is, like a true poet, not made but born. And there is no species indigenous to Warrington. If, there- fore, it were not imported we should never have smallpox in Warrington.

It seems to me that the true test is this: Is War- rington in the best possible sanitary condition to repel an invasion of the migratory microbe? lam afraid that it must be admitted that the town is not in that sanitary condition. In truth, the mere fact that not only smallpox but other infectious diseases as well have spread to the alarming extent that they have done is proof that it is not. Speaking my own candid opinion, I should say that there are far too many unpaved and sloppy streets, passages, and yards, too many old and unfit dwellings, and too much Jerry building in Warrington for the town [I to lay claim to high sanitary excellence.

Mr. William Diggle, who, I understand, was pre- sent at the Council meeting on Tuesday night, had the sat ibfaction of hearing Councillor Henry Roberts draw attention to the noisome smells occasioned by the malodorous vans which are u.ed for the convey- ance of certain manure. This is a subject to which Mr. Diggle, in and out of season, has persistently called attention, and whatever may be thought about his views as to the Intercepting Depots, he is assuredly right in his complaints about these vans. We have perhaps semeoccasion to be thankful that we have not this year experienced a long continu- ance of the real old-fashioned bummer weather' which, for those old enough to remember it, is such a delight to think of. That part of the Mersey that flows through Warrington has of late been stink- ing most abominably, and what with the vans and one thing and another,the town has been very much like Cologne, where Coleridge once counted quite a considerable number of well-defined and separate stinks. Talk about the fish forsaking the Mersey at Warrington on account of its pollution; I am sur- prised that the birds do not forsake the air above it ; it is so polluted sometimes.

, Judging from the statement of CouncillorJ. Shaw , Green at the Town Council meeting it would seem that the School Attendance Committee are really very anxious that school children should sit at certain special examinations in order that they may secure "labour "certificates exempting them from further attendance at schools. They are so anxious, in fact, that they seem disposed to censure school- masters for not putting more of their scholars on the lists for these examinations. Now, in my hum- ble opinion the schoolmasters are showing that they have a much better appreciation of what is good I both for the scholars and the community than the School Attendance Committee. Nobody will argue that an early withdrawal from school is good for the child. In whose, interest., then, is the Commit- tee so anxious to get ready this early crop of boy labourers ?

It may no doubt he said that. a boy's earnings are of great use to his poor parents. That is the cry that. Iris been used against all compulsory education, and if it were to be heeded there would be no corn- pellin2 of children to attend school. But, as exper- ience has shown, it is a fallacious cry, for the poor were never so poor and demoralised as when child- ren could be sent to work almost as soon as they could Walk. Bat, apart frotn all that, it is surely the proper business of the School Attendance Com- mittee to get children to school and to keep them there as long as possible. It seem etrange freak ' on the part of art " Attendance " Comm;ttee to urge upon schoolmasters to get children exempted from attendance at school earlier than they otherwise would bp. An Attendance Committtee might very properly leave that to others.

Since I made the observations I did last week concerning the advent in Warrington of a new solicitor from Loudon, connected pith the Salva- tion Army, I have heard some additional particulars as to this gentleman which will be interesting to my readers. I was under the impression that his name was Peace, but it appears that it is Pease, a name eminently suggestive, however, of identity with peace principles. Mr. Percy Duncan Pease— that is his full name—is,it seems, the son of an officer in H.M. military service, Colonel Thales Pease, who was for some time Commissary General in charge of , Portsmouth Gun Wharf, and was selected by the Admiralty in April, 1891, as Storekeeper General I of Naval Ordnance, at a salary of £1,450 per annum.

In the" Examiner "last week there were reported two Cases of convictions of boys for unloosing wag- gons on siblings of the Cheshire Lines Committee, and there was a note pointing out the danger of such practices. I have since read accounts of a fatal railway accident in America which has occurred through identically the same practice on the part of boys. A passenger train was standing on a siding—which was on an incline,as are the sidings in the cases I have mentioned—at Mountain Park on the Central and New Jersey Railway. Some ju- venile male imps of mischief entered the carriages, loosene•I he brakes, and started the train down the incline, nrl to the main line,at a terrific rate. They managed to jump out in time themselves, but the carriages smashed into a coal train, wrecking it, and killing the fireman, the engine-driver and the brakesman having a narrow escape. A more terri- ble disaster was only averted by promptly telegraph- ing and signalling all down the line. Considering the danger to human life,th us instanced,l think the magistrates were by no means too severe with the daring and adventurous youngsters I have men- tioned. They seem to take as naturally to playing most dangerously with railway waggons as they did a few years before to playing with the toy waggons of their infantile days. They were divert- ing themselves thus on a Sunday too, and Watts's , hymn lines about Satan finding mischief for idle I hands to do were well illustrated In their case on ' this supposed to be the least satanic but most idle day in the week. One day's rest and recruitment is a fine thing for the human race generally, but, strangely enough, there seems to be about as much I mischief on that day as—indeed more than—on any I other day in the week.

The Countess of Carlisle, who gave such a strong impetus to the Women's Liberal movement, in Warrington, last year, by her appearance in connec- tion with the Liberal bazaar, and created such a favourable impression of her ability as a champion of the cause of true political reform,has been show- ing in a very practical way that her Liberalism is I not merely a matter of politics. She has been hav- ing thousands of poor children, hundreds at a time, at the castle of the Earl of Carlisle, and has there been making them happy to their hearts' content. 1"Our old nobility" would stand considerably higher in the estimation of the public if their common hu- manity with the poorest of their fellow-creatures were more extensively recognised after the fashion of the Countess of Carlisle.

I hear that the Longford Wire, Iron, and Steel Company, Limited,have just completed the furnish- ing of the New London and Noi-th-Western Rail- way Station at Euston with Wood's patent spring wire setters. Last week the same Company secured the order of the Metropolitan Asylums Board for 600 bedsteads and Wood's patent wire mattrasses :

and also an order from the Royal South London Eye Hospital to furnish it throughout with special, operating bedsteads, fitted with the patent wire mattresses. It will, perhaps, be remembered that the Prince of Wales laid the ioundation stone of this institution last year.

It is said that there was, in the Bank Quay direc- tion, a very narrow escape from a premature burial the other day. A child had been pronounced to be , dead, and the preparations for the funeral had gone so far that the body had been placed in a coffin, when suddenly, and to the intense amazement of those near it, the supposed " corpse " cried out in a manner which provebl unmistakeably that life was not quite extinct. The child, however, only lived a few hours longer.

It will cheer the hearts of the temperance people of Warrington, to know that at the present time the whole of the Nonconformist ministers in War- rington are total abstainers. I hear that during the coming winter, vigorous action will be taken in the town in regard to temperance work. Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., has promised to address a meeting in Warrington, on October 2Gth, in connection with the United Kingdom Alliance, and it is expected that Mr. William Crosfield, M.P., will preside upon the occasion. I have no doubt that such a meeting will be a great help and encouragement to the temper- ance workers ot the town.

div.head: 100 MILES' RIDE BY WARRINGTON CYCLISTS.
div.p: A 100 MILES' RIDE BY WARRINGTON CYCLISTS.

On Thursday Mr.E. Pickavance started on a pneu- matic safety trom the headquarters of the Warring- ton Cycling Club at 9 35 a.m., and travelled the 100 miles' route via Nantwich in seven hours four mine. Mr. J. Wadington, another member of the club, did the same distance a few days ago in six hours fifty- nine minutes. The club offers gold medals to mem- bers whe do it under seven hours fifteen minutes, and other members are expected to try to lower the above Warrington records.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION FINANCES.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION FINANCES.
REPORT BY THE CLERK TO THE GUARDIANS.

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of 11 Guardians on Wednesday, the Clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton) read a statement as to the finances of the Union, which contained the following :—The esti- mate of contributions required for the half year ending at Lady Day 1893 was submitted to your Board on August 24th. The proportions are therein fixed according to rateable value. The movement made by such value has in the half year been slight; an increase of from £340,181 to £3.11,497, is mainly due to a rural new assessment. For the year 1891-2 we overpaid the calls, with the effect of re- ducing a surplus of £3,094, at Lady Day, 1891, to £1,191, at Lady Day, 1892. We experienced,alike as to Couuty awl Vuion demands, other corresponding troubles, hence it became necessary to strengthen your financial position by a call of £9,649 for the present, and, as you are now advised, by a further call for £8,858 for the next half-year. To enable your Board to examine and compare Union Finance by the light of past experience I annex to the estimates an account in detail of tlnion receipts and dis- bursements in 1891-2. The revenue comprised parish contributions £15,844, County Council grants £4,348, sundry receipts £1,275 making, with the surplus £24,562. From credits are culled items for in-mainten- ances £3,751, out-relief £3,709, maintenance of lunatics £2,899. County, rates £5,300. Fhe total of outlay, less £1,191 surplus, being £23,371. These figures enable an approximate estimate of Union expenditure in connec- tion with relief and of outlay and demands unconnected with relief.

Looking back to a period prior to union administra- tion we find, as has before been remarked, local poor rates, when subject to very light charges other than for I relief of the poor, of 3s. in the £or 6s. yearly. It has I also before been explained by these papers on estimates , that until a quarter of a century back the lowest of Union Calls had been Is. 10d. in the £1 for the year. Continuous diminution of outlay would be out of har- mony with efficient administration, yet it is pleasant to , learm that, in face of new duties, enlarged and im- proved systems, and weightier county demands, the calls for 1891-2 totalled £ls,B44,whereas the once lowest ratio of union levies would have yielded £31,183. The total for 1892-3, of £18,507 would,in like circumstances, have reached to £31,304. In this connection you have the further gratification of knowing that your outstand- ing Loan Debts are sinking, and that a few pence in tbe £ would enable you to be rid of them.

div.head: SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC. IN WARRINGTON. GREAT INCREASE OF CASES. THE NEED OF ISOLATION.
div.p: THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC. IN WARRINGTON. GREAT INCREASE OF CASES. THE NEED OF ISOLATION.

I There have now been no fewer than forty-one cases of smallpox in Warrington. Of these twenty- one have been reported since last Saturday. It iii be seen from this that the disease, instead of diminishing is increasing at an alarming rate. Of the forty-one cases which have come under the notiee of the authorities since July 28th, four have died,twelve are in the hospital, and twenty-five are being treated at their own homes. The cases for the most part have occurred in the Bank Quay district, bat there have been outbreaks so far apart in the town as Winwick-road, Knutsford-road, Nicholson-st., Dixon-st., Golborne-st., and Orford-st.

It is unfortunate that, owing to the prevalence of fever in the town, the demand upon the accom- modation provided at the Infectious Diseases Hos- pital is so great that, as yet, no fewer than 25 cases of smallpox are unisolated. The work of erecting the new smallpox hospital is being pushed forward aa vigorously as possible, men working at it night and day, and until it is completed the dangers ' arising from the lack of isolation will continue. So long as they are unable to give prompt arid effi- cient isolation, the authorities are, of course, seriously handicapped in their endeavours to stamp out the malady, but in other respects, they are going all available means of doing so. Special larrangements have been tirade for vaccination and 'revaccination, infected houses are thoroughly dis- infected, and special attention is given to tlits Icleansing and scavenging of the districts in which the disease has made its appearance. With regard to vaccination, the schools have been visited in order to make sure that the children have been, vaccinated.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATE.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATE.

TEMPT OF PIPES. At the borough police court on Thursday, Robert Rills, a militiaman from Orford Barracks, was charged with stealing, about 9 o'clock, the previous bight; two briar root pipes, trom the shop of James McClue, 47, Horsemarket-st.—The Chief Constable said he went into tAll shop and asked the assistant to look at some pipes, and then walked off with two, without paying,for them. P.C. Sankey noticed him in Horsemarket-st , with two new pipes, and asked him where he got them, and he replied" I stole them "and told him where he had got them. The officer took him to the shop, and his state- ment was confirmed. His object in stealing the pipes was to get discharged from the army.—A militia sergeant gave him at previous good character, and the prisoner wore good conduct stripes. The Seageant said he had stated in the barracks that he would steal something to get discharged.—The prisoner said if he wanted to leave the army he had no occasion to steal, as he could be bought out. He added that the young men had all the favours in the army now and the old men all the kicks. He did not know why he had committed the theft. The Chairmen said be had no doubt it was his own fault as in other cases, if he did not get on in the army. The prisoner was bound ever in his own recognizances for £lO to come up for judgment if called upon.
