div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION v. GARSTON COPPER WORKS. —Warrington journeyed to Garston to meet the finalists for the Liverpool and District Junior Cup in their open- ing game of the season. The visitors travelled with ten men, being minus Kincaid, right full back. Copper Works kicked off about 3.45 p.m., with a strong wind against them, when Warrington soon made tracks for the home goal, but the Garston defence were on the alert The visitors, however, returned to the attack, Denby scozing the first point for Warrington, the home custod- ian failing to stop a grand shot. Returning to the attack the visitors completely bombarded the home citadel, Garston making spasmodic attempts to transfer play to the Warrington end, but failed to get near Jones, the custodian. Garston, however, held their own, half-time arriving with the score unaltered--:Warrington one goal, Copper Works none. After changing ends, in a drizzling rain, the home team assumed the aggressive, J. Roberts scoring for Garston directly a f ter the re-start. The wind now increased in violence, spoiling any exhibition of good football, but the home team kept up a continued fusilade, Davis, Phillips, and J. Mather, playing a very strong defence. At last from a throw in from touch, the ball went straight through, Garston claiming a goal, , stating that it caught a players' head before going through. The plea was allowed. Soon after this, the home side had a free kick for hands right in goal. A scrimmage ensued—a noteworthy feature in the Rugby game, the visitors, however, clearing from hands off one of the home side. The wind spoilt further efforts to play, the sphere travelling back into goal mouth as quickly as it was cleared, the, final result being Garston Copper Works two goals, Warrington one goal. Warrington team : Goal, Jones; full backs, Phillips and Davies ; half backs, substitute, Mather and Bonehill ; forwards, Norman, R. Fennelly, Forbes, Denby, and Johnson. Umpire, Mr. James Mather.

div.head: TRADES CONGRESS.
div.p: THE TRADES CONGRESS.

The Trades Union Congress opened on Monday in Glasgow, when it was stated that there were present 495 delegates representing a million sad a quarter of workers. The Corporation of Glasgow heartily wel- comed the delegates to the city. Mr. John Hodge, pre- sident of the Glasgow Trades Council, was appointed president, and Mr. George Shipton vice-president, of the Council. Mr. Hunter, Glasgow, was elected secretary ; and Mr. Inskip, Leicester, treasurer. Messrs. Judge (Leeds), Jacks and Tait (Glasgow), Ben Tillett (London) and Haslam (Derbyshire) were appointed the Standing Orders Committee. The report of the Parliamentary Committee referred to the recent elections as affording striking evidence of the importance and value of organ- ized labour.

On Tuesday, Mr. John Hodge, the new President, delivered his presidential address. Be dwelt on the progress which trades 'unionism had made in recent years, and argued that it was not subversive of good government, but fended to promote the greatest good of the greatest number. ' The twin curses of the tcoun- try were poverty and drink, and much might be done by social reformers: to remedy the evils resulting from them. He deprecated unnecessary Sunday work, advo- cated arbitration as a mode for settling industrial dis- putes, urged increase of labour organisation so as to include women, and advocated the nationalisation of railways and land. He counselled those who wished to gain a legal eight hours day to more usefully spend their time in securing better organisation and the ad- vancement of many local movements which had a direct bearing on the labour cause. A long discussion took place on the motion of Mr. S. Woods, M.P., cen- suring the Parliamentary Committee and secretary fer, not carrying out resolutions of the Congress urging for- ward the Miners' Eight Hours Bill. Mr. J. H. Wilson, M.P., and Mr. Fenwick, M.P., having explained, the action of the committee, the motion was defeated oy 289 to 121. oi

On Wednesday a nuinbeid 'resolutions were fidoted calling for various alterations in existing laws. In the morning the principal subject of discussion was labour representation, and it was resolved, upon the motion of Mr. Keir Hardie, M.P., to instruct the Parliamentary Committee to prepare a scheme dealing especially with financial difficulty, the same to be subjected to the unions in time for full consideration previous to the next Congress. It was resolved, by 141 votes to 140, that a scheme should be promoted for independent labour re- presentation. It was afterwards agreed to support at the next election only candidates pledged to the pay- , ment of all members of Parliament out of the ConsoliD dated Fund, and of returning officers' expenses out of the rates. The Parliamentary Committee were WI structed to endeavour to bring about the trade union' rate of wages at all Government works, an amendment of the jury laws so that workmen should be entitled to. become jurymen and reqpive 10s.daily for their services.' and the abolition of the qualification for seats on boards, of guardians and local boards. A subscription of 2.30' was made by the delegates and visitors for the sufferers by the recent Aberkenfig explosion.

.t I On Thursday the Congress resumed business at 't3tiia- gow, among the visitors during the day being Lord Rosebery and Sir Charles Dilke. Some conversation took place regarding Mr. Keir Hardie's qualification. The chairman of the Standing Orders Committee stated that no question had come before them as to his quali- fication, whereupon Mr. Keir Hardie said people who made calumniating statements ought to have the courage to formulate them. A delegate who was not allowed to discuss the qualifications of certain delegates left the Congress. Several alterations were made in the standing orders, the most important being a reduction in the con- tribution, enabling poorer societies of unskilled labour to send delegates to the Congress. A long discussion took place on the proposal to hold a Special International Congress for considering the best means to bring about an international eight hours day. The Congress decided to support the holding of a Special International Con- gress immediately. Mr. Fenwick, M.P., and Mr. Chisholm Robertson were nominated for the Parliament- ary secretaryship, and a resolution was adopted in favour of a Bakers' Eight Hours Bill.

div.head: STRANDING OF A MINX
div.p: STRANDING OF A MINX

_ STEAMER. 500 PASSENGERS RESCUED. The Isle of Man Steam Packet Company's steamer Mona's Isle went ashore at midnight on Tuesday at Scarlet Point, near Castletown, Isle of Man, while pro- ceeding from Dublin to Douglas, ,with 500 passengers on board. Alt the passengers, however, were rescued and proceeded to Castletown, where they were hospitality entertained by the inhabitants, Miss 'Baker, a young lady from Nottingham, has sup- plied the following statement :—When we left Dublin at ten minutes past sir the weitber. was very fine,•and: we made good progress until half•past nine, when it became so foggy that we could scarcely See 4 hand before us. Every precaution was takers by the *Min and crew. We, proceeded very slowly and fog signals and rockets were frequently, sent oft. Ithink eight rockets were fired. ' A little before eleven o'clock the steamer Ciiine to a dead stop, having apparently gone' upon smooth' rocks or on to the shore. We had hot tbe-slightekt idea where we were. For a few momenta .there was considerable confusion, as might naturally be expected, with so many passengers on board, but ,there was no approach to a panic. Of course for a this we thought it was all up with us, but the captain and crew (all except one man) behaved splendidly, and we soon quieted down on his,assur- peas being given that there was no danger. The pie& svaiiquite smooth,'but the vessel rolled considerably from side to side. There were plenty. of lifebelts on board, and one was. given to each of us. All the small boats were lowered, tilt we ' cOuld 'not get into them. Plamately two ,ladders were tied together. All the ladies, I beliave, "got down by means of these ladders on to the rocks, and from there 'waded to the Shore. I think the men, or most of them, got down on to the shore by, baskets running on a rope. When we were all ashore we trooped off to Castletown, to get to which we had to cross two cornfields and a grass field; so that we were not far from the town. We reached Castletown at half-past two in the Morning. We were' sheltered in the Town Hall there, where the neigh- bours very kindly supplied us with hot coffee. We left Cistletewn for Douglas by a train at ,ten minutes past. seven, and were in Douglas by eight o'clock, none the worse for our adventure. On Wednesday morning the Tynwald attempted by means of two hawsers to tow the Mona's Isle into deep water, but the attempt was unsuccessful. On Thursday, an attempt was made at high water to drag the Mona's Isle off the rock on which she stranded near Castletown. It was unsuccessful.

A GROCER AND HIS SCALES.—Thomas Lea, grocer and provision dealer, Church-Street, was summoned by W. D. Laird, Inspector of Weights and Measures, for selling bread from a cart without being provided with the proper weights and scales. Defendant pleaded guilty, and said he was away on that day and the boy who drove the cart neglected to put the scales in the vehicle. —A fine of is. and costs Bs, 6d. was imposed. A FISHMONGERS' Row.—William Green, John Duckett, Michael McGrath, John J. Webb, and John Massey, fish dealers, were summoned for assaulting another fish dealer named John Salt on the night of the 30th August. The defendant waylaid him in High-street, knocked him down, and kicked him, and he took refuge in a butcher's shop.—Green stated that Salt sent for him, and when he went to the place of meeting, Salt struck him a blow on the chest and said "That's what I want you for." They then fought, and afterwards Salt ran into the butcher's shop.—The oth3r defendants said they were not present at all.—A boy named Phillips said there was " nobody but their two selves " at the fight.—The Bench dismissed the case. AN T.hscr..E.ss LopoiNo Howsz.—Thomas Kelly, lodging house keeper, Fryer-st., was summoned at the instance of James Percival, nuisance inspector, for not causing the floors and passages and staircases of his house to be swept and washed as required by law. Mr. F. A. Lake prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Improvement Com- missioners. Dr. McDougall, medical officer of health, deposed to the filthy condition of the house on Thurs- day, the Ist September.—The defondant denied the charge, but called no evidence to disprove it. He was fined 20s. and costs as. 6d. DRUNKENNESS.—John Moreis, Allan Ackeriny, and J3hn Green, were each fined for this offence.

FOOTBALL.

••• Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than teo o'clock on Wednesday morning.

WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S V. ECCLBSTON ROY/MS.—OR Saturday the Saints started their season with the Rovers at Eccleston. The visitors won the toss and played. with the wind. The Rovers started, and the Saints were soon pressing, and after good forward play the ball was passed to Hampson who rounded his opponents and scored near the corner flag, the point not being improved The Rovers dropped out, but could make no headway against the wind, and the Saints were soon near their line, where Bennett dribbled over, the kick at goal fail- ing. Again the Rovers kicked off, and very soon Hamp- son, after some loose play, picked up, and rushed over behind the posts, Roughley this time placing a goal. Half time score: St. Mary's, 1-2-3; Rovers, nil. On turning round, the Rovers having the wind, the game was more even. From some off-side play by the Saints, a free kick was given to the Rovers, Harris kicking a good goal. Nothing more being scored, the game ended in a win for St. Mary's by 1-2-3, to the Rovers, one goal (penalty), 4 minors. RUNCORN Av. STOCKPORT A.—On Saturday the Run- corn " A " team paid a visit to Stockport, the match being witnessed by a large crowd. Unfortunately the weather was inclement. The visiting forwards by smart foot-work forced their opponents to defend. Scrimmag- ing ensued for some minutes on the home lines, until some bad passing amongst the Runcorn backs gave Stockport a chance to clear, of which they availed them- selves by rushing the ball through their opponents. Speakman, however, saved at a critical moment, Walker being almost over. Faulkner dribbled well away, and prevented Smith from getting in his return. Clucas was again very prominent by a pretty dribble, and, passing between Faulkner, Tudor, and Antrobus, gained but little ground, as the home forwards, who were greatly superior in the pack, rushed the ball clean into the visitors' 25, when some fumbling play by their backs enabled Olden to cross the line. No goal resulted. This reverse seemed to have disorganized the Runcorn- isms, as in the next few minutes another irresistible rush by the Stockport forwards overcame all opposition, Walker scoring. Again the place was unsuccessful. Half-time was shortly called with the score—Stockport, two tries; Runcorn, nil. Resuming, play was of a very scrambling order for a long while, both sides being very eager. Warder stood out very prominently with his judicious kicking, time after time taking the ball clean away from the feet of the Stockport forwards, and re- turning to touch. Some quick passing between Liggatt, Burrows, Parrott, and Grainge ended in the latter scor- ing the final try, Smith failing at the place. The game ended in a win for Stockport by three tries and three minors to one mixer. Runcorn team :—Warder, full back; three-quarters, Speakman, Antrobus, and Dunva- band ; half backs, Faulkner and Tudor; forwards, Derbyshire, Clucas, Moores, Evans, Taylor, Lightfoot, Gayter, Clarke, and Unnson.

RUNCORN v. STOCKPORT. On Saturday the football season was opened on the Irwell ground, Runcorn, when, notwithstanding the inclemency of the weather, there was a good attendance of spectators. The Runcorn team differed materially from that which" last season represented the club, as will be seen from the following list of players :—Hough- ton, back; Pendlehury, Crompton, and Robinson three- quarter backs; Abram and Hollingworth, half2backs ; Hampson, Shaw, Williams,O. Hughes,Taylor, J. Davies, Langley, Riley, and Lee, forwards. Stockport was represented as follows: Massey, back; T. Haslam, F. Saville, Ashton, and Murray, three-quarter-backs; Noble, Dain, Bailey, Speet, Downs, Morton, Williams, Abbey, forwards. Stockport won the tees, and Riley kicked off in a blinding shower of rain. For a while the play was in midfield, but although Pickard gained a slight advantage by kicking up the field, Houghton relieved, and the play became located in the visitors' 25. pain dribbled out of danger, but again the Runccrn- ians were on the ball, Evans, Abrams, and Hollingworth being prominent. Closely following this episode Crompton essayed a drop at goal, which failing, a minor ensued. Following the drop-out the play for a while was of an even character. At length Stockport made a demonstration, Houghton again coming to the fore in the nick of time. A moment later Noble renewed the attack, but although Houghton was caught napping, the home forwards relieved the pressure. Saville, however, again attacked by means of a free kick, which yielded a minor point. Following the drop- out Abrams got away in a spirited run, and passing to Crompton a wide space of ground was gained. Stock- port cleared, Pickard further improving the advantage by means of h, free kick. 'Again Saville distinguished himself, only to see Houghton punt to midfield. Later on Runcorn were pressed, and Robinson touched down. Half-time result: Stockport, two minors; Runcorn, one minor. Following the interval Noble re-started, and pressure was brought to bear upon the Stockport line. Abrams almost got over, but the play was quickly located in midfield, the hornesters now having the rain- storm at their backs. Dain, however, dribbled effec- tively, and for a moment Runcorn were placed on the defensive. After scrimmaging a while, Pendlebury ran through a knot of opponents, bringing about a series of desultory scrimmages in midfield. The turf, however, was saturated, and neither side could make material headway. The forwards at this time did the bulk of the work. In this Stockport, although playing only eight men in the pack, conspicuously held their own. The play continued of a desultory but even character, Massey doing excellent defensive work for the visiting side. Ashton and Saville were again conspicuous, and the Runcern line was endangered until Pendlebury cleared. At this juncture Runcorn obtained a free kick for palpable infringement of rule, closely following which smart passing by Hollingsworth and Abrams brought about a vital change, for now Crompton, who finally received the ball, dashed brilliantly away and scored, but Houghton failed in his attempt at goal. Towards the end the visitors made determined efforts to repair the disaster, but although they were awarded a free kick, and later on had the ball in close proximity to the Runcorn line, they failed to profit by their exertions, and the score remained unchanged, Final result : Runcorn, one try, one minor ; Stockport, two minors.
WARRINGTON v. DEWSBURY.

The opening of the football season in Warrington took place on Saturday, when a crowd, numbering nearly 4,000 assembled, in spite of the unfavourable state of the weather, to witness the game with Dewsbury. It was to be regretted that rain fell nearly the whole pro- gress of the match, for not only were matters rendered uncomfortikble for the spectators, but the players were seen to such's disadvantage 'that those who had braved the elements Were disappointed at the poor show made by the rival teams. Several improvements have been made on the Warrington ground, the sixpenny side of the ground having been provided with raised footboards, and no effort has been spared for the comfort of the spectators. A delay occurred in the start, the Dewsbury team arriving three-quarters of an hour late, the fire at the oil stores in Salford having delayed them. Owing to some misunderstanding in the time of starting, Mr. H. Williamson, the referee, failed to put in an appear- ance until after the match was concluded, and Mr. Plumpton,_of Widnes, officiated in his stead.

It was after four o'clock when Warrington made their appearance, and a ringing cheer welcomed them, whilst Dewsbury were received in a like manner. The visitors attacked the pavilion goal, and the kick-off rolled into touch barely five, yards past the half-way flag. Some sharp rushing by the Tykes eventually reached the quar- ter flag, but the Bates Ind Heesom checking the progress, Evane, Fair. Turner, and 11011Xle3 dribbled the oval back to ' half . way, where an Injudi- cious kick to Scott 'allowed that custodian to clear easily. Scott was the recipient of a wild pass and was floored before he could make headway, whilst a ringing cheer was sent up when James Bate got away, but the enthusiasts were doomed to disappointment, for he was pulled up five yards from the line. A spell of scrambling play by each get of forwards was relieved when Stadden ran along the popular side and tested Boscow, only to find that player at his best. The War- 1 ringtonians continued to press the Tykes, but beyond 1 forward play and dilatory passing the game was a trifle weary to watch. Jackson attempted a pass, but the relief was brief, far Ashton led his men firmly in one rush, and Heesom next sent the oval touch in goal. Soon after the drop-out, the Bates and Heesom passed neatly, but ffenworthy with a tong 'dribble reached the home quarters. Donohue, Berry, and the brothers, Turner forced the game back to its original quarter, and Barnes and James Bate engaging in a tackle of Conway, the last-named Warringtonian fell, and on examination it was found that his collar-bone was broken. !Evans took the vacant place at half, whilst Holmes was drafted to three-quarter. John Bate and Evans passed well, but Heesom dribbled with a pass to Barnes. The, latter, however, punted across the field, but the proffered chance was not taken. Stadden and Randall changed the venue, and there ensued a monotony of scrimmages and struggles on the Dewsbury. line. ' Jolley made an effort which was worth notingTiatid-Btadden making his mark, the ball was punted to Bosaow, Who plabed it again on the visitors' lines; and half-time was 'called with Warrington only credited with a minor. Frank Turner re-started, and another series of scrambles were witnessed. The players seemed ,a trifle mixed, and apparently did not seem to realize is to which side they belonged. After ten minutes had elapsed the Warringtonians realized their position, and some neat kicking by lieesom, aided by smart 'dribbles on the part of Jolley and ' Berry, caused Scott • some anxiety ; the last-named forced a minor, but something more substantial wail forthcoming a tew moments later. ' when Ashton, taking advantage of a mull by S'ott and. Oates, got in; the popular Warrington skipper ribbling over single-handed, and scoring the first tr) of the season. Fair. Turner failed at the difficult place. The Dewsbury hearts now sank below zero, althongh they were dangerously near scoring on.lionteral Occasions, especially when Randall got clear from a line:out and

passed to Kenwortby, who fell a victim to Boscow's safe embrace. Fair. Turner asserted himself a few minutea later, and a spell bf passing by the forwards was instru. mental in the game being on the Tykes' lines, and Evans got away from! a scrimmage and ran over strongly. ,The scoring did not end here, for another mill by the War.. ringtonuins, flaw Jolley complete the day's scoring. Evans made another effort near the call of time, and although Nevins claimed a try, the point was over-ruled, and the game ended—Warringtpn, 0-3-2; DewsburY. Teams :—Warrington: J. 13oscow, back; J. W. Evans, F. Heesorn, and T. Barnes, tbree-quarter backs; James Bate and Sohn Bate, half backs; -H. Ashton (captain), Fair. Turner, Frank Turner," W. Nevins, J. Jolley, W. Bandies, T. Donohue, W. Berry, and J. Holmes, forwards. Dewsbury: Scott, back Cites, Brown and Conway, three-quarter backs; Stadden, Jackson and Burns, half backs; Kenworthy, Randall, Abel, Butterworth, Pickard, Hodgson, Holdroyd, and Garforth, fcirwards.

div.head: DOUGLAS ,TRiiGEDY..
div.p: THE DOUGLAS ,TRiiGEDY..

EXTRAORDINARY EVIDENCE. A shocking tragedy occurred on Saturday at Douglas, Isle of Man, and has caused an intense sensation. It appears that a gentleman of means', named George Barker Cooper, and belonging to Manchester, where he is a member of a well-known firm, having offices also in Liverpool, was staying at the Regent Hotel with his wife.. On Saturday morning the chambermaid. told Mr. Walden, the manager of the hotel, that the couple were quarrel- ing. Subsequently be heard that a slight scream, Yellowed by a thud, bad attracted the attention of the chambermaid, and he thereupon went to the bedroom, accompanied- by the head porter, and demanded admittance, Cooper opened the door and said.his wife had fainted. Sbe was lying naked ob the left side near the bedstead. Mr. Weldon did- covered that the woman was dead, whereupon Cooper who had sat down on the side of the beg, remarked that she was in a dean faint. A wound was found on the upper part of the breast, and the police were summoned. Cooper made no effort to leave. At the inquest deceased was identified as a former barmaid at the Central Hotel, Douglas. The inquest was adjourned to enable spa-mole/re exam- ination to beheld.

On Monday the Douglas Coroner resumed the inqueit on the body of Edith Annie Cooper, who was found dead on Saturday morning, in a bedroom at the Regent Hotel. Cooper was present in court. Telegrams had been received from the prisoner's father and the de- ceased woman's mother, asking that the inquiry should be adjourned in order that they might be present and hear the medical evidence. Counsel for the prisoner also asked for an adjournment in order that an inde- pendent post-mortem examination might be made in his behalf. After some discussion the inquest was adjourned till next day. On Tuesday the inquest on the body of Mrs. Cooper was resumed in Douglas, before Mr. S. Harris, coroner and high bailiff. Evidence of the utmost significance was given. The Coroner was anxious to know whether Mrs. Cooper was drunk when she arrived in Douglas on Friday night, and the witness to whom he put the ques- tion replied with an indignint and decided negative. Dr. O'Malley gave evidence as to the cause of death, which was shown beyond the possibility of doubt to have been a stab that penetratod the left lung and the heart. The medical man also spoke to finding extensive bruises on the face, head, and body of Mrs. Cooper. These had , been caused by recent blows. Further and most import- ant light was thrown on the case by the evidence of a barmaid at the Regent. This young woman, seeing that Mrs. Cooper was looking very ill, asked the prisoner on Friday night what he had been doing to her. She replie,4 that he had given her "a good thrashing with a horse- whip," and; further, that he "intended to pay the little d— out." The inquiry was adjeurned. - COMMITAL OF THE ACCUSED.

On Wednesday the inquest on the body of --Edith Annie Cooper, was resumed. George Barker Cooper, a Man- chester merchant and husband of the deceased, waa again present in cus.tody.—The first witness was the steward of the steamer Mona's Isle. He contradicted the statement which had been made that the deceased was drunk when she arrived at Douglas in the steamer on Friday night.—Police-constable Whitfield, who arrested Mr. George Cooper, said that when lie MP/ the deceased lying on the floor, he said to the accused," Why, she is dead. Who has done this ?" Cooper replied, " I don't know. I have been to Dumbell's flank in company with Mr. Bradshaw, and on my return I found her like this." Witness asked if he found her on the floor, and Cooper answered that he found her in a faint on the bed and got her on the floor and poured some water on her. Be afterwards said, " I must go "and made for the door.— , Police-constable Warren and Dr. O'Malley corroborated Whitfield's evidence.—Police-constable. Warren said that as Cooper_was leavinge nom he exclaimed, "Oh, my God ! let me kiss her efore ram taken away." The nightdress worn by the deceased, covered with blood, was hare produced, and Warren said that he found it on the floor with one Of the sleeve a torn out. The con- stable also produced ir wash-hand basin three-parts filled- with bloodand.a knifes which he Mild he found lying beside it. The sheet, pillows, and bolster were also smeared with blood, and the cuffs of the shirt which Cooper was wearing at the time had, .blood on them. There was blood, too, on the -wardrobe floor, and an, attempt had apparently been made to Wash' the blood- stains from 89418, towels and handkerchiefs, and a por- tion of thedeceased's underlineri appeared to have been used to wipe thellobr.—Mr. Brookes; 'Manager of ,the firm of g..T.iind -F. Ceoper, of Mancliestet; tit Which the , deceased's father is the principal partner, wasimalled to prove that on Friday- -last they received a draft from Cooper's solicitors of the settlement. Which he was going. to make upon his wife.—The Coroner then summed up, and during his address to the jury Cooper fainted, and had to be removed from the Court--After the, consul- tation, the jury returned a verdict of" Wlil Murder." —The verdict was received with applause on the part of those in court.—The prisoner was then formally com- mitted on the coroner's warrant for the wilful murder of his wife. The body of Mrs. Cooper was on Wednesday morning removed by her father to Birmingham for in- terment in the family grave there.

div.head: DECEASED'S ANTECEDENTS.
div.p: THE DECEASED'S ANTECEDENTS.

The deceased woman, Edith Annie Cooper, was a native of Shirley, near Birmingham, and was married to Cooper ten monthB ago. Her Maiden net& was Cooper aid she was the daughter of Mr. William Cooper, a gen- tleman of independent means residing at The Oaks, 'Shirley. Mrs. Cuoper was abOu t twenty-five years' of age, a good-looking and highly accomplished young lady, and was educated at a private school at Shirley. After leaving school she remained at home with her piurents,: her two brothers and sister, for,some tine i , and then accepted a situation as barmaid at the Central Restab- rant, Corporation,st. _There She Stayed a. long time,but. loft about three years ago, and subsequently took an engagement as barmaid- at the' Central Hotel, Douglas. There, it is believed; she first made the acquaintance of her husband. From Douglas she removed -to•--London, where she lived' with some relatives • but • about eighteen months ago she returned to Shirley, and remained at home until her marriage. She was occasionally visited by Copper, Co whom it was well known in the village she was engaged, and the marriage was fixed for a particular date, but was postponed on account of the perious illness of her sister. Cooper was much older thao his wife, being a man between thirty and "forty veers of age, a gentle manly looking-ilidivianal,-ffis black Moustache and "im penal", giving him "the appearanee of a Frenchman. About ten months ago the deceased wee married tocooper at Shirley ChurclA the ceremony being performed by the Vicar,the Ree.Chas.l3urd. Deceased and- her husband visited Shirley several times after the marriage, and the deceased. whose,: pleasant and, lively disposition had made her a favourite in the village, alwaye , ap- pealed to be Very happy. She was last seen at Shirley .about six weeks ago, and then she told several friends that she was going- to spend her holidays with he/, husband in the lide of Man. Her, untimely death op Saturday morning ha,s caused a great , sensation at Shir- ley, and also at the Central Restaurant, where she was so kindly remembered, and there were many expres- sions of regret when the news of the alleged murder was confirmed, and of sympathy for her parents and friends. INTERMENT OF THE VICTIM'S REMAINS., There was a pathetic scene:in the early hours of Thurs- day morning in the churchyard of Shirley, Bil-mingham. The body of Edith Annie Cooper, the victini It the Douglas tragedy, arrived on We'dneSday night, arid,was placed before the'altar where -ten °months ago, she mar- ried Cooper.--At seint.eclocs on Thursday morning, a little prpeespion, , including the father,, mother, sister, and twct ethers, walked 'Ed thechuiehi *herb the 4.lergy7, man who conducted the marriage ceremony offiCiated. There were only a dozen spectators. The grave-digger, beadle, sexton,' and bellringer, were the bearers of the. coffin. No,bell was tolled. The scene was over before the little hamlet was awake. , . , . , At Douglas, on Thursday, George 13. J.„ Cooper, who stands committed on the , Coroner's inquisition for the murder of his wife, was taken before the High Bailiff. Some of the evidence given, before the Coroner was repeated, and the prisoner wee remanded until Friday.

div.head: . THE CHOLERA,
div.p: . THE CHOLERA,
ENGLAND ALMOST FREE.

A London news agency was informed by the Local Government Board Department on Saturday that "with one or two exceptions, where convalescence is not yet completed, there Is not now a single case of cholera in England or Wales." As a matter 0 fact, however,there are two convalescents lot Liverpool alone, one being under treatment in Parkhill Hospital and the other at 'the workhouse. Latest inbeiligence, however, is Co the effect that the patients are progressing satisfactorily. It was on Stmday ascertained that there were several cases of cholera on board a vessel which had arrived in the Mersey after calling _at Hamburg, where two of the crew had died. The vessel. was placed iro quarantine. • •The Liverpool Landing-stage on Saturday is describsd as presenting a forlorn appearance owing to the embargo which has been put upon emigration to,' the United States. It is anderstood that the emigrants now in the city will be forwarded by slow steamers, which will undergo the prescribed twenty days' quarantine on the othereide._

A death from cholura occurred at the Tyne Port Hos- pital on Monday morning. The victim was landed at Newcastle on Sunday night from the steamer Elbe,which had arrived from Hamburg. On Tuesday, on the arrival of the steamer Oldham, at Grimsby, one of the saloon passengers; was found suffering from cholera, and was removed to the hospital ship. The fruit brought in the boat wig be returned, ancl the fish she carried destroyed. The Vhssel has been disinfected, and will remain in river forty-eight hours to guard against infec- tion.

The Marytaboo° Vestry on Tuesday passed a resolution expressing the opinion that Her 'Majesty's Government should be called upon to WO immediate steps to stop the immigration of pauper Miens into this country. RAVAGES ABROAD. • . THOUSANDS DYING IN RUSSIA. Additional cases of cholera are reported frvin New York. One death ,occurred on 'Tuesday at the quaran- tine station there. The Montreal Provincial Board of Health has prohibited all ccrramunication with Hamburg, Antwerp, and Havre. A large. number of, deaths from cholera occurred in Paris on Monday and neiday. The morality in Russia continues to be of an appalling character. At New York there were two fresh cases of cholera on board the steamer lying in quarrentine on Wednesday, but no death had been reported; whileten Tuesday therq had been eight cases and one death. It is generally believed that, in 'spite of the stringent regulations made in Canada, British and Scandinavian immigrants will be allowed to land.

The figures relating to choleraic disease in Paris are not quite satisfactory. On Tuesday there were 31 deatha in the capital and 21 in the banlieue. At Havre there were 20 cases and 7 deaths on the same day. Our Antwerp correspondent telegraphs that the total of deaths in that city now amounts to 26, and sin the suburbs.

• The cases reported at Hamburg on Tuesday numbered 702, and the deaths 333. There are no fresh cases re- ported in Berlin. Professor Virchow has published a most interesting report of his investigations in Russia. He expresses his belief in the accuracy of the official re- ports. In the whole of Russia there were 4,779 cases and 2,348 deaths on Sunday, and in St. Petersburg 138 cases and 34 deaths on Tuesday.

div.head: TERRIBLE SCENES IN HAMBURG.
div.p: TERRIBLE SCENES IN HAMBURG.

The Special Commissioner sent by "The Morning" to Hamburg alleges that while the Board of Health there returns the deaths at 2,676, the actual burials registered at the cemetery of cholera victims is 4,795. He visited mortuaries in which there were rows of fifty corpses laid oh the stone floor, each body wrapped in a disem- fected sheet and nothing else. They were afterwards put , int* rough pine coffins , and carted to the cemeteries. In one mortuary he saw a pile of bodies come in ordinary everyday clothes, men and women some naked, some wrapped in disenfected sheets,.and so numerous that they overlapped each other. He saw fifty gravediggers digging graves, and fifty more cover- ing the coffins laid in those graves, and at times the arrivals were so numerous that at ene time there were dozens of coffins uncovered. The gravediggers at one cemetery were increased from 27 to 200, and then could not complete with the epidemic. No mourners showed a desire to -enter the cemetery, and the corpses were brought in beer wagons and furniture vans, there being no hearses available. Some of these conveyances car- ried as many as forty corpses at one . time. The gravediggers and the "corpse carriers" have it all to themselves, and day and night they are at their ghastly work. On the road to the cemetery are many bier-halles and other resorts of entertainment. On ordinary days those were generally more or less crowded. Now they are always empty. One proprietor said," We do noth- ing new but listen to the ratttle of the dead cart." This is not cheerful music. Efforts are made to miry the great mass of the victims at night, that the people may not obtain a true conception of the strength of the epi- demic. INFECTED SHIP AT QUEBEC.
QMSBEC, WeDNeeDar.—The Wandrahm, from Ham- burg, arrived at the quarantine ground with cholera aboard to-day. Immigrants are forbidden to enter the province. FRESH CASES AT NEW YORK.
/*Taw YORS, THURSDAY.—Eigiat fresh cases of cholvra have occurred on board the steamship Normannia and two fresh, cases on the Rugia.

div.head: SULLIVAN V. CORBETT FOR £9,000.
div.p: SULLIVAN V. CORBETT FOR £9,000.

DEFEAT OF: SULLIVAN. • J. L. Sullivan, of Boston, met James Corbett, of San ' Francisco, at the Olympic Club, New Orleans, on Wed- inesday nights to box for 45,000 dollars and the heavy- weight championship of the world. Sullivan on enter- ing the ring, weighed 15 stones, whereas his opponent I scaled only /33t. 81b., but the latter is 10 years younger, his age being 28. Betting was generally in favour of the Boston boaster, the odds being five to three against I the-FrisCiirnan: The struggle commenced a few minutes after nine o'clock, and lasted an hour and 'lB minutes. Sullivan had decidedly the worst of the encounter. • In the last pound Corbett felled him to the ground, and his attempts to rise were said to have been pitiful. He crawled to the centre of the ring, and made what is described as a " manly speech.' Again he tried to rise, but had not enough strength left to do so. A Central News telegram received from New Orleans, this morning, says that the result causes general satis- faction ; " Sullivan's bra.ggartism has disgusted almost everybody."

J rernem.___ ‘nat on Sunday, ~...ugust some.labourerel on a walk near Althorpe Railway Station in the vicinity of Northampton, noticed a disagreeable smell of a peculiar nature, as though proceeding from /lead flesh. The labourers began to search, and finally discovered the headless, armless body of a woman in, 5. .pack secreted in a ditch, by the side of the main road from Northampton to Rugby. The bag was cove red with rank vegetation. The feet had been tied together .and then pressed backwards, and the body was thrown forward as as to occupy the smallest possible space. with a quantity of lime thrown in. The body was iwrapped in coarse canvas, which in turn was placed in. an old sack. It was fully clothed except as to the feet. Decomposition had s') far proceeded that it was impos- sible to guess even at the cause of death. On Saturday night, with the assistance of the Hirming ham City Police, the Northampton County Police arrested in Northampton Market-square :Anelrew Macßae, a grocers' assistant at Birmingham; charged on suspicion with being Concerned in the murder of a woman unknown whose mutilated and headless body wasiound in a ditch, near Althorlie Railway Station a month ago. Fer several weeks Macßae has been in the rsle of Man on a holidfsy. He returned last week, and on Saturday, for the first time, resumed charge of his brother's stand- ingln Northampton Market. He went to the Isle of Man directry after the body was found, and pleaded illness for not returning before. The arrest was quietly effect- ed. The prisoner was brought before a magistrate ou Monday and remanded until Saturday. At the resumed inquest on Monday week, a piece of sacking was produced by the po ' liCa in which the body was wrapped. It bore on it a small label with the name and address, E. M. Rae, Northampton. The police gave evidence that the arms of deceased, both of which were still missing, had been sawn off apparently by a bacon - '

saw. -- Fresh facts have transpired regarding the Althorpe murder. The clothing found on the deceased has been identified as having belonged to Ann Pritcha,•d, of 30, Ba!sail Heath, Birmingham. She and her infant child disappeared from Northampton. Mcßae, who is in custody, has been identified as having stolen some of the deceased's clothing. On Wednesday the Northampton police made what is thought to be an important discovery. In searching Ithe Dychurch-lane warehouse, belonging to Mcßae 's IbrOther, for whom the prisoner was manager, the police found a number of pieces of bone in the cooper firePlam These were in the ashes, and were very small and cal- cined. They will be submitted to an expert to ascer- tain, if possible, whether they are human bones, the sug- igestinti being that they are remains of the missing arms of thewoman Pritchard. Mean w hile nothing whatever his been discovered of the missiog head or of the babe. A ' man mined John Hall has come forward with all an- nouncement that a month Ago the prisoner got him to remove from the warphouse a quantity of lire ; this evidence is considered of importance. because the body when found on the roadside near Althorp Station was covered with lime. It is also known that the prisoner I hired a horse and trap and drove out of Northampton ' on July 26, six days after Pritchard's disappearance,and within a week of the time at which the body mist have been deposited in the ditch.

• PARENTAGE OF ROBERT BRUCE.—This great Mall the saviour of Scottish independence at a most nafigerous crisis—was the son of Brace, Lord of Ninandale, by a lady who was Countess of Carrick ne her own right. It appears that the first acquain- tance of his parents and their subseqttent marriage ,t,°°k Place through fortuitous circumstances, so that his existence, and consequently the indepen- dence of his country, may be said to have depended epon mere accident. The particulars are thus related by Mr. P. E. Tytler, in his late work entitled :Scottish Wortities," published as part of Murray's .r.arally Library:—" It appears that a short time utter his return from the crusade, Bruce was riding through the beautiful domains of Turn- berry, Castle, the property of the widowed Conn- 'ells of Carrick, who, in consequence of the death sf her husband, had become a ward of the crown. The noble baron, however, if we may believe an ancient historian, cannot be accused of having visited Turnberry with any view of throwing himself in the way of the Countess of Carrick; and, indeed, any such idea in those days of jealous wardship would have been highly dan- gerous. It happened, however, that the lady her- self, whose ardent and impetuous temper was not !Mich in love with the seclusion of a feudal castle, had come out to take the diversion of the chase, accompanied by her women, huntsmen, and falcon- era; and this gay cavalcade came suddenly upon Bruce, as he pursued is way through the forest alone and unarmed. The Knight would have spurred his horse forward, and avoided the encoun- ter, but he found himself surrounded by the attend- lints ; and the Countess herself riding up, and, with gentle violence, taking hold of the horse's reins, re- [reached him in so sweet a tone for his want of gal- aatrY in flying from a lady's castle, that Bruce, ena- Moured of her beauty, forgot the risk which he ran, ittii,d suffered himself to be led away in a kind of triumph to Turnberry. He here remained for fifteen ;',E_qs, and the adventure concluded, as might have been anticipated, by his privately marrying the Youthful countess, without having obtained the concurrence of the king or any of her relations. Alexander 111., however, although at first indignant lit this bold interference with the rights of the crown, was a benevolent prince, and on the pay- bent of a large feudal fine, extended his forgive- begs to Bruce. The eldest son of this marriage of sudden and romantic love was Robert Bruce the Younger, Earl of Carrick, and afterwards King of Scotland. The second was Edward Bruce, Lord of Galloway, who was crowned king of Ireland in 1316; and besides this regal issue, the Countess of Carrick, who appears to have proved a faithful and affectionate wife, bore her husband three more sons and seven daughters." CONFINING JURORS FROM MEAT AND DRINK. The Gothic nations were famous of old for the quantities of food and drink -which they; consumed. Theancient Germans, and their Saxon descendants 20 England, were remarkable for their hearty meals. Gluttony and drunkenness were so very common, that those vices were not thought disgraceful; and Tucitus represents the former as capable of being 1?; easily overcome by strong drink as by arms. Intemperance was so general and habitual, that no .elle Was thought to be fit for serious business after 'tiinner. ; and, under this persuasion, it was enacted ib the laws, that judges should hear and determine causes fasting, and not after dinner. An Italian author, in his antiquities, plainly affirms that this gnlation was formed for the purpose of avoiding the unsound decrees consequent upon intoxication; and Dr. Gilbert Stuart very pertinently and ingeni- ?_usly affirms, in his Historical Dissertation concern- `ng the Antiquity of the British Constitution, P. 238, that, from this propensity of the older Pitons to indulge excessively in eattrig'and 'drink= !rig, has proceeded the restriction upon jurors and Jurymen to refrain from meat and drink, and to be even held in custody, until they had agreed upon their verdict. Se.axisit POLITENESS.—Near Naval-Moral, we °let a Spanish family of rank travelling, a sight Very uncommon. The ladies and female attendants Were seated in a large, heavy, old-fashioned carriage, covered with carved work and tarnished gilding. This vehicle was drawn by eight mules, ,W,hich two fine.looking men on foot guided solely °Y the voice, calling out their names, to which they aPPeared by their movements to answer with great docility. The gentlemen of the party rode with the male servants, all conversing familarly together; Rod the last often put their heads into the carriage- Window, and spoke to the ladies. The Spaniards, I have often observed, however exalted their rank, are exceedingly kind and affable to their servants and inferiors. And, indeed, the lower classes have much ratural politeness; nor is there anything in their or manner which disgusts or offends. They have no vulgarity in their freedom, nor ser- ,-. A..'"itY in their respect. I have often sat round the fire of a, posathe amid Spaniards of all classes, Wnoni chance had assembled together, and been " quite charmed to mark the general good humour, ' °ad the easy, unembarrassed propriety of behaviour Of the common peasants.—Recollections of the Peninsula. INTRODUCTION OF THE BUG FAMILY.—It is generally supposed that the bug was first introduced to this country in the fir-timber which was imported for the purpose of rebuilding London, after the great fire of 1666. It is said that bugs were not • own in England before that time; and many of these insects were found almost immediately after- Wards in the newly erected edifices. This may Probably be true, as in many of the remoter parts of the country they are unknown to the present day— or at all events extremely rare; and it is pretty well known that they generally attack newly arrived The from the country with the greatest severity. "Ile female lays about fifty eggs at a time. These • eggs are white, and at first are covered with a 'dawns matter, which afterwards hardens, and fixes there wherever they are laid. The young bugs come forth in about three weeks. The usual times of lay- ing are the months of March, May, July, and Sept- !tuber. Two hundred young ones may be produced ~,Lrolia every female bug that lives through the season. htls it may be seen what a numerous increase 4there may be of those disgusting vermin, when vtoper care is not taken to destroy them. PRIVILEGES OF THE KING'S SMITII.-0110 Of OIL historians observes that, immediately preceding the Conquest, the art of working in iron and steel had arisen to such a state of imarovement, that even the horses of some of the chief knights and barons Iv._,ere covered with steel and iron armour. Artificers 5",40 wrought in iron were so highly regarded in %.,'",ose warlike times, that every military officer had Lm's Smith, who constantly attended his person, to "'eeee his arms and armour in order. The chief smith was an officer of considerable dignity, in the 12..eurt of the Anglo-Saxon and Welsh kings, where 4ie enjoyed many privileges, and his weregeld was 4,2unch higher than that of any other artificer. In ~'•ne Welsh court the king's smith sat next to the 'momestic chaplain, and was entitled to a draught tr every kind of liquor that was brought into the , all—a privilege which many artificers of his class 44 our own day will not be disposed to make light 14----Lardner's Cyclopedia. between the AND ENGLISH.—The national precedence is'tween the English and Scotch may be settled ,e"3;- this, that the Scotch are always asserting their 7_°Periority over the English, while the English "-lever say a word about their superiority over the .uotele. The first have got together a great number 114 facts and arguments in their own favour; the ,s-st never trouble their heads about the matter, but ee taken the point for granted as self -evident.-- 41421itt.8 " Characteristics. MIC:IAEL ANGELo.—Michael Angelo's seal repro- • *el:tee three rings enclosed one within the other, as tXPressive of the union which he had made in the mind of the three arts of painting, sculpture, and 4tchitectute. Michael Angelo lived to a very great, yet ilealti ly old age. In the beginning of the 18tis te:tttrF, the Senator Buonarotti caused the vault to °reined at Florence in which his body was gp-I)ositeel. It was found perfect; and the dress of L'een velvet, and even the cap and slippers in which I,:_was buried, were entire, He appeared to have 11 a small, well-set man, with a countenance of -••••eat severity. • t seem cot to hear remarks which are intended v;', „annoy you is a species of negative insincerity is in many cases commendable. It dis- aNints and battles the insulter, and prevents a ofitless war of words. Such dissimulation may L'e the means of preventing a breach of the peace --and the "easier way is the best" when the other, • ay 18 not imperative.

014 WITVZ-Dut impecunious writer applied to a " Sor a loan. The latter put him off till he Z)4l,_id inquire about his character, which he found ,w-,'%• very bad, so far as paying borrowed,money 1,n7 ocncerned. On again meeting the would-be Twer, the gentleman began to make excuses, " I'm really sorry, my dear sir, but—" 'rY for what ?" asked the wit. "That I can't tr,yYp have the money." "Is that all? Then, 1,0 sear fellow, don't be unhappy ; you ought to Yi=lad of it." - -

THE RELIGIOUS CARD-PLAYER.

,• A private soldier by the name of Richard Lee was taken many years ago before a magistrate of Glasgow for playing cards during divine service. The account of it is given as follows :—A sergeant commanded the soldiers at church, and while there the parson read the prayers and took the text. Those who had a Bible took it out,Qout this soldier hid neither Bible nor Common Prayer-book, but pulling outs pack of cards, he spread them before him. He first looked at one card and then at another. The sergeant of the company saw him, and said—" Richard, put up the cards; this is no place for them." "Never mind that," said Richard. • • When the services were over the constable took Richard a prisoner, and brought him before the Magistrate. "Well," said the Magistrate, " what have you brought the soldier here fort" "For playing cards in church." "Well, soldier, what have you to say for yourself ?" "Much, sir, I hope." "Very good ! if not; Iwlll punish you severely." "I have been," said the soldier, "about six weeks on the march. I have neither Bible nor Common Prayer-Book. I have nothing but a pack of cards, and hope to satisfy your Worship of the purity of my intentions. Then, spreading the cards before the Bailie, he began with the ace. " When I see the ace it reminds me that there is but one God. When I see the deuce it reminds me of Father and Son. " When I see the three it reminds me of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. When I see the four it reminds me of the four evangelists that preached— Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. "When I see the five it reminds me of the wise virgins that trimmed their lamps. l'here were ten, but five were wise mid five were foolish, and were shut out. "When I see the six it reminds me that in six days the Lord made heaven and earth. "When I see the seven it reminds me that on the seventh day God rested fret:l the great work which he made, and hallowed it. "When I see the eight it reminds me 'of the eight righteous persons who were saved when God destroyed the world—viz., Noah and his wife, his three sons, and their wives. "When I see the nine it reminds me of the nine lepers that were cleansed by our Saviour. There were nine out of ten who never returned thanks. (I"When I see the ten it reminds me of the ten ' commandments which God handed down to Moses lon the table of stone. " When I see the king it reminds me of the great King of 'Heaven, which is our God Al- mighty. "When I see the queen it reminds me of the Queen of Sheba, who visited Solomon, for she was a woman as he was a man. She brought 50 boys and 50 girls, all dressed in boys' apparel, for King Solomon to tell which were boys and which were girls. The king sent for water for them to wash. The girls washed to the elbows, and the boys to the wrists; so King Solomon told by that." "Well," said the Bailie, "you have described every card in the pack except one." What is that?"

_ "The knave," said the Bailie. "I will give your-Honour a description of that too. ityOu will not be angry." I will not," said the Bailie, "if you do not term me the knave." "The greatest knave is the constable who brought me here.' "I do not know," said the Bailie, "if he is the greatest knave, but I know he is the greatest fool." "When I count how many spots there are in a pack of cards, I find 365, as many days as there are in a year. When I count the number of cards in a pack I find 52—the number of weeks in a year. I find there are 12 picture-cards in a pack, repre- senting the number of months in a year, and on counting the tricks I find 13—the number of weeks In a quarter. So you see a pack of cards serve for ,Bible, almanac, and Common Prayer-Book.

div.head: OTHER STRAWBERNY
div.p: THE OTHER STRAWBERNY

An officer who was patrolling Mullett Street the other day (says the Detroit Free Press) saw a crowd of people at a corner, and he hastened his steps to discover a man sitting on the ground with his back to a tree, while a score. of wqmen and boys surrounded him. When the officer made inquiries as to what had happened, a short, stout woman with her sleeves rolled up confronted him and replied : "He's my husband. He's a good. for-nothing, lazy-bones of a man, and we've had a row." "What about ? " ," Well, I've had to cuppert Mm by wasiling for the last year, and he's been humble enough up to a week ago. Then he took fifty cents of my money and went to a fortune-teller. She told him that I would die very soon, and that he would marry a strawberry blonde with $50,000 in cash." "Seventy-five thousand dollars, my dear," sighed the man on the grass. You shut up! He came home stepping high and feeling smart, and half an hour ago he had the cheek to tell me that I stood in his road. In fact, he wanted to know when I was going to die I" "I merely inquired," groaned the husband. ` "And I merely left my suds and jumped into Mm," she continued. "It was a pretty even thing in the house, but when I got out where I could swing my right I gave him a couple below the belt and tied him up. Strawberry blonde—s7s,ooo---- second marriage—humph! I'm his strawberry I %1 hen I get through with him rn make that fortune-teller see strawberries for the rest of her born days 1" "Well, be gentle," cautioned the officer, as he

passed on. "Oh I wont hurt nobody nor nothing," she replied ; and as the officer passed on she lifted the man to his feet and banged him up the steps into the house in a double-entry style of book-keeping that rattled the shingles.

div.head: "DOING" THE MARRIED MAN:
div.p: "DOING" THE MARRIED MAN:

"Now, Henry," said the bride, "I want you to understand distinctly that I do not wish to be 4taken for a bride. lam going to act exactly as if ot were an old married woman; so, dearest, do not ,think me cold and unloving if I treat you very practically when there is anybody by." "I don't believe I can pass for an old married man. lam so food of you that I Lin bound to show it; I am sure to betray myself." "No, you musn't It's easy enough. And 1 insiet that you behave Just like all old married men do. Do you hear ?" "'Well, darling, I'll try; but I know I shall not succeed." On the first evening of their arrival the bride retired, and the groom fell in with a whist party, with whom he sat playing cards until 4 o'clock in the morning. His wife spent the weary hours in weeping. At last he turned up, and met his grief-stricken bride with the hilarious question. " Well, ain't I doing the old married man like a daisy?" She never referred to the subject again, and every- body knew after that that they had just been married.

THE PENNY 'BUSES.

Sir,—Now that fever and smallpox are raging in our midst may I call attention to the penny 'buses which daily ply along our streets. I should like to know if they are ever disinfected, for this, to my mind, is at the prose..t; time not only advisa- ble, but absolutely necessary. Only yesterday, I saw the mother of a child, who on the 6th inst. died from smallpox (not in the hospital. but at its parents' house), get out of one of these 'buses in company with another woman. I have reason to know that she canoe straight from home,aad thus into the 'bus, which was fairly filled. I doubt whether her fellow pa:_- sengers would have felt very comfortable had they known:this. Surely danger lurks here, so, for the public safety, no harm would be done if disinfectants were freely used daily —Yours truly, CAUTION. Warrington, Sept. Bth, 1892.

div.head: BREWSTER SESSIONS.
div.p: BREWSTER SESSIONS.

Sir,—lt is to be hoped that at the Adjourned Sessions on the 20th inst., the justices if the borough will reverse the decision of the Licensing Committee to grant full licenses in the cases of Battersby-lane and Bewsey, and at the same time cancel ths renewal for those in Buttermarket-street, which they (the justices) reported upon a few years ago as not required. Battersby-lane at present is without the contamination of glaring drink shops, and the inhabitants instead of wishing to have one thrust on them, are almost unanimous in their desire to prevent it. The ironworkers of Bowsey are also opposed to having increased temptations forced amongst them.

With a view of convincing the Bench that the Borough, instead of needing more licensed houses, would be more benefitted by a great reduction of the numbr of exist- ing ones, I think the clergy of the different denomina- ations and all interested in the true welfare of the in- habitants, should use their influence to the utmost to

get property owners and ratepayers to come forward on the 20th inst., and testify that any further increase would not only depreciate the value of their property, but tend to increase drunkenness and immorality. Everyone is aware that the brewery influence in War- ington preponderates in the Church, on the Bench, and in the Council. Those magistrates and Councillors, therefore, who are desirous of improving the condition of the borough by opposing the temptations to drunken- ness, vice and crime and raising the people above the influence of Bung, deserve and desire the hearty support of all true-minded citizens, irrespective of party or creed.—Yours faithfully, A RESIDENT. Warrington, September 7,1892.

div.head: MR. JOHN PEERS ON EVOLUTION.
div.p: MR. JOHN PEERS ON EVOLUTION.

Sir,—lt is long since I came to the conclusion that Mr. John Peers knows everything,especially about evolu- bon. Of course I couldn't come to any other conclu- sign, seeing that Mr. Peers is always telling us how • much he itnOwi and hp .7 little everybody else knows. But ' there is occasionally just Jupiter nods sometimes, arta n. a slight shakiness about the evolutim.r.y infcrmation.... which the Sage of Penketh imparts to us. For IL.qtanc' in his letterlast week he modestly tells us that " transi- tional forms nit being so well adapted to their environ- ments would quickly become extinct after leaving their , modifications to their descendants." There is an appear- ance of intense profundity about this deliverance on evo- lution. In fact, the more I think of it the more profound and incomprehensible it appears. If "transitional forms" are not so well adapted to their environments how do they come to exist at all? Is it a case of the evolution of the unfit from the fit—in other words, the survival of the unfittest ? If that be what Mr. ,Peers means then he must be a kind of topsy-turvy, upside-down evolutionist. If, on the other hand, be simply means that the" forms" he refers to were not so well adapted to their environments as those which succeeded and dispossessed them,why should he speak of them as " transitional ?" I should have thought that, .according to evolution; all forms, whether extinct or extant, were merely transitional. If there be any- thing in evolution, even Mr. Peers and the other inhabi- tants of Penketh will, in the course of ages, give place to a higher type of humanitV ; but I cannot see why, a long time hence, any fossil remains that may be found in that locality should be labelled and put into a museum as specimens of a " transitional" type of man, which, "not being so well adapted to their environments, quickly became extinct after leaving their modifications to their descendants." That would be an undue dispar- agement, as! think the people of Penketh have a right to claim that they are neither more nor less" transitional" than those who have gone Wore or those that come after. You will, perhaps, excuse me for sending you these few lines. I do SO only because lam of opinion that a severely scientific thinker like Mr. Peers—to whom we naturally turn for all abort the latest " ism " —should be extremely precise in his choice of language. —Yours, kc., Warrington, September 5, 1892.
THEEBAW.
MAN'S RESPONSIBILITIES AND ANIMAL RIGHTS. -

Sir,—ln my proposed crusade against an accentuated form of cruelty to animals, I have now the glorious cer- tainty of assured victory ! Well may the cowardly tor- mentors of animals tremble in the secret dens when they learn that W. H. Butler is" quite with me " in the case of morality and humanity v. pseudo-scientific cruelty. After this I can forgive him anything I Even being called a Pharisee does not make one sad, you see ! In return for this avowal of kindly fellow-feeling—which in very truth I vahie=—l :will not accede to his request to show him the relevanee of his bracketed quotation of my words in hialetter. It would be unkind of me to show Mr. Butler what everybody but himself can see. "Oh wad some Power the giftie gie us," &c. But now, sinking all minor differences and little bickering,let us stand shoulder to shoulder in determined antagonism to the continuance of this most foul blot on the morality of our time. My object in writing is to bring before your readers some facts as to that worst of all forms of cruelty to animals—vivisection. For I believe that the facts have only to be widely and gener- ally known for the great heart of my country to be so stirred that it will put down its foot upon this iniquity and utterly overthrow it. I feel assured that we in whose midst and tor whose ostensible benefit these iniquities are wrought cannot, without blame, remain unrecognizant of the fact that if we are net active an- tagonists of this diabolical practice we are to some ex- tent passive participators in the moral guilt involved. My contention is that we—mankind—have no moral right to torture living animals for experimental purposes —that no conceivable end can justify these means of obtaining it. But for the fear of making the reader heart-sick by the detailed enumeration of the horrible cutting and mangling of the living and quivering tissues—the sawing, scraping, and boring of bones, the baring and slicing away of the internal organs, with other manifold maltreatrzients, I could a tale unfold which should make every humane reader ashamed of the so-called civilization that permits these scientific barbari- ties. Suffice it to take one from a series of experiments upon living horses, which I extract from the August issue of "The Zoophilist " !—"Experiment ax. Old horse, laid on litter unable to rise, but nevertheless acutely sensitive. The spinal marrow is bared (by means of a mallet and chisel) in the occipito-atloidian interval. An enormous quantity of liquid escapes, as in the case of all worn-out horses. . . . From the firs" moment, and at whatever point I scratch the pcsterior cord, and however lightly, I provoke immediately signs of the most violent suffering. kter a few minutes this high impressionability is a little quieted,and I can ascer- tain that the pain is most lively when I excite the pos- terior cord nearest the line of emergence of the sensitive nerves of the first cervical pair. . . . The animal is so excitable that it is very difficult for me to see whether the deep prickings of the posterior cord are effective. Hardly had the point of the needle touched the surface of the cord than the animal agitates itself violeatly, and I am unable to hold the needle so as to pierce the marrow." And so on through 80 cases "consecrated "by this—well—original physiological researcher. I have another name for him and his work, but will leave the

reader to affix his proper appellative. I have heard and read about the rights of man, but had this poor old horse no rights, after a life of painful toil in the service of man? Was this a fitting close to such a life? Denied the final mercy of speedy slaughter; bound down in helpless anguish, tortured to death! Here I wish to ask—has man the right of torture as well as that of slaughter? And if so, whence does he obtain it? I strongly deny that he has such a right. On resuming the subject—as I propose to do—l will quote details of the visit of a gentleman to one of these scientific shambles.—l am, .kc., JOHN PEERS.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATO-WAY. SET- TIMBER TO 1892:, ;..
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATO-WAY. SET- TIMBER TO 1892:, ;..

ance, if they ever existed, is necessarily involve.' in it. A negative argument indeed! Is Mr. Peers really ignorant that Darwin himself was disturbed and con- founded to an almost overwhelming extent by it ? and that it extorted the confession "that he who rejects these views on the nature of the geological record will rightly reject my whole theory." (Origin of Species p. 342). And have not Huxley, Lyell, and a whole host of Dar- winians, to say nothing of adverse scientists, every- I where, felt and acknowledged this fact to be a real difli- ?

Mr. Peers may rest assured that no sensible Darwinian even will do other thin smile at his simple and ineffi- cient attempt at explanation as " that transitiana forms not being so well adapted to their environments 0) would quickly become extinct"! 1 Such an explana- tion is a mere subterfuge—is scarcely consistent with the theory it seeks to support—and will certainly never rank among the "Survival of the fittest."

I am sorr-y Mr. Editor to have to trespass upon your space, but my critic's allusion to that precious specimen of monstrosity in the Museum, the Archteopteryx which so affected his scientific friend of " the marrow bones," is really irresistible. His corvert should have conipleted the burlesque as he rose from his knees with the grave query—" Am not I thine ass ?" Now let it be remem- bered that this instance of the Solenhofen monster has been before the scientific world for over 30 years, that very diverse opinions have been held respecting it, that even Huxley speaking of this and similar types of birds admits that their total amount of approxim,.tion to the reptilian type is but small, and " the gap between rep- tiles and birds is but very slightly narrowed by their existence ;" and, further, he remarks " birds are no more modified reptiles than reptiles are modified birds, the vptilian and ornithic types being both in reality somewhat different superstructures raised upon one and the same ground plan" (quoted by Dawso in " Chain e: Life "p. 180). The fact of derivation then of one type from the other cannot be affirmed, and I throw back in Mr. Peers' own words "a flat contradiction to his most baseless assertion "that this and a few other such specimens are intermediate forms at all between species and species, such as we should expect in untold myriads if the theory in question be true. Let my friend be patient, and keep cool in his dealings with the subject. If I understand correctly he may hear of announcements before long which are likely better to serve the purpose of his argument ; but let him remember that my summary has to do with facts and not " dogmas," and is founded upon the statements of distinguished scientists. Darwinian evolution will have to be very much modified, ere these statements can be disposed of satisfactorily. lam perfectly indifferent as to the ultimate discoveries of science evolution-wards. The atheistic tendencies of Darwinian evolution I abom- inate, and the use made of it by such men as Haeckel, Otto Schmidt, and Strauss shows bow, under its blight- ing influence, men can descend from the light of reason to the category an I outer darkness of fools. On the other hand a theistic evolution—if all the out- standing difficulties can be removed—would to my mind immensely enhance our views of the glory and wisdom ef the Creator, and since commonsense assures us that evolution can only possibly be a method of creation I feel certain, as stated in my paper, that it may ulti- mately prove to be the best and truest interpretation of the first chapter of Genesis.—Yours &c., JOHN DIGNUM. Penketh, Bth August, 1892.

div.head: BEWARE OF LICENSING JOBBERY.
div.p: BEWARE OF LICENSING JOBBERY.

Sir,—lt is quite time a change was made in the manner of conducting Licensing Sessions if we are to have a repetition of " Greenall Whitleyism " versus every other interest, as from your correspondent last week, "One who hates jobbery," it looks as if the whole of the Licensing Justices had committed themselves to a policy of deciding all matters in favour of the big brewers. I cannot see what justice there is in their decisions, and how it is intended to benefit the public in any manner whatever, as I am sure the Battersby Lane and Bewsey districts do not wish to have Messrs. Greenall and Whit- ley and Co.'s commodities forced upon them in this manner: that is simply because a brewer has some licenses that the public don't require, as their offering to give them up is prima facie evidence that the public do not require them. I think Councillor Bolton saw the gravity of the case when it became a question of drawing the Licensing Bench by offering licenses, as he refused to name the three licenses he offered to give up. I have no doubt he was in possession of information that led him to think his application would be refused whatever he might offer to do or give. If his application was refused, he knew , his offer to give up licenses might be construed (accord- ing to what he stated in court) into evidence that the public do not require them. Now, I think the justice of the case would be met if the magistrates would refuse to confirm the grant of these two new licenses on the 20th of September, and do away with all these " very valuable" licenses that are of no use to the public (and very little to a brewer except for trucking purposes) at the next Brewster Sessions.

If a brewer chooses to buy all the houses in a particu- lar district, so that he can have all the trade to himself, and finds that the trade could be carried on with more profit to himself in one half of those,houses, what does it matter to him which particular houses do all the trade ? Take a business view of the case ; suppose there are ten public houses in the district, the letting value of the houses would be considerably more if there were only five houses; and those five which had lost their licenses could be turned into valuable shops. Now where would Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company suffer any injustice if the licenses they offer were suppressed? It would make their other houses more valuable in those neighbourhoods. Licensing Justices would be perfectly justified in doing in Warrington what is being done in Liverpool. They would be conferring a benefit on Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., by suppressing these licenses, and saving them the trouble of again offering them as an inducement to gain new valuable licenses. As shown by your correspondent, "A War- ringtonian," they could at once convert them into valu- able shops, but I am afraid very little may be expected from that Licensing Committee, who do everything to please those who have helped to place them on the Bench. A CONSERVATIVE.

LICENSING REFORM.—VALIJABLE SUGGESTIONS. • Sir,—Your remarks in last week's issue, favoring some means of dealing with the evils of the liquor traffic; such as that adopted in Not way, have my warm sympathy. It is quite time that respectable and well meaning citizens should unite their forces in the interest of the town, and adopt some definite policy, with a view to prevent the gross abuses arising from the present lieensing system. In rejecting the panacea offered to us by teetotallers, without attempting to meet the diffi- culty in any other way, we practically give our sup- port to those who are united by self-interest, in upholding the present state of things, while at our feet lies a principle of action which I venture to think, if well understood, would meet with the support of a very large majority. The principle to which I refer, is that of taking the retail sale of all intoxicants out of the hands of private traders, not with a view to prohibition, but in order to eliminate from the trade the incentive of personal interest, so that no man should be better for inducing his fellows to spend their money in drink. There may be many ways in which this could be done, and with a view to elicit the expression of opinion, I • to make the following suggestionspui, : ,Jeg ,• Company should be formed with the all licenses in the town, and all rights dr objecttothe soafleacoqfuIn iinr toficatimi ink. 2.—The proceedings of the ComPn' should be strictly subject to some popularly elected bcidyl, preier; I Licensing Board elected for that purpose by the rate- ' payers, 3.—Nut more than five per cent. per annum interest on capital should be paid to shareholders. Profit above this amount to be given in grants to charitable institu- tions, &c., not supported by the rates, or to.the Imperial I Exchequer. 4.—The Company should acquire the licenses on the best terms possible, the question of compensation or otherwise to be dealt with when it arises, by which time Parliament may have clearly defined the powers of licensing authorities. 5. Every house belonging to the Company should be under a manager who shall have no interest in the sale of intoxican`-. 6.—Clubs and hotel, (if not tept by the Compaay) should t 3 supplied with liquor at the same prices as I individuals, that is, at strictly retail prices, in order to debar them from making any profit on it. 7.—The Company should thoroughly examine and test all the liquor they supplied, and should employ a staff of officers to examine the drink sold to clubs, &c., to prove its identitywith that supplied by the Company) and in order to ensure the supply of nothing but a pure and wholesome beverage. This programme, it is medic s to add, is not possible in the present state of the law, but the change of the law is only a question of time, and by taking steps towards the formation of a Company to carry out such a programme, we should do more probably than could be done in any other way to help the public to realise that a seheme of tkis kind is within the range of practical politics, and thus e w for changes in the law which might be necessary in order to carry it out. The raising of capital would probably be a matter of no difficulty. The Norwegian Companies make a profit of 125 per cent, per annum, which is the very best 'guarantee that they are able to pay 5 per cent. interest ; and as everyone will acknowledge that money can be. made in the drink trade, especially by a Company hav- ing a monopoly, there is little doubt that the excellent security would raise the shares at once to a premium and no one having money to invest would wish to be left out.
Trusting that this matter will not be allowed to drop, I remain, yours truly, Latchford, 9th, September, 1892.

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.

CUURCH ACCOUNTS —The accounts of the St. Mary's Mission Church to Easter Day have been circulated. The receipts amount to £B7 10s. lid., of which £5B Os. lid. were collections. A list of subscriptions to the Cadishead Mission Church building fund had also been circulated, together with the expenditure. The Lob- scriptions, collections, grants from National Society and Church Building Society, and the bazaar amounted to £952 3s. Bd., all of which had been expended in the mission-room off _Liverpool-road.

THE WARES.—The Wakes commenced on Saturday, and during the day the village was visited by many persons. The heavy showers which fell occasionally acted as a deterrent to the proceedings. In consequence of the unfavourable weather the Ist and 2nd teams did not play. On Sunday many friends and relations paid their annual visit to Cadishead. On Monday afternoon and evening the showmen and stall-holders on the re- creation ground were kept busy. The horses were well patronised.
