Taarr.—At the Lyinm Police Court, on Tuesday even- ing, before Dr. Brabazon, Arthur Harris, John Harris (father and son), and John Welch, of Manchester, were charged with having stolen an Inverness macintosh and a blue cloth overcoat, the property of Mr. Jacob McGill, Lymm,on the 31st of August.—Miss McGill identified the property.—Samuel Brookes stated that one of the men offered him the coat for sale.—Sergeant Griffiths said that he and Sergeant Wynne received the prisoners into custody from the Present police.—The prisoners were remanded.

Local. BOARD MEETING.—The usual monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday evening at the Board's offices, when the following were present—Mr. James Gregson (in the chair), Messrs. James Holt, Brazendale, F. Swallow, H. Harrison, R. Whitelegge, J. T. Ridgway (law clerk), W. Mullard (clerk), W. Severs (gas manager), and J. Mort (surveyor). The Law Clerk stated that he had received a letter from Mr. Underwood complaining of a nuisance in front of his gateway.—Mr. Holt said that a while ago the Board had. placed a grid in front of the gate to prevent the flooding, and now Mr. Underwood complained of the smell.—The Surveyor stated that Mr. Underwood had since said that he would rather be drowned than poisoned. (Laughter.) —The matter was placed in the hands of the Surveyor. —A meeting of the Fire Brigade was held on the 27th o; August, when the fireball was rung, and the brigade had a practice both at the Dam and in the village.—The Law Clerk read a letter from Mr. Moston, the captain of the brigade, in which he tendered his resignation. He said that it was with regret that he did so after holding the position for so long a time, but increasing years com- pelled him to take that actien.—The resignation was accepted.—lt was proposed by Mr. Harrison,seconded by Mr. Holt, and carried,that the Board advertise for a new captain at a standard salary of £s.—Mr. Brazendale thpught they wanted a new bell, as there was no distinc- tion between the sound of the fire-bell and the school- bell.—Mr.Holt suggested that the bell be properly hung, and it would then act properly. This was ordered to be done.

THU SPORTS AND GALA .—The first annual athletic sports and gala were held in afield kindly lent by Mrs. Weir, of Cockshot Farm. .The committee for carrying out the arrangements consisted of Messrs. E. Barnham and G. and T. Houghton, Mr. W. F. Pennington being the secretary. The entries for the various events num- bated upwards of 70. The handicapping was done by the committee, Mr. C. Allen was the starter, and Mr. E. Barnham the judge. Despite the unfavourable weather, there was a fair attendance, and considering the wet state of the ground some good racing took place. THE NEW RECTOR.—The new Rector of Croft (the Rev. , H. I. Wadeson, M.A.), read himself in at the afternoon I service on Sunday, when there was a good congregation. The prayers having been read by the Rector, and the lessons by Captain Withington, and the hymn " For ever with the Lord," sung, the rev, gentleman ascended , the pulpit, and said he was required to read tc them the j 39 articles of religion, and his declaration to the same, after which he would give a short discourse. He then proceeded to read and afterwards made his declaration. He took for his texts the words "We preach Christ crucified." Service will be hold in the church on Sunday afternoon until the Rector takes up his residence in the parish. CIIILDREN'S TREAT.—This popular annual treat, took place on Saturday, under very unfavourable circum- stances with regard to the weather. The committee this year consisted of Messrs. H. Hankinson, IJ. Flatton, R. Sanderson, W. Sanderson, and IH. Shaw, Mr. S. Stretch being the hon. I treasurer, and Mr. S. Taylor the hon secre- tary, whose arradgements gave every satisfaction. Generally tJI the children in the parish from three to 15 years of age receive tickets free, all above that age pay- ing fid. each for their tea. The children assembled at the Board School at one o'clock in the afternoon, and at two they formed a procession, and, headed by a banner and the Leigh Vmunteer Band, they paraded the village under the superintendence of the committee and officers, and Mr. Cawthorne (the schoolmaster), Mrs. Savage (infants mistress), and Miss Stretch (assistant teacher), the I route taken being from the school up Heath-lane as far as the Plough Inn, and back a,gain past the school to the j Smithy-brow, and thence to the school again. Upwards , I of 200 children and young people were in the procession j ! and their neat and clean appearance was much com- mented upon by a large atienber of persons on the route. At four o'clock they sat dawn to an excelleat tea in the schoolroom. After tea, an adjournment was made to a field, kindly hmt, by Mr. E. W. Sankey, of Heath Farm, one of the rns3inbers of the School Board, where one or two race:, and various games took place, and the band played an excenentselection of music for dancing until nearly dusk, under the conductorship of Mr. Charles , Wood,

div.head: TECEINICAL INSTRUCTION AT
div.p: TECEINICAL INSTRUCTION AT
EARLESTOWN.
BY A SCIENCE TEACHER.

The syllabus of til-e—daTse-s-i-n---cajlection with the Viaduct Institute is now before the public. This working-men's college, as it ma' be termed, is doing a great work in the town, and many that are young men now will feel grateful in later life that such an Institution existed for their benefit. It will be seen from our advertising columns that the fees that will secure admit.sion to these classes are very small. The classes may be divided into three groups viz : The Science and Art group, the Com- mercial Group, and the almestic Science classes to • women. In the first group we have the Art Class, in which is taught freehand, model, and per- spective drawing; and in the Science Classes: Machine corst •uction and drawing, building con- struction, and thawing, practical plane and solid geometry, applied mechanics, steam, magnetism, and electricity, mathematic), and chemistry. The Commercial group consists of classes in book- keeping, elementary, end advanced, and sl'orthand. The Women's Classes comprise cookery, laundry work, and dressmaking. Taking the Science and Art group it will be seen that the Vlach-et Institute Techn;cal Instruction Committee have established a most complete course of study for all engaged in enginee-ing work of any kind. A workman may gain that knowledge of materials and of principles upon which his daily work is based, without which knowledge lie is a mere human tool, plodding along the rut into which he may somehow or other have fallen. Equipped with this knowledge, he feels the impulse of guiding principles within himself, he improves rapidly in skill, and finds a pleasure in his work. Although the classes at the Institute may fairly be described as large some of the subjects, yet if one half of the young fellows about the place, that ought to be in them were in them, we are afraid that the !nstitute would not be large enough to accommodate them. There are about the place from half-a-dozen to half-a-score of decidedly large works. From the wagon works alone the Building Construction Class ought to be crowded out, for, bear in mind that the general principles of carpentry form a very large portion of this subject, and a know- ledge of the different kinds of joints and of the framing and fitting of timber generally would be of great service to every workman employed there; a knowledge, too, of the different kinds of timber, their growth, modes of preservation, and characteristics would be acquired, and, above all, the power of depicting by plan elevation and section any and every object that can be made of timber would be secured. Then we have the Vulcan Foundry's Slee's Engineering Works, Vicar's Engineering Works, and others from which an ample supply of students for the Machine Drawing, Mechanics' and Steam Classes ought to come, and in addition Mc- Corquodale's and the Sankey Sugar Works ought to help materially in the same direction. However, it so happens that the students in these classes are young peope troubled,as all young people are, more or less, .with ill-defined desires and wavering reso- lutiona. As a rule, they feel deep down in their hearts that they ought to be studying in these classes, but on the surface they seem to he deterred by being unable to see clearly of what use the knowledge to be gained there will be in their daily life, or in what way it may influ- ence their future. We will attempt to show in what way they may gain from both these points of view, but let us first look at it in a more general way. We find people of mature years, who have the means, encourag- ing the practice of cricket, football, and other outdoor games in this country to a remarkable degree. The young people themselves largely look at these games as affording them fine fun and amusement generally. Their elders, however, do not lo.it at them exclusively, or even chiefly, from this point of view, but rather from that said to have been held by the Iron Duke, who is reputed to have said that the battle of Waterloo was won upon the cricket fields of England. In spirit this remark was no doubt a just one,and we ourselves largely believe in it. The physical and even moral development that results from the practice of these games has had an enormous effect upon the development of the English nation,and given us such as start in the race ofinations as bids fair to leave us the final victors, and places the whole world at our feet. Now is it not possible that study may have the same effect upon our brain develop- ment that physical exercise has upon our bodily growth? All authorities agree that this is so, and, our own observation, independent of them,wouldlead us to think so. A steady course of study spread over a series of years leads to the acquirement of the power of clear thinking and of the habit of continuous thought that characterises the man who is a leader or governor of men. So that if a youth is not quite able to see that the subjects brought under his notice will be of worldly benefit to him to-morrow morning or next week, he may cheerfully join some class or other, in the certain faith that he is doing a good thing fer himself by so doing. Besides getting this increase of brain power and brain reserve he will also be acquiring that habit of study and that power t.f study which can only be acquired in early years, and which will enable him at any time of life to give himself thoroughly to the acquirement of know- ledge in any particular direction. This is really what is meant by training. This is indeed the first and f,treatest object of education from the highest point of view, though we are afr...id that the importance of edu- cation, as expressed by the term " training "is not so highly thought of as it ought to be by time English as a nation. We are, however, rapidly rising to this concep- tion.

In addition to all this it is quite obvious that the knowledge to be gained in these classes is useful in all that appertains to the production or control of machinery, and it is the good workman who, in addition to his manual skill, possesses some scientific knowledge, that will be promoted to the position of foreman or manager at his place of employment. Of this there can be no doubt. Too many examples have fallen under our notice to permit us to do so. It is important, however, that a student on first joining these classes should begin aright. Students often make serious mistakes by choosing some subject that seems to apply at once to their daily occupation. Now, so far as the science group is concerned ,there can be no doubt that the first subject for all engineering students is drawing. No real progress can be made either in mechanics,steam, or any other subject in which machine.; have to be con- sidered without a knowledge of drawing. At the same time, or immediately after, should be taken elementary mathematics, for the necessary calculations cannot be made in the later subjects without a knowledge of frac- tions, mensuration, and at least square root. After this course has been taken the study of steam and mechanics can be taken up with an absolute certainty, with regu- lar work of course, of acquiring a thorough knowledge and passing the examination. At most if not all of the large institutions in the ceuntry this course is insisted upon. It is offered here merely as advice. With regard to drawing itself James INT's myth, the inventor of the steam hammer and many other useful mechanical appliances, says in his autobio- graphy, popular edition, page 122, "Mechanical drawing is the alphabet of the engineer, without this the work- man is merely a hand ; with it he indicates the posses- sion of a head," and again on page 56 he says, "A few strokes of the pencil convey ideas which quires of writ- ing would fail to impart. This is one of the most valu- able gifts which the man who has to do with practical subjects can possess " ; and still again on page 97, "This accomplishment of accurate drawing, which I achieved for the most part in my father's workroom (his father was an artist and draughtsman) served me many a good turn in future years with reference to the engineering work, which became the business of my life." Now what more can we say to urge young fellows to put in an appearance during the coming winter P It is true he will have to exercise some amount of self-denial. If he has a fondness forroaming about the town at night, seeking the lastest good thing in the betting line concern- ing the next football match or horse-race, we fear he will find the habit interfered with, but to his great benefit no doubt. He will, however, find a truer pleasure and have opened to him a higher ideal that will make a man of him.

....... Space will not admit of us saying much more concern- ing the Commercial group and the women's classes, any more than to say emphatically that any youth engaged in commercial pursuits, and with leisure, who fails to attend one or more of these classes is blind to his own interest and determined to pull the wrong way.
THE FEARFUL FATALITY AT WIDNES,

Yesterday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse,the county cormier, held an inquiry into the circumstances of the death of Henry Stone, aged 42, Dominick Kelly. aged 33, and John -Routledge, aged 46, who were killed at Hutchinson's Chemical Works, Widnes' on the 11th August, by the falling of a vitriol chamber. Mr. H. S. Oppenheim was present on behalf of the United Alkali D3mpany. The deceased and some other men, were employed in pulling' down several vitriol chambers, and on the day in question, they had partially demolished one, when the whole affair collapsed, burying the three men under the ruin% Several other men were also injured. After a full consideration of the evidence, the jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death."

div.head: EISTEDDFOD AT RHYL.
div.p: THE EISTEDDFOD AT RHYL.

The Eistoddfod proceedings at Rhyl were opened on Thursday with a gorsedd of bards. Sir Watkin Williams Wynn presided over the Eistiddfod proceedings, and his Presidential address referred to the influence exercised by the Eisteddfod in shaping the national character of Wales. In the evening Dr. Joseph Parry's new oratorio, "Saul of Tarsus/ was performed for the first time. 4. It was on Monday decided by the Accringten Town • Council to purchase the pa and water works at the price of £713,220.

THE AUTUMN EXHIBITION AT LIVERPOOL. This year there is a capital exhibition in the Walker Art Gallery. There are few annual pic- ture shows of which it can be said that so many of the pictures are distinctly interesting. At this includes some sculpture—in the gallery, and at Liverpool there are nearly fourteen hundred works— least 150 of these are well worth looking at. The interesting things of the show seem to us divisible into several distinct groups. There is some sculpture, including the finest piece of work produced in England this year; there are at least a dozen portraits that deserve mention of one kind or another; there are interesting things by the men who are defined by the self-chosen name of "impressionists ; " there is a larger number of fair landscapes by artists not laying any particular claim to this title; there is again, a somewhat larger number of interesting " figure-subjects," and, lastly, there are the pictures fly men with well-snow!' names.
DEATH OF MR WINTERBOTHAIf, M.P.

Mr. A. B. Winterbotham, LiN‘lal member for East Gloucester, died on Thursday evening at his residence, Norman Hill, Dursley. Tire, ve days ago he was taken to London for the purpose uf undergoir an operation. Although this was successful, he gradually sank. The deceased, who was universally respected, leaves a widow, two sons,And a daughter. Fla was a director of the firm of Messrs. Hunt and Wintert,otharn, and had bean an active politician for 30 years.

MR. JOHN PEERS AND HIS EVOI UrION.

Sir,—l have always given Mr. Peers credit for being a man of considerable information, and for having amassed by great and laudable industry a multitude of facts bearing upon various branches of sciektific subjects Here, however, my admiration of him ceases. The , moment my good friend begins to make use of his many acquisitions, that moment his weakness shows itself. In nothing is this mote conspicuous tnan when he under- takes to criticize, or to reason upon, his acquired know- ledge, and to draw inferences from his facts. Nearly all his attempts in this line are to my mind consummate ' failures. He never seems to take, the touble as a critic to understand an opponent's real position. He reasons upon narrow and partial knowledge ; and jumps to con- ' elusions which his facts can never warrant. My paper, a summary of which appeared so far back as February last in the Examiner, and which Mr. Peers has only just j now noticed, is entitled "On Evolution,and some of the objections to Darwinism." He has a copy of the whole , of it in his possession, and it is simply incorrect and unfair to represent me as " versus Evolution." Had he read it more carefully he would have drawn a juster inference ; viz—that, whilst opposed to the Darwinian ferns of evolution with Its atheistic tendency, I express nowhere any opposition to the theistic theory advocated by so many Christian scientists. The strongest opinion I ventured to offer was that some of the objections to Dar- winism given in my summary—notably those numbered 6, 7,8 and 9 " appeared to me to be almost fatal to any theory of evolution, and would seem rather to confirm the doctrine of special creations than otherwise." Mr. Peers, however, thinks that I aim " dogmatic " in the statements made in my summary, a sample or two of which he gives with his usual accuracy. "Take 5 and 6" he says. Well; what about number 5 ? Has John Peers heard what Darwin himself says he had not heard, "of any single fact of transmutation of one species into another being recorded in all hist/n..7/ ?" What does he suppose that this means but human his- tory, which goes back, say from four to five thousand years? Another, but distinct objection, is number 8. "The testimony of the rocks is entirely against the as there are no intermediate forms between species and species left us, which must have been in myriads of examples if this theory were true." Now, here we are, face to face with a very crucial point in the evolution theory ; and the extremely foolish remark of my critic touching "a negative argument" does nothing to meet its force. It is no question about not seeing a thing and, therefore, not believing it, as my critic says, with a most ridiculous illustration : The intermediate forms are part and parcel of the theory.and their appear.

ALLEGED STABBING FATALITY IN. LONDON. Charles Blackman was committed for trial at the West London Police Court on Thursday, charged with the manslaughter of a friend named James Bond. It Wao alleged that they were drinking together, and that when Bond endeavoured to get Blackman to bed the latter stabbed him in the chest and abdomen with a penknife. - the wounds proving fatal. It was stated that theyoung' men had been much attached to each other, and the prisoner wept bitterly throughout the proceedings.

"TOUCII. AND Several Communications—some of them received late—are crowded out. John L. Sullivan has met his match. He has been knocked out of time as champion boxer and champion braggart. It will do him and his friends good to take a back seat. ----- Mr. C. L. Fenwick, the Chief Constable of Ches- ter, has written a thoughtful letter upon the Bishop of Chester's proposal to nationalise public- houses. He believes in "one man one license;" and regards compensation as out of the question; but would give a few years' grace. The whole subject is beginning to excite the attention which it merits. 'There is some fear that Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., may retire from public life in consequence of the losses and crosses he has had to endure in fighting Various costly libel actions. Such a result would be a misfortune to Ireland at this juncture. He has struggled manfully—not in his own interests, but in the interests of the public; and the public Should come to his rescue.

SUCCESS OF A WIDNES BRASS BAND. At a brass band competition, on Saturday, at Uphol- land, the Widnes Subscription Bann gained the filth prize. If you want a lucky wedding ring go lo 51, HIGH-sT.,wher• you will gets present with it.—Advt. RUNCORN TONIC SOL.FA CHOIR. 'rhe first practice for" Judas Maccabreus " took place on Monday evening in the Ellesmere st. schoolroom. The attendance was very good, and the rehearsal was an excellent one for a first night. Beth Parrca.sma's Shops are under personal supervision.and customers may rely upon receiving every attention.—tidet. WORKMEN'S EXCURSION FROM WIDNES. On Saturday the employes of the Liverpool Silver and Copper Company, Widnes, held their second annual excursion. A most enjoyable day was spent at Mar- bury Hall, the residence of Mr. A. Hornby Lewis, Chair- man of the Company. TolePH PRITCHARD is prepared to wind and keep in repair, private clocks from 10s. per annum.—Advt. TREAT TO CHOIR BOYS AT RUNCORN. Mr. J. Littler, conductor of the Runcorn Parish Church choir, on Saturday, took the choir boys to Manchester, and a very pleasant time was spent at Belle Vile Gar- nens. A capital tea was provided. ARCHMASONRY AT RUNCORN. The annual meeting of the Bridgawater Chapter was held on Wednecday evening, at the Masonic Hall. The following officers were appointed :—Comp. J. R. Digges Z ; T. H. Annet H. ; W. R. Wass P.Z.J. ; A. Linaker P.S. ; W. Upton B ; J. Goff N; J. J. Waterworth and W. Hankinson assist. S. PRITCHARD'S have now stood the test far 50 yaars,and quality and first-class workmanship are still guarantaed.—Advt. GOSPEL UNION MISSION, RUNCORN. Mr. Cain, the Evangelist, who had been in charge of this Mission for twelve months, has been presented with a handsome " Bagster's Teacher's Bible, on the occasion of his departure to Winsford. Mrs. Cain, his wife, was presented with a purse of money. Mr. Windsor is now the missionary in charge. When in want of a chaste and elegant wedding or birthday present go to PRITCHARD'S, Si, liigh-st.—Advt. THE LICENSE OF THE THEATRE ROYAL, RUNCORN. A special sessions was held at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, for the purpose of hearing an application by Mr. Henry Caddick for the renewal of the license of the Theatre Royal. The magistrates on the bench were Messrs. James Reynolds, C. Reynolds, A.Thomas, and G. L. Davies.—Superintendent Atherton had no objection, and the license was granted. Mr, H. Coward and Mr J. J. Waterworth were bound over as sureties for the good conduct of the theatre. JesEPH PRITCHARD keeps spectacles to snit all sights from a shilling a pair.—Advt. ALLEGED SHOP DOOR THEFT AT WIDNES. On Wednesday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Mr. LI. Wade Deacon, Patrick McCreese, Marsh-street, was charged with stealing a pair of trousers, a vest, and a muffler, the property of Floratia Syred, pawnbroker, Widnes. George Owens assistant to Mr. Syred said he saw prisoner running down the street with the articles under his arm. Witness gave chase and blew a whistle. Prisoner then dropped the clothes. They were worth 14s. 6d. Prisoner was committed for trial. JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- st., and 4, Bridge-st., Enneorn.—Advt. FARNWORTH C.E.T.S. On Saturday, the annual demonstration was held in connection with the Earn worth branch of the Church of England Temperance Society. Unfortunately, the pro- cession was much interfered with owing to the heavy showers of rain which fell throughout the afternoon. A special service was held in the church, and an appropri- ate sermon preached by the Rev. Mr. Matthews, vicar of Earlestown. Tea was afterwards provided in the schools, which was followed by an entertainment and a spirited address by Mr. G. A. Pilling (Liverpool). JOSEPH PRITCHARD has the best stock if ladies' silver and gold watehes in the town.—Adrt. ASSAULT ON THE MATRON OF 'THR WORKHOUSE. On Thursday morning, at Runcorn Police Court, be- fore Major Hazelhurst and Mr. J. Handley, Hannah Manning, an inmate of the Dutton Workhouse, was charged with absconding from the place with cloth- ing belonging to the Guardians, on the sth instant, and further with assaulting the matron, Ellen Cunnah, on the previous day. The latter offence, consisted of strik- ing the face of Mrs. Cunnah. The former charge was dismissed, but for the assault the prisoner was sent to goal for 14 days without hard labour. If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen. take It to PRITCHARD'S.—Advt. THEFT FROM A RUNCORN SHOP. On Wednesday morning, at the Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Hazlehurst, George Gladys, navvy, was charged with stealing is. Oid., the , money of James Allen, tripe dresser, Church-street, Run- corn, on the sth inst. About one o'clock OR the after- noon of the date named, the prisoner was seen by a boy named Frederick Massey behind the counter of the prosecutor's shop, taking the money out of the till. P.C. Juett apprehended the man, who, in answer to the charge, said, "It is quite right ; this is what! took," handing him is. Oid. The prisoner was committed to gaol for 14 days. Go to PRITCHARD'S for the best five guinea watch a work- Inman can have.—Advt. "AN UNNATURAL FELLOW" AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Edward J. VVaterson, of Widnes, was summoned for the arrears of an order made upon him in respect of his wife from whom he is separated.—Mrs. Waterson said far two years and six months the prisoner had never been near her or his children. On March 7th last, she obtained a separation order, and prisoner was ordered to pay 6s. per week. He had not paid her a penny. He was now £6 in arrears. He had not worked for three years, but lived with his father, who kept a post office at Widnes, and had a good business. He was an able-bodied man.—Mr. James Rey- nolds stigmatised the prisoner as an unnatural fellow, and sentenced him to two months' imprisonment. JesEnt PRITCHARD'S Bale shop is 51,High-st.. his workshop 4, Bridge-Bt.—Advt. FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTION AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Wm. A. Kneale, 15, Dobsim-st., Liverpool, and Sydney War- hurst, Londcn-road, Liverpool, were charged with ob- structing the footpath in Widnes-road on the 2nd inst. Kneale was also charged with committing a breach of the peace on the same date. Warhurst did not appear. —P.S. McGregor said the defendant was employed by the Colonial Meat Co., in Widnes-road, and on the 2nd inst. those summoned, in company with a number of men, were driving about the town in a waggonette, and throwing a quantity of bills about. In the evening the crowd increased until neither vehicles nor foot-passengers could pass.—Defendant said he did not know he was doing wrong.—Fined ls. and costs. Warhurst was fined £1 and costs, or one month in default. JeallPH PR/TCHARD. Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51. High- it., sad 4, Bridge st., Buncisra.—Advt. •

PENDING ELECTIONS. In last night's " Gazette " the sneaker notifies his intention of issuing writs six days hence for elections in South Bedfordshire and South Leeds. • THE CHOLERA. Last night's " Gazette " contains over six columns of quarantine notices, referring to various parts of the world rendered necessary by the cholera outbreak at Hamburg. A PUBLICAN PUNISHED. William Connor, landlord of the Rising Sun, White- chapel, was yesterday fined £7O, and had his license forfeited, for receiving alid harbouring uncustomed whisky. 4111.• EXTENSIVE FORGERIES. George Coloquhoun, manager for Messrs. Mann, George, and Co., was committed for trial at Cardiff, yesterday, charged with forging bills of exchange for nearly 211,000. Bail was refused. TRAGIC AFFAIR AT CItEWE. _— A JEALOUS HUSBAND SHOOTS HIS WIFE AND HIMSELF. Yesterday morhing a man named Walter Powell, a boilermaker, living in Flag-lane, Crewe, shot at his wife and then shot himself. Jealousy is assigned as the cause of the trouble. Mrs Powell may recover, but the man's case is considered hopeless. -to KILLED BY A CYCLIST. -- A young man named Hutton, residing at Audley, Blackburn, died yesterday of injuries received in a cycling accident on Tuesday last. Deceased was stand- ing on a crossing when a bicyclist named Gill came round the corner and ran into him, dashing him so violently to the ground that he was shockingly injured about the head, death resulting from concussion of the brain. THE FRODSHAM MARSH OUTRAGE. THE wrist IN COURT. Yesterday morning at Frodsham, Charles Bungle, navvy, was charged en remand with attempting to mur- der Emily Dukes at Frodsham Marsh on August 15, by , beating her about her head with a poker. Prosecutrix, who has been dangerously ill from the effects of the assault, was now to appear, but looked pale and weak. Prisoner lodged with her in a hut on the Ship Canal last winter. He went away and returned on August 15, and committed the assault in a fit of jealously. 111. THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS. The Congress was resumed yesterday morning, and a long discussion took place on the eight hours' question. It was proposed that the legal eight hours' day should be adopted at the option of the trades. To this an amend- ment was moved to the effect that the eight hours' day should be compulsory, except where a particular trade decided by ballot to be exempted. On a division the amendment was adopted by 205 to 155. The Congress, by a large majority, agreed to meet next year in Belfast,
